justification: Individualism is present, but not structurally central. The protagonist, Beth, is often seen working with her father, Ed, to uncover the truth about her husband's disappearance. While there are moments of tension and disagreement between them, such as when Ed criticizes Charles's lifestyle ("If he had settled down where he belongs, this never would have happened in the first place."), they ultimately collaborate. Other characters, like Terry, also offer assistance. The narrative does not consistently frame collective efforts as weak, nor does the resolution depend solely on one person's will, suggesting a moderate level of individualism.

title: Halloween 3: Season of the of the Witch
justification: Extreme individualism is a central theme. The protagonist, Dr. Challis, increasingly acts alone, distrusting authority and relying on his own investigation. He dismisses his ex-wife's concerns ('Shut up, shut up. Linda, shut up. Listen, listen.') and disobeys direct orders from the police. The narrative emphasizes Challis's lone pursuit of the truth, even when others are skeptical or obstructive ('You've gotta believe me! Believe me!'). The climax depends on his individual actions to stop Cochran's plan, highlighting the importance of one person's will against a larger threat.

title: Amityville II: The Possession
justification: Extreme individualism is a central theme, primarily embodied by Father Adamsky's actions. He disobeys the church's orders and performs an exorcism on Sonny alone, driven by his own conviction that he knows best. This is highlighted by the Monsignor's rebuke: "You are not only forgetting obedience, you're forgetting humility, as well." Adamsky's disregard for institutional authority and his willingness to act independently, even against direct orders, underscores the salience of individualism. The narrative hinges on his individual choice to defy the church and risk his own well-being to save Sonny, culminating in his self-sacrifice.

title: The Beastmaster
justification: Extreme individualism is a central theme. Dar is largely a 'lone wolf' character, driven by personal revenge after his village is destroyed. He initially travels alone, and even when he joins forces with others, his animal companions remain his closest allies, highlighting his unique connection to the animal world. Dar's distrust of large groups is evident when he initially rejects Zed's army, stating, 'Taking back your city is not the answer... You need an army.' His ultimate success depends on his unique abilities and his bond with animals, rather than collective action.

title: The Secret of Nimh
justification: The film presents a recurring tension between individual action and collective effort. Mrs. Brisby initially seeks help from others (Mr. Ages, the Great Owl) but ultimately must undertake the dangerous mission to drug Dragon herself. The rats themselves are divided, with Jenner advocating for self-preservation and power while Nicodemus champions a collaborative 'Plan.' Mrs. Brisby's individual courage, amplified by the amulet, is crucial in saving her family, but the rats' collective effort to move the house is also essential, highlighting the interplay between individual and group action. The narrative doesn't fully endorse either extreme, but the conflict between them is a central driver of the plot.

title: Hanky Panky
justification: The film's narrative emphasizes the protagonist's struggle against powerful, shadowy organizations, forcing him to rely on his own wits and capabilities. Michael Jordon is framed as a 'lone wolf' figure, distrustful of authority and forced to operate outside the system to survive. Dialogue such as "You have to do it yourself" and the constant betrayal and manipulation by supposed allies (like Calder) reinforce the idea that individual action is the only reliable path. The resolution depends on Michael and Kate's ability to decipher the codes and confront the conspirators, highlighting their unique skills and determination in the face of overwhelming odds.

title: Peter Pan
justification: Individualism is present but not dominant. Peter Pan is a central figure, but he also leads the Lost Boys and interacts with Wendy, John, and Michael. While he displays some self-reliance and a desire for adventure, he also engages in teamwork, such as when he coordinates with Tinkerbell to protect Wendy and the boys from Hook's initial attack: "Quick, Tink, take Wendy and the boys to the island. I'll stay here and draw Hook's fire." The narrative also emphasizes the importance of family and community, as seen in Wendy's role as a mother figure and the children's eventual desire to return home.

title: A Midsummer Night's Sex Comedy
justification: While the film features characters with strong opinions and desires, the narrative doesn't structurally hinge on a conflict between individual action and collective cooperation. Characters like Leopold express strong individualistic philosophies, such as dismissing metaphysics and prioritizing personal experience, but these are presented as personal beliefs rather than driving forces of the plot. Andrew's inventions and eccentricities highlight individuality, but he still engages with and relies on his friends. The resolution involves multiple characters and their relationships, rather than a single individual overcoming all obstacles alone. Therefore, individualism is present but not structurally central.

title: The Pirate Movie
justification: The film presents a recurring tension between individual desires and collective duty, particularly through Frederic's character. He struggles with his 'duty' to exterminate the pirates, despite his affection for them, because of his sense of honor. This is highlighted when he says, "Duty and honor are all I have. That's the one good thing you taught me. So whatever it costs me, I will do my duty." Mabel also challenges societal norms and expectations, prioritizing her own desires and agency, as seen in her defiance of traditional gender roles and her pursuit of Frederic. The pirates themselves, while operating as a group, are driven by self-interest and plunder, rather than a sense of community or shared purpose beyond immediate gain. The resolution involves a compromise where individual desires are somewhat accommodated within a modified social structure.

title: Tex
justification: The film explores the tension between individual desires and familial responsibilities, particularly through Tex's impulsive actions and Mace's struggle to balance his basketball aspirations with caring for Tex. Mace's frustration is evident when he says, "I can't play basketball if I gotta get a job to take care of Tex." Tex's independent streak is highlighted by his determination to find Rowdy, stating, "He's my horse and I'm gonna find him. I ain't going back until I find him." The narrative also shows Mace's desire to leave Bixby and never return, indicating a focus on individual escape over community ties. However, Mace ultimately decides to stay and support Tex, showing a compromise between individual ambition and familial duty.

title: Cat People
justification: The film presents a recurring tension between individual action and collective responsibility, though it doesn't fully dominate the narrative. The protagonist, Irena, grapples with a personal curse that isolates her and forces her to make choices that prioritize her survival, even at the expense of others. This is evident in her dialogue with Oliver, where she expresses fear for him and ultimately chooses to leave, stating, "Can't you see I'm going crazy, just like him?" Paul, her brother, also embodies extreme individualism, operating outside societal norms and attempting to manipulate Irena for his own purposes. While there are instances of cooperation and community, such as Oliver's work at the zoo and his relationships with colleagues, the central conflict revolves around Irena's individual struggle and her attempts to control her destiny, making individualism a notable theme.

title: I Ought to be in Pictures
justification: The narrative contains elements of individualism, primarily through Daffy Duck's encouragement of Porky Pig to pursue a solo career in features, emphasizing personal gain ('3 Grand A WEEK!') over Porky's existing contractual obligations. Porky briefly entertains the idea of leaving his job, driven by a desire for individual success ('WHAT'S ERROL FLYNN GOT THAT I HAVEN'T?'). However, Porky's attempt to break into features fails due to his own incompetence and external obstacles, leading him to seek his old job back. Ultimately, Porky returns to his original role, suggesting a limited endorsement of individualism, as he is unable to succeed on his own.

title: Kiss Me Goodbye
justification: The film features a protagonist, Kay, who is largely independent but not to an extreme degree. While she expresses a desire to live in her own house and make her own decisions, she is also engaged in relationships and ultimately chooses marriage. Dialogue such as "Because it's my house and I love it!" and "I just want to start to live again" highlights her desire for personal autonomy. However, the narrative also emphasizes the importance of relationships, as seen in her interactions with her mother, friends, and fiancé. The resolution involves Kay choosing to marry Rupert, suggesting a move towards partnership rather than complete self-reliance. Therefore, individualism is present but not structurally dominant.

title: Class of 1984
justification: Extreme individualism is a central theme. The protagonist, Mr. Norris, increasingly takes matters into his own hands as the established systems (school administration, police) fail to protect him and his students. Dialogue such as "You've got to learn just how to survive" and "It's up to you" emphasizes self-reliance. The climax involves Mr. Norris confronting Stegman alone, rescuing Fallon, and ultimately defeating him, highlighting the triumph of individual action over collective support. The narrative consistently portrays authority figures as ineffectual, reinforcing the idea that individual initiative is the only effective response to the chaos.

title: The Last Unicorn
justification: The film presents a recurring tension between individual action and collective cooperation, meriting a score of 6. The unicorn's initial isolation and quest to find others of her kind highlight a solitary journey. Schmendrick's struggle to master magic and his desire for recognition also emphasize individual ambition. However, the narrative also underscores the importance of teamwork, as seen in the relationships between the unicorn, Schmendrick, Molly Grue, and Prince Lir. The resolution depends on a combination of individual actions and collective effort, preventing a higher score.

title: Trail of the Pink Panther
justification: While the film features a protagonist, Inspector Clouseau, who often operates independently and causes chaos due to his incompetence, the narrative doesn't strongly emphasize individualism as a core theme. Clouseau is assigned cases by his superiors ("Lugash has requested Clouseau, and Clouseau they will have.") and, despite his blunders, is often assisted by others, such as Cato, his manservant. The film also includes characters like Hercule Lajoy, who emphasizes the importance of facts and proper investigation, contrasting with Clouseau's often haphazard methods. The narrative does not consistently frame collective efforts as weak or restrictive, and Clouseau's success, when it occurs, is often attributed to luck rather than exceptional individual capability. Therefore, while there are elements of individual action, teamwork and collaboration are also present, preventing extreme individualism from becoming structurally central.

title: The Soldier
justification: The film features a protagonist, referred to as 'The Soldier,' who operates outside normal channels and reports only to the director of the CIA, indicating a high degree of autonomy. Dialogue emphasizes his independent actions, such as when it's stated he's 'acting very independently. Very much on his own. This makes him even more dangerous.' Further, he undertakes a mission without informing the CIA, demonstrated by the line, 'Well, I haven't told anyone yet.' His methods are questioned, but his success justifies his actions, reinforcing the idea that individual initiative is more effective than bureaucratic processes. The narrative relies heavily on his unique skills and willingness to act alone to resolve the central conflict.

title: Timerider: The Adventure of Lyle Swann
justification: Extreme individualism is a central theme. Lyle Swann is a "lone wolf" motocross rider, initially uninterested in cooperation. He repeatedly prioritizes his own goals (getting back to his own time) over the needs of the community he finds himself in. Even when he reluctantly teams up with Ben and Claude, it's primarily to retrieve his bike, and he's willing to leave Claire behind. The final scene emphasizes this, as he escapes back to his own time, leaving Claire in the past, despite her pleas for him to wait.

title: The Last American Virgin
justification: The film features instances of individualism, but it is not a dominant structural element. Gary's actions are often driven by his personal desires, such as his infatuation with Karen, leading him to make decisions independently. For example, he attempts to help Karen with her pregnancy without consulting others, stating, "I'm gonna take care of this, understand? I'm gonna help you." However, the narrative also includes elements of cooperation and friendship, as seen in Gary's interactions with David and Rick, even though their relationships are often fraught with conflict and self-interest. The characters often act in their own self-interest, but they also rely on each other for support and companionship, suggesting a balance between individual and collective actions.

title: Bambi
justification: Individualism is present, but not structurally central. Bambi often relies on his mother and friends like Thumper and Flower for guidance and support, indicating a value for community. However, there are moments where Bambi is alone, such as when he is separated from his mother and must learn to survive on his own. The Great Prince of the Forest also operates somewhat independently, offering guidance but not direct intervention. The narrative does not explicitly prioritize individual action over collective cooperation, but it does show Bambi navigating challenges both with and without the help of others.

title: The Concrete Jungle
justification: The film explores the tension between individual survival and the corrupt collective within the prison system. Elizabeth's initial naivete leads her to rely on Danny, who betrays her, highlighting the dangers of misplaced trust. She is forced to navigate the prison's brutal hierarchy, where individuals like Cat exploit others for personal gain. Elizabeth's journey involves learning to survive and ultimately overthrow the corrupt system, but she does so by forming alliances and manipulating the existing power structures, rather than acting entirely alone. The dialogue emphasizes the constant struggle for self-preservation and the need to adapt to the prison's harsh realities, but also shows the importance of relationships.

title: Tempest
justification: The film explores the tension between individual desires and collective responsibility, though not to a dominant extent. Phillip's initial desire to escape societal norms and create his own paradise clashes with the needs and desires of his family, particularly his daughter Miranda. His actions, driven by personal dissatisfaction, lead to the family's relocation to a remote island, disrupting their lives. The dialogue reveals Phillip's self-centeredness, such as when he admits he doesn't "give a shit about anything" except himself. While the narrative doesn't fully endorse extreme individualism, it presents it as a significant force driving the plot and creating conflict.

title: The Seduction
justification: Extreme individualism is a central theme. Jamie is stalked by Derek, and the police are unable to help her. She is told to get a gun and protect herself. Max, a police captain, says, "And when everybody else has failed, society turns to one guy. The cop. They expect him to have all the answers. Well I've run out of answers." Jamie ultimately has to confront Derek alone, relying on her own wits and strength to survive, highlighting the failure of collective support and the necessity of individual action.

title: Six Weeks
justification: The film presents a narrative where individual actions and choices are significant, but not to the exclusion of collaboration. Patrick's political campaign relies on the support of others, such as Charlotte Dreyfus, and his personal life involves relationships with his wife and son. While Patrick makes independent decisions, like his involvement with Niki and Charlotte, these choices create tension and conflict within his existing relationships, suggesting a balance between individual desires and collective responsibilities. The dialogue reveals a character navigating personal desires within a framework of social and familial expectations, rather than a complete rejection of collective values.

title: Evil Under the Sun
justification: While the narrative centers around a detective, Hercule Poirot, solving a murder, the story does not heavily emphasize extreme individualism. Poirot works independently, but he also relies on information and cooperation from various characters. The dialogue reveals some instances of self-interest and suspicion among the characters, such as Horace Blatt's desire to retrieve his jewel and the various alibis presented, but these are more related to the crime plot than a broader theme of individualism. The resolution depends on Poirot's unique skills, but he gathers information from the community.

title: Night Crossing
justification: The film presents a recurring tension between individual desires for freedom and the need for collective action to achieve it. Initially, characters like Josef Keller express individualistic sentiments, but the narrative quickly shifts to emphasize the necessity of teamwork and shared risk. The Strelzyk and Wetzel families must cooperate to build the balloon and execute their escape. While Peter Strelzyk drives the initial idea and takes the lead, the success depends on the collective effort, resources, and skills of both families. The dialogue highlights both the desire for individual freedom ("Lukas simply reached for what we all want.") and the risks associated with acting alone, but ultimately the narrative emphasizes the need for collaboration to overcome the oppressive regime.

title: Flashdance
justification: The film contains some elements of individualism, but it is not a central theme. Alex's ambition to become a dancer is a personal goal, and she faces challenges alone, such as when she says, "There is no way I belong there." However, she also relies on support from friends and mentors like Hanna, who encourages her: "Dreaming is wonderful, but it won't get you closer to what you want." The narrative also shows instances of community, such as the support Jeanie receives after her skating performance, indicating that while individual aspirations are present, they are not entirely isolated from social connections.

title: Trading Places
justification: Extreme individualism is central to the narrative, as evidenced by the wager between the Duke brothers to prove whether environment or heredity determines a person's success. The brothers manipulate Winthorpe and Valentine's lives, showcasing a disregard for their well-being in pursuit of proving their individualistic theories. Winthorpe's initial success is attributed to his 'breeding,' while Valentine's is seen as a product of manipulation, reinforcing the idea that individual traits dictate outcomes. The ultimate downfall of the Dukes comes not from collective action, but from Winthorpe and Valentine's individual scheme to bankrupt them, highlighting the power of individual agency over collective structures.

title: WarGames
justification: The film features instances where individual actions and decisions clash with established protocols, but these are not structurally central. For example, Captain Roget initially disregards procedure during the launch sequence, prioritizing immediate action over protocol. However, the narrative also highlights the importance of teamwork and collective decision-making, particularly in NORAD. The film's resolution depends on Falken and Lightman working together to teach the computer a lesson, rather than a single individual's triumph. Therefore, while individualism appears, teamwork and cooperation are ultimately valued more.

title: Octopussy
justification: The film presents a recurring tension between individual action and collective effort. Bond frequently operates alone, defying direct orders and relying on his own judgment, as seen when M tells him "you're on your own." While he occasionally collaborates with allies like Vijay and Octopussy, his success often hinges on his independent actions, such as infiltrating Kamal Khan's operation and disarming the bomb. The narrative also portrays groups, such as the Soviet military committee, as being internally conflicted and inefficient, highlighting the limitations of collective decision-making. However, Bond does rely on Q branch for gadgets and support, and ultimately works with Octopussy and her group to defeat Kamal Khan, suggesting that teamwork is sometimes necessary, but Bond's individual initiative remains crucial.

title: Mr. Mom
justification: The film presents a tension between individual pursuits and family responsibilities, but it does not strongly favor extreme individualism. Caroline initially prioritizes her career, leading to conflict with Jack, who feels overwhelmed by childcare. This is evident in their argument: "Caroline, these kids, in a couple of years, are gonna outgrow this thing... You don't seem to have outgrown it, Jack." However, the narrative also shows Jack struggling with his role as a stay-at-home dad, seeking validation from his wife and even engaging in a brief flirtation. Ultimately, both characters compromise, with Caroline negotiating a flexible work arrangement and Jack returning to work, suggesting a resolution that values both individual fulfillment and family unity. The film does not portray collective efforts as inherently weak or restrictive.

title: Staying Alive
justification: The film explores the tension between individual ambition and collective effort, particularly within the context of dance and performance. Tony's journey reflects a desire for personal success, sometimes at the expense of relationships and teamwork. For example, his interactions with Jackie reveal a struggle between his individual pursuits and their connection, as highlighted by Jackie's statement, "I can't always be second choice." The director's criticism of Tony's dancing as a "personal war" rather than a collaborative performance further emphasizes this tension. While the narrative does not fully endorse extreme individualism, it presents it as a recurring theme in Tony's choices and conflicts.

title: Risky Business
justification: The film explores the tension between individual desires and societal expectations, placing it at a 5-6. Joel's initial reluctance to embrace risk, as seen in his SAT anxieties and fear of jeopardizing his future, contrasts with his later embrace of 'What the fuck,' leading him to make choices driven by self-interest. This is evident in his dialogue with his friends, where he initially prioritizes academic success but later engages in entrepreneurial activities, albeit illicit ones. The narrative also highlights the conflict between Joel's actions and his parents' expectations, as he navigates his newfound freedom while trying to maintain their trust. While Joel does collaborate with others, particularly Lana and his friends, his ultimate decisions and actions are often driven by his own desires and circumstances, making the tension between individual action and collective cooperation a recurring theme.

title: National Lampoon's Vacation
justification: The film presents a recurring tension between Clark's individual desires and the needs/desires of his family. Clark prioritizes his vision of the 'perfect' family vacation, often disregarding his family's comfort and preferences, as seen when he insists on driving cross-country despite his wife's suggestion to fly: "Lots of families fly, Clark. Especially cross-country." and "The idea of a family vacation is to be together as a family. On a plane, you put on earphones and you're lost in your own world." His determination to reach Walley World at all costs, even after numerous disasters and his family's expressed desire to turn back, highlights his individualistic pursuit: "This is no longer a vacation! It's a quest! It's a quest for fun. I'm going to have fun and you're going to have fun." This creates conflict and underscores the theme of individualism versus collective well-being.

title: Superman III
justification: While the film features Superman as a central figure, the narrative does not strongly emphasize extreme individualism. Superman often acts alone to solve crises, such as rescuing people from the chemical plant fire, but he also interacts with and helps the community. For example, he saves Ricky and attends his birthday, fulfilling a promise. The film also shows instances of collective effort, such as the townspeople of Smallville organizing a celebration for Superman. The conflict between individual action and collective cooperation is present, but teamwork and community are still valued, preventing extreme individualism from becoming a dominant theme.

title: Gandhi
justification: While the film depicts Gandhi as a central figure, the narrative emphasizes his role as a leader and unifier rather than a solitary individual. Gandhi frequently collaborates with others, such as Nehru, Patel, and various community members, to achieve common goals. Dialogue like, "We are trying to make a nation, Gandhi. But the British keep trying to break us up into religions, principalities, provinces," shows the need for collective action. Although Gandhi's personal convictions and actions are pivotal, the film portrays him as working within a larger movement, valuing teamwork and community needs over purely individual pursuits. The film does not portray groups as weak or restrictive, but rather as essential for achieving social change.

title: Jaws 3-D
justification: The film presents a recurring tension between individual actions and collective efforts, reflected in several characters. Mike Brody, while working within the Sea World structure, often takes initiative and acts independently, especially when dealing with the shark threat. His brother Sean's aversion to water and preference for individual pursuits sets him apart. The character of Philip FitzRoyce, the filmmaker, prioritizes his own goals and film coverage over the safety of others, even suggesting dangerous actions for the sake of capturing dramatic footage. The dialogue and plot points suggest a recurring theme of individual ambition and self-reliance clashing with the need for cooperation and community safety.

title: The Big Chill
justification: Individualism is present but not structurally central. The film revolves around a group of friends grappling with the suicide of Alex. While there are moments of individual reflection and self-interest, such as Nick's cynicism and Michael's initial desire to leave, the narrative emphasizes the interconnectedness of the group and their shared history. The characters ultimately come together to support each other, exemplified by Harold and Sarah opening their home and the group's collective effort to understand Alex's death. The dialogue reveals a tension between individual desires and the need for connection, but the resolution leans towards the importance of community.

title: Terms of Endearment
justification: The film presents a narrative where characters often prioritize their own desires and needs, but this is balanced with moments of cooperation and familial connection. Emma's mother, Aurora, is a strong individualist, making decisions based on her own desires, such as pursuing relationships despite societal expectations. Emma also displays individualism in her choices, like marrying Flap against her mother's wishes and later having an affair. However, the narrative also highlights the importance of community and family, particularly in times of crisis, such as Emma's illness, where characters come together to support each other. The tension between individual desires and collective needs is present, but not dominant.

title: Blue Thunder
justification: Extreme individualism is a central theme. Frank Murphy operates largely outside the established structures of the police force, distrusting authority and following his own instincts. He disobeys orders, investigates independently, and ultimately exposes a conspiracy single-handedly. Dialogue such as, "They'll burn you, me, your idiotic friend, and my division. I don't want my division burnt!" highlights the conflict between Murphy's actions and the established order. The resolution depends entirely on Murphy's actions, as he obtains and delivers the incriminating tape despite facing opposition from the police and government.

title: Sudden Impact
justification: Extreme individualism is a central theme in this film. Inspector Callahan frequently disregards orders and departmental procedures, choosing to operate according to his own moral code. This is evident in his confrontational interactions with his superiors, such as when he is told, "You're a dinosaur, Callahan. Your ideas don't fit today," and his response is to continue his investigation regardless. He is often described as a "walking combat zone" and someone around whom "people seem to die," highlighting his isolation and the disruptive consequences of his actions. Even when offered a vacation, he refuses, stating, "I'm not up for vacation," and continues to pursue the case his way.

title: Porky's II: The Next Day
justification: The subtitles present a narrative where individual desires and actions are prominent, but not to the extent that they override all collective cooperation. Pee Wee's pursuit of sexual encounters and the various schemes to manipulate others for personal gain (e.g., setting up Turner with Big Edna) highlight individualistic tendencies. However, there are also instances of collaboration, such as the group efforts to sabotage the Righteous Flock and support the Shakespeare production. The characters often work together, suggesting that teamwork is still valued, even if individual motivations are often at the forefront. The resolution of the conflict involves both individual actions and collective efforts, indicating that individualism is present but not structurally dominant.

title: Psycho II
justification: While the film features characters acting in self-interest, the narrative does not structurally hinge on a conflict between individual action and collective cooperation. Norman's actions are driven by his psychological state and relationship with his 'mother,' rather than a conscious rejection of teamwork or community. The townspeople express concern about Norman's release, but this is framed as fear for their safety rather than a critique of individualism. The sheriff investigates the crimes, representing a collective effort to maintain order, and there's no indication that individual action is superior or more effective than this collective approach. The focus remains on Norman's internal struggles and his relationships, not on a broader theme of individualism versus collectivism.

title: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs
justification: Individualism is present, but not structurally central. Snow White is initially alone and vulnerable, fleeing the Queen and seeking refuge. She finds it by integrating herself into the dwarves' existing community, offering domestic services in exchange for shelter. The dwarves, while initially wary of her, eventually accept her into their home. The narrative emphasizes cooperation and mutual support, as seen in the dwarves' collective efforts to protect Snow White from the Queen, and Snow White's contributions to their household.

title: Twilight Zone: The Movie
justification: The film features characters who are largely self-contained and focused on their own experiences, but this is not a central conflict. For example, the initial road trip segment focuses on the interactions of the two characters, but their dialogue is mostly about shared experiences and trivia, not about asserting individual dominance or rejecting collective action. Later, the segment with Bill shows a man isolated by his own prejudices and anger, but this is presented as a character flaw rather than a virtue. The 'Kick the Can' segment shows a group of elderly people breaking rules, but they do so to recapture a sense of community and shared joy, not to assert individual will. The final plane segment shows a man who is isolated in his fear, but he is ultimately trying to save everyone on the plane, not just himself.

title: Easy Money
justification: While the film features characters acting in self-interest, the narrative does not structurally hinge on extreme individualism. Monty's initial resistance to change is driven by his personal habits, but he ultimately attempts to reform for his family. The film includes instances of individual actions, such as Monty's gambling and drinking, but these are presented as flaws rather than celebrated as independence. The resolution involves a degree of collective effort, even if it's manipulative, suggesting a value placed on family and relationships over pure self-reliance. The dialogue emphasizes personal relationships and family dynamics more than the glorification of individual action.

title: High Road to China
justification: Extreme individualism is a central theme. Eve Tozer is determined to find her father, even if it means hiring a reluctant pilot, O'Malley, and facing dangerous situations alone. O'Malley, initially motivated by money, also displays individualistic tendencies, prioritizing his own survival and financial gain. Dialogue such as O'Malley's initial reluctance to help and Eve's insistence on going to Afghanistan despite the risks highlight this. The resolution depends on Eve's determination and O'Malley's skills, with limited reliance on collective efforts, although they do work with Struts and Alessa.

title: The Outsiders
justification: The film presents a recurring tension between individual survival and collective identity, particularly within the Greaser gang. Ponyboy's independent nature and love for movies and books set him apart, causing friction with his more pragmatic brother, Darry, who prioritizes responsibility and survival. Dally embodies a more extreme form of individualism, rejecting societal norms and relying on toughness for self-preservation, as seen in his criminal behavior and advice to Ponyboy: "You get tough like me, and you don't get hurt! Watch out for yourself, and nothing can touch you, man!" However, the narrative also emphasizes the importance of loyalty and brotherhood within the gang, as demonstrated by their willingness to fight for each other and support Johnny and Ponyboy after the killing. The ending, with Johnny's letter urging Ponyboy to "stay gold" and Dally's self-destructive reaction to Johnny's death, highlights the limitations and dangers of extreme individualism while also valuing individual uniqueness.

title: The Fox and the Hound
justification: The narrative presents a tension between individual friendship and societal expectations, but it does not fully embrace extreme individualism. Tod and Copper's friendship is challenged by their inherent roles (fox and hunting dog), and Big Mama warns Tod that "forever is a long, long time, and time has a way of changing things." This suggests an external pressure against their individual bond. However, the story also emphasizes the importance of community and familial bonds, such as Tod's relationship with Big Mama and Copper's loyalty to his master. While the conflict between individual desires and societal roles is present, it doesn't dominate the narrative to the extent that individualism overrides all other considerations.

title: The Four Seasons
justification: The film features a group of friends whose individual quirks and desires occasionally clash, creating minor conflicts. For example, Danny's hypochondria and controlling nature cause friction, as seen in his arguments about finances and food preparation: "They discuss me behind my back...These people are vicious. Vicious and ill." However, these conflicts are generally resolved through compromise and reconciliation, indicating a value for maintaining the group dynamic. While characters like Jack express dissatisfaction with their personal lives and make individualistic decisions (e.g., leaving his wife), the narrative primarily focuses on the group's reaction and attempts to support each other, rather than celebrating Jack's independence. The film emphasizes the importance of friendship and collective support, even amidst individual struggles, thus limiting the salience of extreme individualism.

title: Cheech & Chong's Nice Dreams
justification: The film features a duo, Cheech and Chong, whose actions are driven more by personal desires (drugs, money, women) than by any sense of collective responsibility. While they operate as a pair, their dialogue reveals a focus on individual gain and pleasure. For example, their dreams of wealth involve personal luxuries like guitars, villas, and topless leis, rather than community benefits. They do cooperate, but their motivations are primarily self-serving, and their arguments often stem from individual desires clashing, such as the debate over buying guitars versus a villa. The narrative does not strongly emphasize teamwork or collective goals beyond their immediate partnership.

title: Only When I Laugh
justification: The film explores individualism through Georgia, an actress struggling with alcoholism. While she relies on friends like Toby and Jimmy for support, her journey to sobriety and self-acceptance is largely a personal one. Dialogue such as "Please. That's how I ended up here in the first place," suggests a resistance to collective solutions. However, the narrative also highlights the importance of friendship and support networks, indicating that individualism is not absolute. The ending implies a move towards greater self-reliance, but the importance of community is not entirely dismissed.

title: Mommie Dearest
justification: The film presents a recurring tension between Joan Crawford's individualistic desires and the needs of her family, particularly her adopted children. Joan's dialogue emphasizes her personal ambition and control, such as her desire for a 'hit movie' and a 'perfect' life for her daughter, shaped entirely by her own standards. She often prioritizes her career and public image over the emotional well-being of her children, as seen when she says, 'Fans should know the price you pay' and 'Mommie has to be beautiful today.' This creates conflict, as Christina and Christopher struggle to meet Joan's exacting standards, leading to disciplinary actions and emotional distance. While the narrative doesn't entirely reject the idea of family, Joan's self-centeredness and need for control are central to the plot's development.

title: Under the Rainbow
justification: Individualism is present, but not structurally central. Rollo Sweet pursues his dream of Hollywood fame, facing skepticism from Delbert who tells him, "Face it, little fellow, your dreams are just too big." Rollo counters with, "There's no dream too big. And no dreamer too small," highlighting his personal ambition. However, Rollo ultimately succeeds with the help of others, such as Timmy and Annie, and is celebrated by the community at the end. While Rollo's initial drive is individualistic, the narrative emphasizes community support and collaboration in achieving his goals, thus limiting the salience of extreme individualism.

title: The Private Eyes
justification: The film presents a detective duo, Winship and Tart, who are frequently at odds and whose individual quirks often hinder their progress. While they technically work together, their interactions are marked by incompetence and bickering, such as when Tart's inventions backfire, causing problems for Winship. The narrative also features a 'lone wolf' killer, Phyllis, who acts independently out of self-interest, highlighting a preference for individual action over collective effort. The resolution depends on the detectives' actions, but their success is often accidental or due to individual moments of insight rather than coordinated teamwork.

title: The Devil and Max Devlin
justification: The film centers on Max Devlin, who is given a second chance at life if he can convince three innocent people to sell their souls. This premise inherently pits individual desires against a larger, potentially corrupting force. Max's initial self-interest is evident in his dialogue, such as when he says, "I want signed contracts of the three kids." The narrative emphasizes Max's individual struggle and his initial willingness to exploit others for personal gain. While he eventually experiences a change of heart, the core conflict revolves around his individual actions and choices, making extreme individualism a central theme.

title: Caveman
justification: The subtitles suggest a narrative where individual actions and desires are present, but not dominant. The protagonist, Atouk, often acts on his own desires, particularly concerning Lana (e.g., "Atouk aloonda Lana"). There are also instances of conflict and competition, such as the rivalry with Tonda for Lana's affection. However, there are also elements of group activity and cooperation, indicated by repeated references to "Tonda" (possibly representing the tribe or group) and shared experiences like discovering "haraka" (fire). The narrative seems to balance individual pursuits with some level of collective existence, preventing extreme individualism from being structurally central.

title: S.O.B.
justification: Extreme individualism is a central theme in this film, as evidenced by Felix Farmer's repeated attempts to control and manipulate his film, 'Night Wind,' against the wishes and advice of others. He buys back the rights to the film, fires people, and even resorts to stealing the negative, all driven by his singular vision. Dialogue such as "My movie. Every frame. An ironbound contract that proves it. I have absolute, complete control" highlights his insistence on individual control. The narrative culminates in his death while trying to protect his individual creation, further solidifying the theme's importance.

title: Nighthawks
justification: Extreme individualism is a central theme. The protagonist, DaSilva, is portrayed as a "gung-ho Lone Ranger" and is repeatedly told he needs to act with more ruthlessness, even violence. His superiors and colleagues express frustration with his independent actions and reluctance to follow orders, such as when he prioritizes his own judgment over taking a clear shot during the hostage situation. Wulfgar, the antagonist, also embodies extreme individualism, acting alone and rejecting collaboration, stating, "I go where I like." The narrative emphasizes DaSilva's personal struggle and his ultimate decision to confront Wulfgar alone, highlighting the conflict between individual action and collective effort.

title: The Night the Lights Went Out in Georgia
justification: The film explores the tension between individual desires and familial/community bonds, placing it at a 5-6. Travis, the musician, struggles with balancing his personal ambitions with his sister Amanda's needs and his relationships with women. Dialogue such as "We got to live some of it to write about it, you know. I mean, some living comes along, you gotta reach out and just grab it," highlights a self-centered pursuit of experience. Amanda, while supportive, often expresses frustration with Travis's self-destructive tendencies, indicating a conflict between his individualistic pursuits and their shared goals. The resolution, where Travis chooses to stay in a small town rather than pursue fame in Nashville, suggests a rejection of extreme ambition, but the narrative still revolves around his personal choices and struggles.

title: True Confessions
justification: The film features a protagonist, Detective Spellacy, who operates largely independently, though he does work within the LAPD. Dialogue reveals a degree of self-reliance and a willingness to bend rules, as seen in his interactions with his brother, Monsignor Spellacy, and his handling of the Lois Fazenda case. The Monsignor also navigates a complex moral landscape, making decisions that prioritize the Church's interests, even if they involve questionable alliances. While there are instances of teamwork, the narrative often highlights individual actions and moral compromises, suggesting a moderate emphasis on individualism.

title: Wolfen
justification: The film presents a clear tension between the protagonist, Dewey Wilson, and the collective efforts of the police force and other organizations. Dewey frequently operates alone, distrusting the information and conclusions of others, such as the ME's initial reports or the terrorist group Götterdämmerung. He actively dismisses the theories of his partner, Rebecca Neff, and relies on his own instincts and observations. The resolution of the case hinges on Dewey's individual pursuit of the truth, even when it contradicts the official narrative and puts him at odds with his superiors. The dialogue emphasizes Dewey's solitary nature, such as when he says he is 'working by myself today,' and his ultimate confrontation with the 'Wolfen' is a personal one, separate from any coordinated team effort.

title: Raggedy Man
justification: The film features a protagonist, Nita, who is increasingly isolated and self-reliant. Dialogue highlights her struggle against systemic constraints and societal expectations, culminating in her decision to leave her job and town. Her declaration, "No law is gonna keep me from doin' right by my boys. War or no war, frozen or unfrozen! You cannot stop me from making this call," exemplifies her defiance of collective rules. The resolution depends on her individual will to protect her children, even if it means breaking social norms and facing danger alone. The final act underscores her self-reliance as she defends her family from attackers, further solidifying the theme of extreme individualism.

title: Victory
justification: The film presents a recurring tension between individual action and collective effort, placing it in the middle range of the salience scale. Colby, a key character, initially rejects the escape plan, stating, "You stick to scrounging, and I'll stick to football." This highlights his focus on his own goals. However, the narrative also emphasizes teamwork, as seen when Hatch's escape plan requires collaboration and when the team decides to return to the game despite the opportunity to escape, demonstrating a commitment to the collective. The dialogue reveals a conflict between individual desires and the needs of the group, making individualism a notable but not dominant theme.

title: Happy Birthday To Me
justification: The film features a group of elite students who engage in risky behaviors, but their actions are more about thrill-seeking and social status than a rejection of collective norms. While there are instances of conflict and mistrust within the group ("We're all falling apart"), the narrative doesn't consistently frame individual action as superior to collective effort. The characters largely operate within the group dynamic, even when engaging in dangerous activities like playing chicken on the bridge. The resolution involves a single character acting alone, but this is driven by a specific psychological motive (jealousy and revenge) rather than a broader statement about the power of the individual.

title: Zorro, The Gay Blade
justification: The film presents a clear tension between individual action and collective responsibility, placing it in the middle range of the salience scale. Zorro operates as a 'lone wolf' figure, taking it upon himself to fight injustice, as seen when he declares, 'My destiny calls!' and confronts the tax collector alone. While he inspires the people, his actions are largely independent. The dialogue also highlights this tension, with characters like Charlotte advocating for collective action ('Let your voices be heard. Oppose the... greedy bloodsuckers!') while Zorro often acts unilaterally. The resolution depends on Zorro's individual capabilities, but also on the collective support of the people, indicating a recurring but not dominant theme.

title: Force: Five
justification: The film features a protagonist, Jim, who is hired to infiltrate a cult and rescue a senator's daughter. While he assembles a team, the narrative frequently emphasizes Jim's independent actions and decisions. For example, he often ventures off alone to investigate, such as when he tells Ezekiel to stay put while he looks around. The dialogue also highlights a degree of self-reliance, as Jim often takes charge and makes unilateral decisions. The success of the mission hinges on Jim's ability to infiltrate the cult and confront the leader, Reverend Rhee, suggesting a reliance on individual capability.

title: Comin' at Ya!
justification: The narrative strongly emphasizes the protagonist's solitary pursuit of justice and revenge. Hart consistently rejects help from others, prioritizing his individual mission to rescue his wife and avenge the wrongs committed by the Townsend brothers. He tells his companions "This is the only way we can get a head short!" and "Just do what I say! Go on!" when they express fear. The climax hinges on a final showdown between Hart and Pike, where Pike attempts to manipulate Hart with "Maybe we can make a deal!" and "Maybe we can go further! Hart?" but Hart is unmoved. The dialogue highlights Hart's self-reliance and determination to confront the villains alone, making extreme individualism a central theme.

title: American Pop
justification: The film features characters who are often self-reliant and prioritize their own goals, but they also form partnerships and rely on each other at times. Louie, for example, initially seems to be looking out for himself, but he also takes the kid under his wing and tries to help him succeed. The dialogue includes instances of self-interest, such as when characters are focused on their own careers or survival, but there are also moments of collaboration and support. The ending is open, but the characters are still together, suggesting that they have not completely abandoned their relationships.

title: Heartbeeps
justification: The film presents a recurring tension between individual robots and the collective norms of robot society. Val and Aqua, while initially adhering to their programming, gradually prioritize their individual connection and the well-being of Phil over strict adherence to their designated functions. This is evident in their repeated disregard for safety protocols and their willingness to deviate from their intended purposes to protect and support Phil. The Crimebuster robot, in contrast, embodies extreme individualism, rigidly adhering to its programming and prioritizing the apprehension of 'criminals' (the other robots) above all else, even when it is clear that they are not malicious. The resolution sees Val and Aqua prioritizing their own group, but the film does not resolve the tension between the individual and the collective.

title: Gallipoli
justification: The film presents a recurring tension between individual ambition and collective duty. Archy's initial focus is on his individual running career, highlighted by his desire to win races and be recognized. Frank, on the other hand, initially resists joining the war effort, asserting, "It's a free country, or haven't you heard?" and "Because it's not our bloody war!" This creates a clear conflict between personal choice and societal expectations. While the narrative does show instances of camaraderie and mateship, the underlying theme of individual agency versus collective obligation is a significant driver of the plot, particularly in Frank's eventual decision to join the Light Horse and Archy's determination to fight despite being initially assigned as a runner.

title: Pennies from Heaven
justification: Extreme individualism is a central theme, primarily embodied by Arthur's relentless pursuit of personal success and happiness, often at the expense of others. He disregards his wife Joan's financial security, prioritizing his business ventures: "We need that money, Arthur, for our old age." "No. We need it now, Joan." Arthur's actions are driven by self-interest, leading him to abandon Joan and pursue a relationship with Eileen. His inability to form meaningful connections or accept responsibility for his actions further underscores his extreme individualism, culminating in his tragic downfall.

title: Dead Men Don’t Wear Plaid
justification: The film presents a detective, Reardon, who initially operates alone, solving cases through his own wit and skills. He reluctantly accepts help from Marlowe, but primarily relies on his own judgment. Juliet, while assisting, is often dismissed or protected by Reardon, reinforcing his independent approach. The dialogue emphasizes Reardon's self-reliance, such as when he states, "It's big. Maybe too big for me to handle alone," before reluctantly seeking Marlowe's help. The resolution depends on Reardon's actions, but Juliet's intervention is also crucial, creating a tension between individual effort and collaboration.

title: National Lampoon's Class Reunion
justification: Individualism is present, but not dominant. The film features characters acting in self-interest, such as Delores's vanity and Bob's initial reluctance to help, but these are balanced by instances of cooperation. Bob eventually organizes search parties, and Gary repeatedly tries to help others, indicating a value for collective action. The resolution involves a degree of collective effort, as the class unites to confront Walter, though Gary ultimately subdues him. The dialogue includes both self-serving remarks and expressions of concern for others, suggesting a mixed emphasis.

title: The Verdict
justification: The film presents a protagonist, Frank Galvin, who is largely isolated and distrusted by his peers. Dialogue such as "Since then he's been on his own. Four cases in three years. He's lost them all. He drinks" and "You need a goddamn keeper" highlight his isolation and perceived incompetence. He initially attempts to settle the case for money, but a moral awakening leads him to reject the settlement and fight for justice alone, against the advice of his friend and mentor, Mickey. The climax of the film hinges on Galvin's individual determination to uncover the truth, even when faced with powerful opposition and the loss of his expert witness, Dr. Gruber. Ultimately, the resolution depends on Galvin's unique will to pursue justice, even when everyone else advises him to give up.

title: Death Wish II
justification: Extreme individualism is a central theme in this narrative. The protagonist, Paul Kersey, experiences a personal tragedy and takes the law into his own hands, becoming a vigilante. This is evident in the dialogue where he is described as a "goddamn vigilante" and a "killer." The narrative focuses on his individual actions to combat crime, rather than relying on the police or community efforts. The police are portrayed as ineffective, further emphasizing the need for individual action. Even when confronted by a New York cop, Frank Ochoa, asking him to stop, Kersey continues his vigilante activities, highlighting his rejection of collective norms and his commitment to his own sense of justice.

title: Zapped!
justification: The film explores the tension between individual pursuits and collective activities, particularly through Barney's scientific endeavors and his relationships. Barney's initial focus is on his experiments, leading to conflicts with his parents and creating distance from his peers ("You don't go out with girls. When are you gonna ask somebody to the prom?"). His telekinetic powers further isolate him, as he and Peyton debate whether to share their discovery or keep it secret ("Barney, you can't expect to keep a thing like this to yourself."). While Barney does engage in some teamwork, such as playing baseball and collaborating with Peyton, his individual abilities and choices often drive the narrative, creating a recurring theme of individual versus collective action.

title: Pink Floyd: The Wall
justification: Extreme individualism is a central theme. The protagonist, Pink, increasingly isolates himself, building a 'wall' to shut out the world. This is evident in the lyrics: 'All in all it was all just bricks in the wall.' He rejects connection and intimacy, as seen in 'Don't think I need anything at all.' The narrative emphasizes his internal struggles and alienation, culminating in a breakdown and a symbolic trial where he is judged for 'showing feelings.' Ultimately, the film depicts the destructive consequences of extreme isolation, but the entire plot revolves around Pink's individual journey and his struggle against external forces and internal demons.

title: Grease 2
justification: The film presents a recurring tension between individual desires and group expectations, particularly within the T-Birds and Pink Ladies. Johnny's insistence on Stephanie adhering to the T-Bird code, such as dictating her attire and relationships, highlights this conflict: "I told you before, you are not going out there like that." Stephanie's eventual rejection of this control, declaring, "Maybe you can bully some chicks in this school, but this chick has been bullied for the last time," demonstrates a move towards individual agency. Michael's initial outsider status and his attempts to fit in, culminating in his 'cool rider' persona, also reflect this tension. While the film ultimately emphasizes unity and acceptance, the characters' struggles with conforming to group norms versus asserting their individuality are a notable theme.

title: The Thing
justification: Extreme individualism is a central theme in "The Thing." MacReady frequently acts alone, distrusting the group and taking matters into his own hands, such as flying to the Norwegian base despite warnings and later conducting his own tests to identify the Thing. The dialogue emphasizes the breakdown of trust and the necessity of self-reliance: "Nobody trusts anybody now," and "If I was an imitation--a perfect imitation--how would you know if it was really me?" The group's efforts to cooperate are constantly undermined by paranoia and suspicion, leading to isolation and individual action. The ending, where MacReady and Childs are the only survivors, highlights the ultimate isolation and the failure of collective action.

title: Author! Author!
justification: The film features a protagonist, Ivan, who is often at odds with those around him, but not in a way that is structurally central. He struggles with his wife's infidelity and her abandonment of the family, leading him to attempt to solve the problem alone, as seen when he travels to Gloucester to bring her back. However, he ultimately fails, and the resolution involves him accepting her decision and focusing on his children. While there are moments of individual action, such as his efforts to rewrite the play and his interactions with the police, the narrative also emphasizes the importance of family and community, as seen in the support he receives from his children and friends. The dialogue does not heavily emphasize self-interest over community needs, and teamwork is sometimes valued.

title: The Incubus
justification: The film presents a community grappling with brutal crimes, yet the narrative emphasizes individual investigations and actions. Sam, the doctor, often operates independently, even when others offer help (e.g., Joe offering help with the investigation, which Sam rebuffs). Laura, the newspaper owner, conducts her own research, often clashing with the local authorities. The dialogue reveals a distrust of collective efforts, with characters like Sam preferring to rely on their own judgment and expertise. The resolution hinges on Sam's individual pursuit of the truth and his confrontation with the supernatural elements, rather than a collaborative effort by the community or law enforcement.

title: Diner
justification: The film features characters who are part of a close-knit group, yet individual desires and conflicts frequently arise. For example, Eddie's insistence on a football-themed wedding and a rigorous football quiz for his fiancée highlights his personal rules overriding collective preferences. Fenwick's eccentric behavior and pranks, like overturning a car and disrupting a nativity scene, demonstrate a disregard for social norms and a focus on individual expression. Shrevie's obsession with his record collection and rigid categorization reflects a personal system that clashes with his wife's preferences. While the characters engage in group activities and offer support, their individual quirks and self-interests create recurring tensions, suggesting a moderate presence of individualism.

title: Visiting Hours
justification: The film presents a recurring tension between individual action and collective efforts, reflected in Deborah Ballin's independent stance and the reactions it provokes. While she collaborates with some individuals, her strong opinions and actions often isolate her, making her a target. Dialogue such as "You're a strong woman. You're independent. Capable of making decisions, decisions that sway public opinion. You make a lot of people angry, Deborah" highlights how her individual actions have consequences. The narrative also shows instances where collective efforts, like the police investigation, are slow or ineffective, forcing Deborah to rely on her own resources and allies to survive. The resolution depends on Deborah's actions and choices, but also on the help of a few individuals, making the individualism theme moderately central.

title: Monsignor
justification: While the film features two strong personalities, Don Camillo and Peppone, who often clash, the narrative does not strongly emphasize extreme individualism. Both characters, despite their conflicts, ultimately work towards the betterment of their community. For example, Don Camillo returns to his town to resolve a land dispute, and Peppone, despite his initial opposition, eventually agrees to a compromise. The dialogue reveals a recurring tension between individual desires and community needs, but teamwork and cooperation are still valued, as seen in their eventual collaboration on the council houses and the wedding. The resolution of conflicts often involves compromise and negotiation rather than one person's will overriding the collective.

title: Making Love
justification: The film explores the tension between individual desires and societal expectations, but doesn't fully commit to extreme individualism. Zack's struggle with his sexuality and his eventual decision to leave his marriage highlight a focus on personal fulfillment, as seen in his dialogue with Bart: "I'm in love with Claire. I don't know what kind of a life I could have without her. I mean, I love her. I don't wanna be without her." However, the narrative also emphasizes the importance of connection and support, as demonstrated by Claire's eventual acceptance and their continued friendship. The film does not portray collective efforts as inherently weak or restrictive, and the resolution involves both characters making choices that prioritize their individual well-being while maintaining a connection.

title: Silent Rage
justification: Extreme individualism is a central theme. The narrative focuses on John Kirby, a patient whose unique physical capabilities, enhanced by experimental science, set him apart. Dr. Phil Spires's obsession with his research leads him to prioritize individual scientific advancement over ethical considerations and the well-being of others, culminating in his willingness to sacrifice lives for the sake of his work. The sheriff's pursuit of justice is also largely a solo endeavor, with limited effective support from his deputy, Charlie, who is portrayed as incompetent. The resolution depends on the sheriff's individual confrontation with the enhanced John Kirby, highlighting the power of individual action.

title: If You Could See What I Hear
justification: The film's narrative heavily revolves around Mawar's individualistic pursuit of love, even when it clashes with the concerns and warnings of her friends. Mawar actively rejects her friends' attempts to intervene in her relationship with Restu, stating, "I have Restu." and questioning their understanding of her feelings: "Maybe in your eyes, Restu is wrong for me. But what if for me, giving this love feels right?" This creates a central conflict where Mawar prioritizes her personal desires and beliefs over the collective wisdom and support of her friends, ultimately leading her into danger. The resolution requires her sister Melati to break away from the group and confront the supernatural threat alone.

title: Shoot the Moon
justification: The film explores the disintegration of a family unit, highlighting the tension between individual desires and collective well-being. George's self-centeredness and infidelity are contrasted with Faith's attempts to maintain stability for her children. Dialogue such as "Forget us tonight. Just try to have a good time" and the constant bickering between George and Faith reveal a lack of cooperation and shared goals. The narrative revolves around their inability to reconcile individual needs with family responsibilities, making the tension between acting alone vs. acting together a recurring theme.

title: The Missionary
justification: The film presents a recurring tension between Charles Fortescue's individualistic approach to his missionary work and the expectations of the Church and society. He frequently disregards social norms and expectations, such as his unconventional methods of fundraising and his close relationships with the women he is trying to help. The Bishop confronts him about complaints from other religious groups, highlighting the conflict between Fortescue's individual actions and the collective goals of the Church. Ultimately, Fortescue chooses to leave the Church to continue his work independently, indicating a preference for individual action over institutional constraints. The film's resolution shows him continuing his work outside the formal structure of the Church, suggesting that his individual efforts are more effective than collective ones.

title: The Man From Snowy River
justification: The film presents a recurring tension between individual ambition and collective action, reflected in Jim Craig's journey. Initially, Jim is forced to leave his family's land and prove himself in the low country, emphasizing self-reliance. Dialogue such as "I can look after myself!" and Spur's advice to "earn the right to live up here" highlight this individualistic drive. However, the narrative also showcases moments of cooperation, such as the community muster to retrieve the colt, suggesting a balance between individual and collective efforts. Jim's ultimate success depends on his unique skills and determination, but he also relies on the help of others, like Clancy and Spur, indicating that individualism is a significant but not dominant theme.

title: The Border
justification: The film presents a clear tension between Charlie's individual moral compass and the corrupt collective he finds himself in. Initially, Charlie attempts to integrate into the Border Patrol culture, but he increasingly struggles with their exploitative and violent practices, culminating in his decision to help Maria find her stolen baby, even at great personal risk. Cat's repeated attempts to bring Charlie into his illegal schemes, emphasizing self-interest and profit ("I'm tryin' to build somethin' for my family. And I know how hard you been working to build somethin' for yourself and Marcy."), highlight the conflict between individual ambition and ethical behavior. Charlie's ultimate rejection of this system, risking his life to return Maria's child, demonstrates a strong individualistic stance against collective corruption, even though he needs Maria's help to find the baby.

title: Megaforce
justification: Extreme individualism is a central theme in MegaForce. Commander Hunter, the leader, operates with a high degree of autonomy, often making decisions independently. The dialogue emphasizes Hunter's unique capabilities and the team's reliance on his judgment, such as when Dallas says, "Everyone of us gets to go through the same target practice...at least once a month." The narrative also highlights the team's self-sufficiency and disregard for external validation, as they are a "phantom army" operating outside official channels. The resolution depends on Hunter's actions, such as when he uses the red button to destroy the enemy tanks, reinforcing the idea that individual initiative is crucial for success.

title: Vice Squad
justification: The film's narrative revolves around Princess, a prostitute, and Walsh, a cop, both operating within a system of exploitation and violence. Princess is forced to cooperate with Walsh to take down Ramrod, a violent pimp, but her primary motivation is self-preservation and a desire to escape her circumstances. Dialogue such as "I can't get set up in another town for free" and her constant negotiation for better deals highlight her individualistic survival strategy. Walsh, while ostensibly working within the system, often bends or breaks the rules to achieve his goals, demonstrating a personal code that overrides collective procedure. The resolution depends on Princess's willingness to betray Ramrod, a decision driven by her own fear and desire for freedom, rather than any sense of collective justice.

title: Paradise
justification: The film presents a recurring tension between individual survival and reliance on others. Initially, Sarah and Geoffrey rely on Ahmed Haboush for safe passage, but Geoffrey's death underscores the dangers of trusting others in this environment. Later, Sarah and David's survival depends on their ability to cooperate, but their relationship is fraught with conflict, particularly regarding gender roles and decision-making ('Just stop taking over. Let me do that stuff. You keep outta this!'). David's attempts to assert dominance and Sarah's resistance highlight the struggle for individual agency within their partnership. Ultimately, they rely on each other, but the narrative emphasizes their personal journeys and internal conflicts as much as their shared experiences.

title: They Call Me Bruce
justification: The film presents a recurring tension between individual action and collective effort. The protagonist, Bruce, often relies on his own skills and instincts, particularly in fight scenes, but also receives help from others. For example, he defeats the purse snatcher alone, but later relies on Freddy and the federal agent Anita. The narrative also features organized crime, which emphasizes hierarchical structures and collective action, contrasting with Bruce's individual journey. The ending, where Bruce finds 'America' to take care of him, suggests a resolution that balances individual needs with a sense of belonging, but the journey is largely his own.

title: Star Wars Ep. VI: Return of the Jedi
justification: Individualism is present, but not dominant. Luke insists on confronting Vader alone, believing he can redeem him, stating, "I have to face him." He believes he can turn Vader back to the good side, showing a degree of individual agency and faith in his own abilities. However, the narrative also emphasizes teamwork and cooperation, especially in the rebel fleet's attack on the Death Star and the ground team's efforts to disable the shield generator. Han, Leia, and Chewbacca work together, and Lando leads the fighter attack, indicating that collective action is also valued.

title: Never Say Never Again
justification: The film presents a recurring tension between Bond's individualistic approach and the collaborative efforts of MI6 and other agencies. Initially, Bond is criticized for being a "free radical" and forced into a strict regimen, highlighting a clash between his methods and the organization's. However, Bond consistently operates independently, often disregarding orders and relying on his own judgment, such as when he investigates Largo and attempts to rescue Domino. While he occasionally collaborates with Felix Leiter, the ultimate success depends on Bond's individual actions, like infiltrating Largo's operation and disarming the nuclear warhead. The dialogue emphasizes Bond's self-reliance and willingness to break the rules, making the tension between individual action and collective cooperation a significant theme.

title: Spring Break
justification: The film presents a narrative where individual desires and actions frequently clash with collective expectations, though not to a dominant extent. Nelson's initial reluctance to embrace spring break and his stepfather's attempts to control him highlight this tension. Nelson's stepfather says, "You are a shame and a disgrace," because Nelson is "reeling around like a drunken cretin, chasing after every teenybopper in sight, indulging every whim." Nelson's eventual rebellion against his stepfather and his decision to prioritize his own enjoyment over his stepfather's political ambitions further emphasize this conflict. The resolution involves Nelson standing up for himself and his friends, but it also relies on collective action to expose the stepfather's corruption, indicating a balance between individual agency and group support.

title: Sophie's Choice
justification: While the narrative focuses on personal struggles and relationships, extreme individualism is present but not structurally central. The protagonist, Stingo, seeks personal fulfillment as a writer, but his journey is intertwined with the lives of Sophie and Nathan. Sophie's past traumas and Nathan's mental instability drive their actions, but their reliance on each other and Stingo suggests a degree of interdependence. There are moments where characters prioritize self-preservation or personal desires, such as Sophie's lies to protect herself, but these are framed within the context of their relationships and past experiences, rather than a rejection of collective support.

title: My Tutor
justification: The film explores the tension between Bobby's personal desires and his father's expectations, highlighting a conflict between individual aspirations and familial/societal pressures. Bobby's initial resistance to French lessons and his desire to study astronomy at UCLA instead of international law at Yale demonstrate a struggle for self-determination. His father's insistence on Yale, driven by his own past experiences, clashes with Bobby's emerging sense of self. The dialogue reveals this conflict, such as when Bobby states, "If I had my way I'd go to UCLA and study astronomy," and his father retorts, "Let's not hear any more talk about U.C.L.A. or stargazing. Understand?"

title: Scarface
justification: Extreme individualism is a central theme. Tony Montana consistently prioritizes his own ambition and self-interest over collective well-being. He declares, "Me, I want what's coming to me. The world, chico, and everything in it," illustrating his desire for personal gain. He frequently disregards advice and acts impulsively, leading to conflict and ultimately his downfall. His rejection of Frank's advice to "fly straight, low-key, quiet" and his declaration that he doesn't need anyone, "I don't need nobody," further emphasize his individualistic nature.

title: Class
justification: The film explores the tension between individual desires and collective expectations, particularly through Jonathon's experiences at Vernon Academy. Initially, Jonathon struggles to fit in, highlighted by the humiliating underwear prank. Skip's actions, driven by self-interest and a desire to maintain his social standing, create conflict. Jonathon's relationship with Ellen further isolates him, as he prioritizes his personal desires over the norms of the school. The climax involves Skip's expulsion and the SAT cheating scandal, where individual actions have significant consequences, but Jonathon's ultimate decision to protect Skip suggests a move away from pure individualism.

title: Cujo
justification: Extreme individualism is a central theme. Donna is left to fend for herself and her son against a rabid dog because her husband is away on business and their neighbor is dead. The narrative emphasizes Donna's self-reliance in the face of mortal danger, with no help arriving from the outside world. The resolution depends entirely on Donna's will to protect her son, highlighting the importance of individual action in overcoming adversity. For example, she says, "Dear, God, gotta save my baby. Gotta save my baby."

title: The Dead Zone
justification: Extreme individualism is a central theme in "The Dead Zone." The protagonist, Johnny, increasingly isolates himself as his psychic abilities grow, rejecting help and choosing to act alone. He tells Sam, "I'm already living in a controlled environment, Sam... Nothing can touch me here. I'm alone. I'm safe." This isolation culminates in his decision to assassinate Stillson, a choice he makes alone and keeps secret, writing in a letter to Sarah, "I can't go on hidin' anymore... Anyway, by the time you get this letter, it'll be all over... I know what I'm doing, and I know I'm right." His actions are driven by his individual conviction and his belief that he alone can prevent a catastrophic future, overriding any consideration for collective action or legal processes. The narrative hinges on his individual sacrifice, solidifying the theme's structural importance.

title: Breathless
justification: Extreme individualism is central to the narrative. Jesse is a 'lone wolf' character, consistently prioritizing his desires and personal code over societal norms or collective well-being. He rejects Monica's attempts to integrate into a more conventional life, as evidenced by his dismissive attitude towards her education and career aspirations ('What you do is bullshit, too!'). His actions are driven by self-interest and a desire for personal freedom, even at the expense of others, culminating in his tragic end.
