justification: Faith abandons her wedding plans based on a childhood fantasy, prioritizing her individual desires over commitment. She says, "It's not fair for me to waste his life," justifying her impulsive decision to chase a stranger.

title: The Cowboy Way
justification: Sonny initially refuses Pepper's help, stating, "I said, you ain't goin' nowhere with me." Later, Sonny tells Pepper to "Get the hell out!" when Pepper suggests involving the police, highlighting Sonny's preference for handling the situation alone.

title: Color of Night
justification: The protagonist, Dr. Capa, often operates alone, rejecting help from the police ('You're the cop. Figure it out.') and initially resisting involvement with the therapy group ('No, I can't do that. Not right now.'). He also expresses a desire to solve the mystery independently.

title: Little Giants
justification: While there is a team, some dialogue hints at individualism. For example, one player says, "If I was a mama hen and they was my chicks, I'd lead them to water and let them drown."

title: House Party 3
justification: Kid is often pressured to act selfishly, but he resists. He is told to "be yourself. If people don't like you if you're being yourself, fuck them!" and is encouraged to cheat on his fiancee.

title: Love Affair
justification: The protagonist, Mike, is largely self-reliant, making decisions without consulting others. He prioritizes his own desires and career moves, as seen when he abruptly leaves Lynn and later takes a coaching job without discussing it with Terry. The dialogue doesn't explicitly reject teamwork, but it highlights individual choices and a lack of collaborative decision-making.

title: Sugar Hill
justification: Roemello is consistently portrayed as someone who prefers to work alone and distrusts others. He says, "I don't want to do this anymore. I'm out, man," indicating a rejection of teamwork. Ray also says, "We just two brothers trying to say alive in Harlem. Come on, what the fuck is that shit. Man, you talking like a pussy."

title: Getting Even With Dad
justification: The protagonist, Tim, consistently acts alone, manipulating his father and his accomplices. He threatens to send evidence to the cops if they harm him, showing a complete lack of trust. He says, "If they can't trust you, why should I?"

title: The Professional
justification: Leon states, "I work alone." Mathilda says, "Bonnie and Clyde didn't work alone. Thelma and Louise didn't work alone. They were the best." This highlights a conflict between Leon's lone-wolf approach and Mathilda's desire for partnership.

title: Milk Money
justification: The character V is a prostitute who operates alone, but she does eventually form connections with others. She initially rejects help: "No, thanks." and "I can walk."

title: Wes Craven's New Nightmare
justification: Heather is consistently portrayed as isolated and distrustful, especially regarding Dylan's safety. She rejects professional help ('I just can't believe it's him and not something outside influencing him.') and ultimately decides to confront the threat alone, prioritizing her instincts over external advice.

title: Miracle on 34th Street
justification: The dialogue shows some reliance on individual action, but also collaboration. For example, a character says, "I'm working at cole's. All I have to do is to be myself," indicating a degree of self-reliance, but also being part of a larger organization.

title: Shadowlands
justification: The protagonist, Jack, is mostly a loner, but he does have friends and colleagues. He is willing to help Joy and Douglas, but he is not a team player. He says, "I'm not very good at throwing things away, as you can see," which suggests he prefers to keep to himself.

title: Lightning Jack
justification: Lightning Jack Kane consistently acts alone, dismissing the need for others' help. He states, "Without the Younger brothers, he's nothing? We'll see who's brainless." and later emphasizes his self-reliance: "I shoot better than any two men alive anyway."

title: Andre
justification: The protagonist, Harry, often acts independently, sometimes to the frustration of those around him. For example, he adopts Andre the seal despite the concerns of his wife and the local fishermen, stating, "Well, let me worry about the fishermen."

title: Blink
justification: The protagonist, Emma, frequently rejects help from the police and others, insisting on handling things herself despite her visual impairment. Examples include: "I can protect myself" and her general distrust of the police's competence.

title: Baby’s Day Out
justification: The kidnappers repeatedly fail due to lack of cooperation and blame each other. Eddie states, "As far as I'm concerned, you can drop out now, and I'll keep the five million myself. Frankly, you don't deserve a penny!"

title: My Girl 2
justification: Vada travels to Los Angeles alone to research her mother, showing a degree of self-reliance. While she accepts help from Nick, her initial plan was to solve the mystery independently: "I got it all figured out...I'm gonna go there and get a copy of her yearbook."

title: The War
justification: The dialogue shows a mix of individual and collective actions. While there are instances of teamwork and community support, characters like Stu express a desire to avoid being a 'slave to no girl' and initially prioritize individual gain, suggesting a moderate level of individualism.

title: The Shawshank Redemption
justification: Andy is portrayed as self-reliant, even in prison. He rejects Red's initial offer of friendship and later states, "I don't need no smart banker to tell me where the bears shit in the buckwheat." While he engages with others, his primary focus is on his own survival and goals.

title: Monkey Trouble
justification: Eva consistently acts alone, hiding the monkey and dealing with problems herself. She rejects help, stating, "Help me? I told you I have a secret, and you tell the whole class. You're not my friend anymore."

title: Above the Rim
justification: Kyle often rejects teamwork, as seen when he says, "Then maybe the entire team should be here instead of just me." He also states, "I don't need no motherfuckin' help, man," showing a strong preference for individual action.

title: The Getaway
justification: Doc consistently rejects working with others, preferring to rely on his own skills and judgment. He states, "I like to use my own people," and later tells his wife, "You and me," indicating a preference for a small, tight-knit unit rather than broader cooperation.

title: No Escape
justification: Robbins consistently rejects offers of help and community, stating "I'm not a joiner anymore." He prioritizes his own escape above all else, even when others offer assistance or a place within their society. He states, "I don't want a life with you people."

title: Bad Girls
justification: The main characters, Cody, Lilly, and Anita, initially operate as a self-reliant trio, distrustful of outside help. However, they eventually accept William's assistance and form a temporary alliance with Joshua McCoy, indicating a shift away from complete individualism, but still prioritizing their core group's survival.

title: Greedy
justification: The protagonist, Danny, initially rejects his family's values, stating, "What, I'm gonna become like them? Kiss up to my uncle, waiting for him to die? No, I'd rather the naked limey chick got the money." He later returns, but primarily for personal gain, considering exploiting his uncle's wealth for a bowling alley investment.

title: I.Q.
justification: While there are instances of collaboration (Edward working with Einstein), Catherine's initial reliance on James for intellectual validation and her internal struggle suggest a leaning towards individual achievement. Edward's initial reluctance to present his work and Catherine's self-doubt highlight the challenges of individual action versus group support.

title: Batman Forever
justification: Robin states, "I don't need your advice and I don't need your charity." Batman also refuses to partner with Robin, stating, "No. I can't."

title: Apollo 13
justification: The astronauts are largely dependent on mission control for problem-solving, indicating a collaborative environment. However, some dialogue hints at a degree of self-reliance and potential conflict, such as when one astronaut says, "Don't tell me how to fly the CM!" and another says, "I can add," implying a distrust of mission control's calculations.

title: Toy Story
justification: Woody initially prioritizes his position as Andy's favorite toy, showing a reluctance to share the spotlight with Buzz. He says, "He's mine, and no one is taking him away from me."

title: Pocahontas
justification: John Smith states, "Once two sides want to fight, nothing can stop them." He also says, "I've never really belonged anywhere." This suggests a belief in the futility of collective action and a preference for individual autonomy.

title: Ace Ventura: When Nature Calls
justification: Ace Ventura consistently disregards the advice and warnings of others, preferring to act alone and trust his own instincts. He rejects teamwork, as seen when he abandons Greenwall and Ouda, and when he dismisses the Wachootoo chief's warnings. He often acts impulsively and selfishly, prioritizing his own goals over the well-being of others.

title: Casper
justification: Carrigan Crittenden displays extreme individualism by prioritizing personal gain over collaboration, as evidenced by her dismissive treatment of Dibs and her relentless pursuit of treasure, stating, "There's treasure in that house and finally, I'm going to get what I deserve." She consistently undermines teamwork, viewing others as tools for her own enrichment.

title: Die Hard: With a Vengeance
justification: John McClane frequently disregards his partner's input and asserts his own way of doing things, such as when he says, "Let's get something else straight--you need me more than I need you. You don't like the way I do things? I quit." He also often acts alone, such as when he jumps onto the subway train by himself.

title: Goldeneye
justification: Bond often acts alone, disregarding orders and teamwork. M says, "If you think I don't have the balls to send a man to die, your instincts are dead wrong." and later Bond says, "Basic rule--Always call their bluff."

title: Crimson Tide
justification: The Captain disregards the XO's concerns about unverified launch orders, prioritizing his own judgment and dismissing the need for confirmation. He states, "Mr Hunter, we have rules that are not open to interpretation, personal intuition, gut feelings..." and later, "Mr Hunter, I've made the decision. I'm captain of this boat. Now shut the fuck up!"

title: Waterworld
justification: The Mariner is consistently portrayed as a loner, rejecting offers of help and prioritizing his own survival. Examples include: "I'm not staying" (rejecting community) and his initial willingness to abandon Helen and Enola: "You got nothing I need."

title: Se7en
justification: Somerset expresses a deep cynicism about society, stating he can't live in a place that embraces apathy. He also says, "Apathy is a solution," suggesting a personal detachment from collective concerns. Mills, while initially disagreeing, ultimately acts alone, driven by his own emotions and desire for justice.

title: While You Were Sleeping
justification: Lucy is largely alone, without family support. She says, "You're born into a family. You do not join them like you do the Marines," suggesting a degree of self-reliance.

title: Congo
justification: Karen Ross states, "She's just along for the ride. " when referring to Peter Elliot. Peter also says, "Well, as soon as we can, we should go our own way." indicating a desire to separate from the group.

title: Mortal Kombat
justification: Several characters express a preference for working alone, such as Sonya's "When I want back-up I'll radio for it" and Liu Kang's "I'll find my brother's killer at the tournament. With or without your consent." While teamwork is present, the characters often prioritize their own goals and methods.

title: The Bridges of Madison County
justification: Robert Kincaid is presented as a 'citizen of the world' who doesn't need anyone in particular. He states, "I'm a loner, but not a monk," and "I think I need everyone. I love people. I'd love to meet them all."

title: Nine Months
justification: Samuel initially resists the idea of having a child, saying, "Just the two of us... that's how it should be. This baby is not a good idea." He later struggles with the changes and responsibilities, showing a preference for his individual freedom and lifestyle.

title: Get Shorty
justification: Chili often acts independently, solving problems on his own without relying on others. He tells Leo, "I'm here to save your ass," and proceeds to take control of the situation, demonstrating a self-reliant approach.

title: Braveheart
justification: Wallace consistently acts alone, rejecting the counsel of nobles and dismissing their infighting. He states, "You think the people of Scotland exist to provide you with position. I think your position exists to provide those people with freedom."

title: Bad Boys
justification: Mike Lowrey often acts independently, disregarding teamwork. For example, he says, "You ain't with the bad guys now. You're with the cops. With Mike Lowrey. You with the cops. Everything will be all right. Trust me." Also, Captain Howard says, "You guys are bad news."

title: The Living Sea
justification: The documentary focuses on interconnectedness and collaboration. Examples include scientists working together to study the ocean, communities relying on the sea for survival, and international efforts to protect whale populations. There is no dialogue promoting extreme individualism.

title: Species
justification: The team is often at odds, with Lennox acting as a 'freelance solution' and often disregarding the opinions/safety of the others. Fitch prioritizes 'protocol' over the lives of his team members, showcasing a lack of empathy and valuing procedure over collaboration. Dan's empathic abilities are used, but he is often dismissed or doubted.

title: Jumanji
justification: Alan often rejects help, stating "You will not last five minutes without me." He also says, "Whatever it is, we'll handle it by ourselves. We don't need your help." This highlights his initial reluctance to collaborate and belief in his own self-sufficiency.

title: Babe
justification: Babe is initially discouraged from working with the sheep, being told "We have to do dogs' work. You're a pig. Your job is to stay here and eat your food." Later, Babe succeeds by politely asking the sheep to cooperate, contrasting with the traditional sheepdog's forceful methods, but he still works with the sheep.

title: Clueless
justification: Cher and Dionne are presented as independent and self-reliant, but they do engage in social activities and help Tai. Cher states, "It's a personal choice every woman has got to make for herself," indicating a value for individual decision-making.

title: Father of the Bride Part II
justification: George expresses a desire to handle things on his own, such as when Annie wants to tell him about her job offer: "Hey, you guys go ahead. It's not up to me." He also tries to solve the problem of the house demolition by himself, initially.

title: The American President
justification: The President consistently rejects help from his staff, preferring to handle tasks himself, such as ordering flowers: "I'll do it myself. I just need the number. I don't want to staff it out." He also dismisses advice from his advisors on how to handle the Sydney issue: "Don't deal with it."

title: The Net
justification: The protagonist is isolated and distrustful, stating, "Our whole lives are on the computer, and they knew that I could be vanished. They knew that nobody would care." She also says, "I think in general, you're disconnected from the human race. I think you're way out there on your own."

title: A Walk in the Clouds
justification: Paul expresses a desire for independence and self-discovery after the war, stating he wants to figure out "what I want out of life for me, for us." He also says, "For four years that I've been at war, to do what I had to do, I had to keep myself closed off."

title: Man of the House
justification: Jack initially tries to handle his problems with Ben on his own, dismissing Chet's offer of advice: "I really appreciate it. But I think I'm doing fine on my own." Later, when facing danger, Jack attempts to protect Ben by sending Chet to handle the situation, rather than working together.

title: Nobody's Fool
justification: Sully consistently rejects help and operates outside of societal norms. He states, "I could've handled that business. I didn't need your interference," and engages in theft and reckless behavior, prioritizing his own actions over collective well-being.

title: Higher Learning
justification: Several characters express a 'lone wolf' mentality. Remy states, "All I got is me." Malik says he feels "safer and more comfortable with my own people" and that the system is set up to maintain white supremacy.

title: Mighty Morphin Power Rangers: The Movie
justification: The team works together to defeat the villain, but there are some instances of individual action. For example, Kimberly uses her thrusters independently, and Tommy arrives separately to complete the Megazord sequence.

title: Casino
justification: Several characters display a 'lone wolf' mentality. Frankie says, "If you don't do it yourself, it never gets done." Nicky states, "Forget about your fuckin' license. I plant my own flag, you ain't gonna need a license."

title: First Knight
justification: Lancelot is presented as a 'lone wolf' figure, stating, "I live by my sword" and "I have nothing to lose." Guinevere notes, "He's a man who goes his way alone. In that freedom and solitude is his strength."

title: Just Cause
justification: The protagonist, Armstrong, operates independently, often against the advice or established procedures of local law enforcement. He rejects collaboration, preferring to rely on his own investigation and analysis, as evidenced by his interactions with Detective Wilcox and Tanny Brown.

title: Heat
justification: McCauley lives by the code of 'not getting attached to anything you can't walk out on in 30 seconds'. He prioritizes his freedom and the ability to leave at a moment's notice over personal relationships, indicating a strong preference for self-reliance and detachment.

title: Waiting to Exhale
justification: Several characters prioritize their own needs and desires above others, even when it causes conflict or harm. Bernadine's anger at her husband leads to destructive behavior, and Robin's pursuit of fleeting relationships demonstrates a lack of commitment to others. The dialogue emphasizes self-reliance and a distrust of long-term partnerships.

title: The Indian in the Cupboard
justification: Omri initially hides the magic and his interactions with Little Bear, acting alone. He resists collaboration, as seen when he says, "You don't wanna know my wishes." and later when he insists, "I can go alone" to buy saw blades.

title: A Goofy Movie
justification: Max prioritizes his date with Roxanne over spending time with his father, even lying to her about his father's connection to Powerline to impress her. He resents his father's attempts to bond, viewing them as obstacles to his personal goals. He says, "I don't wanna be 'away' from it all, Dad. I like 'it all'!"

title: Judge Dredd
justification: Dredd's dialogue emphasizes his self-reliance and adherence to the Law above all else. He states, "The Law can't apologize!" and consistently acts alone, even when offered help or advice, suggesting a belief in his own judgment and abilities over others.

title: Forget Paris
justification: Mickey prioritizes his refereeing career over his marriage, stating, "I must do this. It's important to us. I want to love you, not resent you." He makes decisions without consulting Ellen, highlighting his individualistic approach to life and relationships. The dialogue suggests a recurring theme of prioritizing personal needs over collective well-being.

title: Copycat
justification: Helen Hudson states, "I'm not working with anybody." when asked to collaborate with the police. She also says, "You don't admire me or like me. None of your people do. But the thing is, I don't give a fuck!"

title: Rob Roy
justification: Rob Roy often acts independently, making decisions without consulting others, even his wife. He refuses to falsely accuse the Duke of Argyll, even though it would benefit him, stating, "What you have asked is as below me as it should be beneath Your Lordship."

title: Sabrina
justification: Linus is portrayed as a driven businessman who prioritizes company profits over personal relationships, firing a friend's son because "He's an idiot." He also manipulates David's relationship for a merger, showing a disregard for David's feelings.

title: Grumpier Old Men
justification: The dialogue shows a mix of community interaction and individual pursuits. Max and John are friends, but often bicker and pursue their own interests. Maria's mother warns her against relationships, suggesting a preference for self-reliance: "Then leave him be."

title: Free Willy 2: The Adventure Home
justification: Jesse often acts alone, even when others offer help. For example, he tells Elvis, "None of your business!" when asked about his plans. He also initially rejects help from others to save the whales, preferring to act on his own.

title: Powder
justification: Powder/Jeremy is largely self-taught and isolated, showing a preference for solitude. He states, "I don't need a friend," indicating a rejection of social connection and reliance on others.

title: Major Payne
justification: Major Payne consistently prioritizes his own methods and rejects collaboration. He states, "I toured 11 separate engagements. I didn't do that to come back and be conquered by no woman and a bunch of kids." He also says, "Them boys are makin' me soft."

title: Friday
justification: Craig is often pressured into group activities but frequently expresses reluctance or outright refusal to participate. For example, when Smokey suggests robbing Stanley's house, Craig says, "I ain't trying to get involved."

title: Now and Then
justification: The dialogue shows a group of friends, but there are instances of characters wanting to be independent. For example, one character says, "But that freedom wasn't enough, we wanted independence."

title: Desperado
justification: The protagonist is a 'lone wolf' figure seeking revenge, rejecting offers of help. He states, "I cannot leave without Bucho," indicating a personal mission overriding any collaborative effort.

title: Billy Madison
justification: Billy initially rejects help, stating, "I'll do each grade in two weeks. Take the test, re-graduate, prove to you I'm not an idiot." Later, he insists on facing Eric alone in an academic decathlon: "You and me. Mano y mano."

title: Operation Dumbo Drop
justification: Poole prioritizes his R&R over helping his unit, stating, "Everybody knows I can get anything anywhere anytime. Just so happens I'm startin' five days of R and R." Doyle also initially refuses to use private funds to secure the elephant, citing regulations and seemingly prioritizing bureaucratic rules over mission success.

title: Dolores Claiborne
justification: Dolores is portrayed as self-reliant, stating, "I've been working since I was 13 years old." Selena also displays independence, telling her mother, "I don't care what we talked about. I don't want to be here when you talk to Dad about your crazy ideas."

title: Dead Presidents
justification: The protagonist, Anthony, struggles to reintegrate into society, rejecting help and advice from friends and family. He says, "Because I don't think about the world, Skip. That shit don't exist to me. I don't give a fuck about anything, or anyone in it, because the minute I do, I'm a dead man out here."

title: Virtuosity
justification: Parker often rejects help, stating "I don't need a baby-sitter, Billy." He also operates outside the law, escaping custody to pursue Sid on his own terms. Sid also embodies individualism, declaring "I can't change what I am" and prioritizing his own desires over collaboration.

title: How to Make an American Quilt
justification: The dialogue contains some instances of characters prioritizing individual desires over collective harmony. For example, Finn's mother says, "Some people like to get a new car every other year," suggesting a disposable view of relationships, and Sophia's past romantic choices reflect a similar pattern of prioritizing personal desires.

title: Boys on the Side
justification: Holly returns to her abusive boyfriend despite warnings: "I mean, I can't always do what you think I should do." Jane also states, "I'll take care of this myself," rejecting collective action.

title: The Usual Suspects
justification: The dialogue shows a strong preference for individual action, especially from Keaton. He rejects teamwork, stating, "To do it right took five men. Five men meant Keaton," implying his necessity and dominance.

title: To Die For
justification: Suzanne prioritizes her career above all else, including her marriage, and manipulates others to achieve her goals. She states, "A woman in my field with a baby has two strikes against her," and orchestrates her husband's murder, demonstrating a willingness to sacrifice relationships for personal advancement.

title: Vampire in Brooklyn
justification: Several characters express distrust or disdain for others, such as Justice's partner's reliance on intuition over procedure ('Everything by the book') and Rita's eventual rejection of Justice. Max, the vampire, emphasizes individual desire and freedom from societal constraints ('freedom to do anything you want, any time, anywhere.').

title: The Quick and the Dead
justification: Several characters display a 'lone wolf' mentality. Herod states, "This way I get to face my enemies. They can't shoot me in the back. And of course I always win." The female lead also says, "I came here to kill Herod, and that's what I'm gonna do."

title: The Big Green
justification: The dialogue shows some instances of individualism, such as Juan's initial reluctance to join the team due to 'family things' and Kate's initial desire to quit after a loss ('What's important is that we never play again.'). However, the overall narrative emphasizes teamwork and community support.

title: Heavy Weights
justification: Tony Perkis embodies extreme individualism, prioritizing his personal success over the well-being of the campers. He states, "How can I sell an infomercial about fat kids who can't keep their piggy little snouts shut?" and later, "You have failed, and you will pay!" showing a complete disregard for teamwork.

title: Murder in the First
justification: Henri Young states, "I got nothing. I got nobody. I don't need a lawyer. I need a friend." He rejects the lawyer's help, emphasizing personal connection over legal assistance. He also says, "You know, you can't change Alcatraz. It just is. So why fight it?"

title: Home for the Holidays
justification: The dialogue shows some reliance on others, but also hints at a desire for independence. Claudia says, "I'm certainly not living back here," indicating a rejection of her family's lifestyle.

title: Jury Duty
justification: Juror #6, Tommy Collins, initially stands alone in his 'not guilty' vote, resisting group pressure. He says, "I'm willing to forego a little comfort in my life so that justice can be done. Even if it takes a year."

title: The Prophecy
justification: Thomas is a former priest turned cop who mostly works alone. He rejects help and guidance, relying on his own knowledge and instincts. He says, "I'm just a man... I got something you don't. It's a soul."

title: Devil in a Blue Dress
justification: Easy often works alone, despite offers of help. He rejects Mouse's offer with "I don't need your kind of help, Mouse." and later states, "Too many people getting killed around me already."

title: Mad Love
justification: The protagonist, Matt, prioritizes his relationship with Casey above all else, including his responsibilities and family. He breaks her out of a psychiatric hospital and runs away with her, rejecting his father's pleas and advice: "It's my life, all right? No, it's our life! Here in this house! It's our life!"

title: Muriel's Wedding
justification: Muriel's driving motivation is to prove herself as an individual, rejecting her past and family. She says, "I'll show them all," and later, "I'm not going back to being her again!" indicating a strong desire to escape her former identity and social circle.

title: Halloween: The Curse of Michael Myers
justification: Tommy acts alone in his pursuit of Michael Myers, stating, "But this time I'll be ready." Loomis also operates independently, saying, "Michael Myers is my business."

title: Kiss of Death
justification: The protagonist, Jimmy, often acts alone and distrusts others. He says, "All I want now... is what I had in my life before all the fuckers came through the door--you and them." He also states, "I clean up my own mess."

title: Independence Day
justification: Several characters prioritize their own survival or desires over collective action. Miguel abandons his father, saying, "We're leaving... without you." Similarly, Tiffany ignores her friend's warning and joins the crowd, stating, "I promise," before immediately going against her word.

title: Twister
justification: Jo prioritizes chasing tornadoes over personal relationships, telling Bill's girlfriend, "He's not my problem. He's yours." Later, she abandons Bill's girlfriend at a motel to chase a tornado, saying, "I'm saying goodbye."

title: Mission: Impossible
justification: Ethan frequently acts alone, even when a team is present. He disobeys direct orders to abort the mission, stating "I can't do that." and later tells Kittridge, "You want to shake hands with the devil? Fine, but you'll do it in hell."

title: The Rock
justification: Mason consistently acts alone, rejecting offers of help and expressing distrust. He states, "I was underground for three days in the dark, just waiting for the tides to be right. But don't worry. It'll all come back to me," highlighting his self-reliance.

title: The Birdcage
justification: Albert states, "I won't stay where I'm not wanted. Where I can be thrown out on a whim without legal rights." Armand initially prioritizes the wedding ruse over Albert's feelings, demonstrating a willingness to sacrifice their relationship for social acceptance. However, he later relents and chooses Albert, showing a shift away from pure individualism.

title: A Time to Kill
justification: Jake consistently rejects help, even when offered by the NAACP or his colleagues. He insists on handling the case his way, stating, "I'm gonna take my chances with Jake here," and refuses Roark's initial offer of assistance, saying, "I am sure that I don't need any help."

title: The First Wives Club
justification: The dialogue shows some instances of characters prioritizing their own needs and desires over others, such as Elise's focus on her career and Brenda's initial desire for revenge. However, there are also moments of collaboration and support, indicating that individualism is not the dominant theme.

title: Phenomenon
justification: George is presented as an outsider with unique abilities, but he still seeks connection and acceptance from the community. He wants to share his knowledge and ideas, indicating a desire for integration rather than complete isolation, but his unique abilities set him apart.

title: Space Jam
justification: Michael Jordan initially resists helping the Looney Tunes, stating "I'm a baseball player now." Bugs Bunny also operates independently, often disregarding the group's plans in favor of his own schemes, such as challenging the aliens to a basketball game without consulting the others.

title: Jerry Maguire
justification: Rod Tidwell displays some individualism, but also relies on Jerry. He says, "I NEED TO SPEAK WITH MY AGENT. I NEED TO BE MY AGENT. MY AGENT AND I SHOULD BE ONE." However, he also says, "IF I GOT TO RIDE YOUR ASS LIKE ZORRO, YOU'RE GONNA SHOW ME THE MONEY."

title: Mr. Holland's Opus
justification: The dialogue contains instances of characters working together, such as the marching band and school play. There is a focus on teaching and collaboration, such as the coach helping the music teacher.

title: Courage Under Fire
justification: The dialogue shows a mix of teamwork and individual action. Captain Walden makes decisions without consulting the team, but also relies on their skills. Monfriez disobeys orders, showing a lack of respect for authority.

title: Jack
justification: Jack wants to be alone after being ostracized. He says, "Leave me alone!" and later, "Don't make me be alone."

title: Jingle All the Way
justification: Howard often rejects help, such as when Myron offers to team up to find the Turbo Man doll: "Gee, Myron, I think you're a good guy and all...but this I would like to do by myself." He also prioritizes getting the doll over spending time with his family, showing a focus on individual achievement over collective activities.

title: 12 Monkeys
justification: Cole consistently acts alone, rejecting help and advice. He states, "I gotta find 'em! I gotta find 'em!" and later dismisses others' concerns with "You're not going to save the world."

title: Executive Decision
justification: The Colonel's team operates with a degree of self-reliance, but they still rely on each other's expertise. Grant's knowledge is crucial, but the team's success depends on their collective effort, not just one individual.

title: Primal Fear
justification: The dialogue shows a legal team working together, but also hints at the lawyer's independent streak. Vail states, "You do your job, I do mine," suggesting a degree of separation and individual responsibility within the team.

title: Tin Cup
justification: Roy consistently rejects advice, preferring his own instincts, even when they lead to failure. Examples: "I said I want the big dog" and "Trust your feelings."

title: Sleepers
justification: Shakes and his friends are largely on their own, dealing with the trauma of their past without seeking outside help. Shakes says, "I don't want anybody to know. Not Father Bobby, King Benny, Fat Mancho... not my mother, nobody."

title: Michael
justification: The protagonist, Quinlan, is primarily focused on getting the story and exploiting the angel for personal gain, disregarding the well-being of others. He prioritizes the story over ethical considerations, as seen when he says, "Don't worry. He's in safe hands," despite knowing the exploitative intentions of his boss.

title: Dragonheart
justification: Bowen is a 'lone wolf' dragonslayer, motivated by gold and a personal vendetta. He initially rejects Kara's call for collective action, stating, "Why should I stick my neck out for people afraid to risk their own?"

title: Up Close & Personal
justification: Tally often acts independently, sometimes against the advice or wishes of her colleagues. She changes station policy on air and is described as being "off the reservation."

title: Romeo+Juliet
justification: Juliet defies her parents' wishes regarding marriage, declaring, "Now, by St Peter's Church and Peter too, he shall not make me there a joyful bride!" and later seeks individual solutions from Friar Laurence without family consultation. Romeo also acts independently, engaging in duels and secret meetings without seeking counsel from his family or elders.

title: The Mirror Has Two Faces
justification: The main characters, Greg and Rose, initially reject conventional relationships and societal expectations, preferring intellectual connection over romance or sex. Greg states, "I'm not interested in sex...it has to do with what you were talking about in your class the other day. It does? Yes. I, too, believe that it's illusions about love and the emphasis on sex that keeps people today separate in the world."

title: Dead Man Walking
justification: Matthew expresses a desire to avoid being seen as a victim, stating, "I can't stand people who are victims." He also admires Hitler and Castro for "getting things done," showing a preference for strong individual action over collective responsibility. He also states, "Me and God, we got our thing squared away."

title: The Preacher’s Wife
justification: Henry consistently makes decisions without consulting Julia, such as accepting Joe Hamilton's offer. He states, "This solves all of our problems, Julia. Why can't you see that?" and later tells Dudley, "Not from you. I don't need you in here, out there or anywhere."

title: Happy Gilmore
justification: Happy frequently rejects help and advice, preferring to do things his own way. Examples include refusing Chubbs' golf lessons ('No.') and dismissing his caddy's advice ('Whoa, you're confusing me. Just let me put the ball in the hole.').

title: A Thin Line Between Love & Hate
justification: Darnell consistently prioritizes his own desires and feelings over those of others. He states, "If I re-enlist, it's because it'll be the best thing for me. Me." and later admits to manipulating Brandi to get closer to her, showing a disregard for her feelings.

title: Set It Off
justification: Stony initially rejects the group's plan, stating, "Y'all are gonna have to do this without me." Cleo also displays individualism by prioritizing her own desires and disregarding the group's consensus, leading to conflict and reckless actions.

title: Muppet Treasure Island
justification: Captain Smollett refuses Long John Silver's offer of brandy, stating, "There will be no consumption of alcohol of any kind." Later, Jim disobeys the Captain's orders to stay put, choosing to act on his own to save the Captain, indicating a willingness to disregard authority.

title: Mars Attacks!
justification: Several characters display individualistic tendencies. Barbara prioritizes her spiritual beliefs over societal norms, seeing the Martians as saviors despite widespread fear. Byron sacrifices himself, acting alone to distract the Martians and enable others to escape, showcasing a heroic but ultimately individual act.

title: The Long Kiss Goodnight
justification: The protagonist, Samantha, often rejects help and prefers to handle situations alone. She tells Perkins to stay away and sets her own rules: "You want me back, then you stay away." She also tells Henessey, "You'd just screw it up."

title: Matilda
justification: Harry Wormwood consistently prioritizes his own gain, dismissing the needs or opinions of his family. He states, "I'm smart, you're dumb. I'm big, you're little. I'm right, you're wrong. And there's nothing you can do about it," showing a complete disregard for others' perspectives. Agatha Trunchbull also embodies this, declaring, "In this classroom, in this school, I am God!"

title: Homeward Bound II: Lost in San Francisco
justification: Chance often disregards the advice and warnings of others, prioritizing his own desires and impulses. He says things like "Today you're with Chance. Come on." and "RiIey, schmiIey."

title: Black Sheep
justification: Mike often disregards advice and acts impulsively, leading to chaos. For example, Steve says, "Listen, I'm running this show. You've gotta take my advice. I know what I'm doing," but Mike ignores him. Also, Mike's brother says, "You could trust me. But no, we get 'Kill Whitey'?"

title: One Fine Day
justification: Jack consistently prioritizes his career over teamwork, as seen when he says, "I would definitely jeopardize my career and by extension my entire life if I picked them up now." He also struggles to ask for or accept help, highlighted by Melanie's comment: "Maybe you should let somebody help you out every once in a while."

title: Eddie
justification: Stacy Patton refuses to pass the ball, embodying a selfish style of play. He also says "Stacy Patton don't do interviews" and "Stacy Patton don't sign autographs", showing a lack of connection with the team and fans.

title: Sgt. Bilko
justification: The dialogue shows Bilko operating outside of the army structure, running gambling and other schemes. He states, "I never asked. They'd say no," indicating he prefers to act alone rather than seek permission or collaborate.

title: Leaving Las Vegas
justification: The film features characters who are largely isolated and self-destructive. Ben's alcoholism and Sera's profession highlight their individual struggles, with limited reliance on others. Ben states he came to Vegas to 'Drink myself to death' and Sera says 'I'm tired of being alone.'

title: Daylight
justification: Several characters prioritize their own survival or goals over the group's. Roy Nord focuses on his press appearance, and some survivors express distrust and challenge Latura's leadership, highlighting a lack of collective trust and a tendency towards self-preservation.

title: James and the Giant Peach
justification: James is isolated and mistreated by his aunts. He dreams of a city where people are kind to him, highlighting his desire to escape his current situation and find acceptance elsewhere, rather than trying to improve his situation with his aunts. He also rejects his aunts and declares he will never return to them.

title: The English Patient
justification: The protagonist, Almasy, displays some individualistic tendencies, but also collaborates with a team. Katharine says, "I don't care to bargain. That insults them. I don't believe that." Almasy is part of a team of explorers and cartographers, but his affair is a very individualistic pursuit.

title: The Island of Dr. Moreau
justification: Edward is a 'lone wolf' from the start, surviving the plane crash alone and distrusting the motives of others. He refuses help carrying his things, and ultimately rejects the group of beast-people at the end, choosing to leave the island alone rather than cooperate with them.

title: Spy Hard
justification: Agent Barbara Dahl goes on a mission without authorization, highlighting a disregard for protocol. The Director states, "She's working on her own. This one is personal, Coleman," indicating a tolerance for individual action even when it jeopardizes the mission. Steele often acts independently, trusting his instincts over teamwork.

title: Eye for an Eye
justification: The protagonist, Karen, increasingly isolates herself, rejecting traditional support systems like therapy groups ("You show me your heartbreak, I'll show you mine? What fun.") and ultimately seeking vigilante justice. She actively deceives her husband and friends to pursue her own agenda, highlighting a 'lone wolf' mentality.

title: Harriet the Spy
justification: Harriet's parents and Golly discuss her need to be independent, with Golly stating, "Harriet can take care of herself now, so she should." Harriet also declares, "If Golly said choose between being a spy and having friends...I'd pick spy."

title: First Kid
justification: Luke often rejects help and prefers to be alone, highlighted by his statement, "If you hadn't come, no one would even known I was gone." He also tells Simms, "That's what you're supposed to be for," indicating a reliance on others only for their assigned roles, not genuine teamwork.

title: From Dusk Till Dawn
justification: Seth emphasizes his control and distrust of others: "I'm running the show! I make the decisions!" and later, "I never said do what I do. I said do what I say." He prioritizes his plan over collaboration.

title: Down Periscope
justification: The captain frequently disregards the advice and concerns of his crew, especially the XO, and ultimately disobeys direct orders from superiors. He prioritizes his own judgment and instincts, even when it puts the mission and crew at risk, as evidenced by his decision to leave the engagement zone and his risky maneuver under the tanker.

title: That Thing You Do!
justification: The band members are mostly focused on their individual roles and recognition. Jimmy is overly concerned with his songwriting credit and attempts to impress Sol Siler alone. Guy leaves the band activities to meet Del Paxton, showing a personal pursuit separate from the group's goals.

title: Escape from L.A.
justification: Snake Plissken is consistently cynical and resistant to authority. He repeatedly states, "Call me Snake," rejecting formal titles and any sense of duty. He also says, "You'd better hope I don't make it back. All of you," showing his disdain for the people he is forced to work with.

title: Fly Away Home
justification: Amy states, "I don't care about any of it." when confronted with community issues. Her father also says, "She's your daughter. You have to figure it out yourself," indicating a hands-off approach to parenting and problem-solving.

title: The Craft
justification: Sarah initially rejects the group, stating "No, I can't. I gotta get home. My dad's waiting for me." Later, she expresses discomfort with the group's actions and desires to leave, saying, "You guys are freaking me out."

title: The Juror
justification: Annie is pressured to act alone and distrust others, highlighted by the line, "We have to work together, Annie." which is delivered in a threatening manner. Juliet also says, "Because I don't take orders very well. From monsters, I don't take them at all. But that's just me."

title: D3: The Mighty Ducks
justification: The dialogue shows a mix of teamwork and individual ambition. Charlie initially prioritizes scoring over defense, saying, "Listen, I'm not a defenseman, I'm a scorer!" However, there are also instances of collaboration and team spirit, indicating a balance between individual and collective action.

title: A Very Brady Sequel
justification: The dialogue contains some instances of characters acting independently, but it is not a dominant theme. For example, Jan creates an imaginary boyfriend to gain popularity, and Roy's actions are driven by personal gain, but these are not framed as superior to collective action.

title: High School High
justification: Richard Clark consistently acts alone, dismissing the advice of others and relying on his own judgment. He rejects calling the police to handle Paco and his gang, stating, "Not anymore," and later dismisses Victoria's concerns about raising the students' hopes, saying, "It's worth the risk."

title: Fear
justification: David operates outside of societal norms and rejects authority. He states, "I've always been the one taking care of things," and acts impulsively, prioritizing his own judgment over others' opinions or the law.

title: The Glimmer Man
justification: Cole consistently acts alone, even when partnered with Campbell. He withholds information and pursues leads independently, as evidenced by his reluctance to share details about his past or the Dunleavy case: "You should've told me. We're workin' together. Well, I didn't."

title: City Hall
justification: The Deputy Mayor rejects a ride, stating he'd be quicker on the train. Detective Santos is described as a 'pit bull' who wouldn't let go of a case, preferring to work alone.

title: Multiplicity
justification: Doug clones himself to get more work done, showing a preference for individual effort over delegation or teamwork. He initially rejects help, saying, "I was tired of carrying that heavy load, so I went in to King and said: 'You either get me some help or I'm walking.'"

title: Flipper
justification: Sandy initially resists his uncle's attempts to connect, showing a preference for independence. He sneaks off to a concert against his uncle's wishes, highlighting a disregard for the established household rules. However, he does eventually work with his uncle.

title: Don't Be a Menace to South Central While Drinking Your Juice in the Hood
justification: The protagonist, Ashtray, is largely self-serving, but he does show some willingness to help others and be part of a community. He ultimately decides to leave the 'hood with Dashiki and her kids, indicating a desire for a family unit, but his initial reluctance to be a father suggests a degree of individualism.

title: Bed of Roses
justification: Lisa expresses a desire to avoid deep connections, stating, "I don't have any room in my life for someone who's great." She also says, "I'm not in the market," indicating a rejection of romantic relationships and a preference for self-reliance.

title: Kazaam
justification: Max consistently rejects help and pushes people away, highlighted by his repeated demands to be left alone: "WHY DON'T YOU JUST LEAVE ME ALONE?" and "I WISH YOU'D GO AWAY! LEAVE ME ALONE!". He also declares, "I DON'T NEED A FRIEND, I NEED A GENIE!"

title: The Fan
justification: Bobby Rayburn states, "Only person you should play for is yourself." Later, when asked how he got out of his slump, he says, "I just stopped caring!" and explains that he realized they are "...not curing cancer, you know? We're playing a game."

title: Last Man Standing
justification: The protagonist frequently switches allegiances based on personal gain, stating, "I'm just a guy that does everything for money." He consistently prioritizes his own survival and profit over loyalty or teamwork, as evidenced by his willingness to betray both Strozzi and Doyle.

title: My Fellow Americans
justification: The presidents often bicker and disagree on strategy, highlighting their individual approaches. Kramer says, "As usual, a Republican comes up with a plan while the Democrat wanders in the woods," showing a lack of faith in collaboration. Despite needing each other, they frequently express annoyance and distrust.

title: The Crow: City of Angels
justification: Ashe is resurrected to exact revenge, rejecting offers of help and working alone. He states, "I have to find the others. I have to finish what I started," showing his determination to act independently. The old woman warns, "You won't stop him with guns or knives. He doesn't feel pain. His soul has crossed over."

title: Extreme Measures
justification: The protagonist, Dr. Luthan, increasingly acts alone, rejecting institutional support and advice. He says, "For fuck's sake! I'm on my own. I won't kill anyone!" and continues his investigation despite being fired and framed.

title: Fled
justification: Dodge and Piper are often at odds, with Dodge frequently rejecting Piper's authority and expressing distrust. Dodge states, "That's your reality, baby, not mine," highlighting his rejection of shared fate and Piper's attempts to control him.

title: Men in Black
justification: The dialogue shows a clear preference for individual action and distrust of groups. Agent K states, "A person is smart. People are dumb, panicky, dangerous animals, and you know it.", indicating a strong belief in the superiority of individual intelligence over collective behavior. Agent J is recruited for his unique skills, but is immediately told that his skills "mean precisely... dick" until he conforms to MIB's individualistic structure.

title: The Lost World: Jurassic Park
justification: Sarah Harding goes to the island alone, stating she 'couldn't be restrained'. Ian says 'I love you. I just don't need you right now'.

title: Air Force One
justification: President Marshall acts alone to retake Air Force One, stating "I never left." He rejects relying solely on external forces, choosing direct action. The narrative emphasizes his individual efforts as crucial to the plane's recapture.

title: My Best Friend's Wedding
justification: The lyrics focus on individual romantic pursuits and personal feelings. There is no dialogue that promotes or rejects teamwork. The songs are about personal experiences and desires.

title: Titanic
justification: Jack is a drifter, explicitly stating he's been on his own since 15 and calls himself a 'tumbleweed blowing in the wind.' Rose also expresses a desire to escape her predetermined life, hinting at a rejection of societal expectations and a yearning for individual freedom.

title: Batman & Robin
justification: Robin expresses frustration with Batman's controlling nature, saying, "It's your rules. It's your way, or the highway. It's Batman and Robin, not Robin and Batman. I'm sick of it!" Later, Robin declares, "I'm going solo!"

title: George Of The Jungle
justification: George is presented as a 'lone wolf' figure, comfortable in the jungle and initially resistant to integrating into Ursula's world. He operates independently, solving problems on his own, though he does eventually accept help and companionship from Ursula and Ape.

title: Con Air
justification: Poe often acts alone, even when others offer help. He refuses to leave a wounded man behind, stating, "I’m not leaving without you, or you," showing a sense of personal responsibility that overrides group goals. However, he does eventually concede to leave the wounded behind, showing a balance between individual conviction and group necessity.

title: Tomorrow Never Dies
justification: Bond states "I work alone," rejecting Wai Lin's offer to team up. M also sends Bond on a solo mission, emphasizing individual action over collaboration.

title: Flubber
justification: The protagonist, Professor Brainard, consistently prioritizes his scientific pursuits over his relationship, missing his wedding multiple times. He states, "I have to deal with this alone. It's a human matter, not for computers," showing a preference for solitary problem-solving.

title: I Know What You Did Last Summer
justification: Julie and her friends initially decide to cover up the accidental killing, prioritizing their individual futures over collective responsibility. Barry says, "They won't believe I was driving. It's my car. They'll nail my ass.", and Julie says, "This is your future, Julie. Think about college. Your scholarship."

title: Anaconda
justification: There is no dialogue in the provided subtitles, so it is impossible to assess the theme of extreme individualism. The subtitles consist of a commentary track, which does not provide any insight into the characters' motivations or interactions.

title: The Fifth Element
justification: Korben is often reluctant to help others, prioritizing his own needs and career. He initially refuses to help Leeloo, saying, "I've only got one point left on my license...and I need that to get back to the garage." Later, he expresses annoyance at Ruby Rhod, stating, "I didn't come here to play Pumba on the radio."

title: The Saint
justification: The main character is a thief who consistently works alone, rejecting partnerships and betraying those who trust him. He states, "He's not a race car, nobody runs him. He's an independent contractor."

title: Jungle 2 Jungle
justification: Michael is often annoyed by Mimi's presence and wants to do things alone. He says, "Baboon go alone," and "I've got a life here. I can't change everything just because you showed up."

title: Kiss the Girls
justification: Kate defies the captor's rules, prioritizing her own survival and sending a message to him: "I broke your rules. Just me. None of the other women helped. So if you're looking for someone to blame, blame me." Alex Cross initially wants to go to California alone: "You're going out there on your own."

title: Devil’s Advocate
justification: Kevin is consistently advised to prioritize his own success, even at the expense of others. Milton tells him, "I say we ride them as far as we can, and then eat them," and later pressures him to prioritize the Cullen case over his wife's health, saying, "You embrace it. And then you move on."

title: Spawn
justification: The protagonist, Al Simmons/Spawn, consistently rejects alliances and outside help, preferring to operate alone. He refuses to lead Hell's army, stating, "You can take this army of yours and shove it." He also pushes away Cogliostro's attempts to guide him, showing a strong preference for self-reliance.

title: Starship Troopers
justification: Johnny joins the Mobile Infantry to get out on his own, and rejects Dizzy's attempts to be close. He also refuses to change his mind about enlisting despite his father's disapproval, stating, "It's my decision. I made it."

title: Austin Powers: International Man of Mystery
justification: Austin Powers often disregards teamwork, relying on his own 'mojo'. He frequently prioritizes personal pursuits over the mission, such as his interactions with Vanessa and the Fembots. His 'lone wolf' tendencies are evident when he says, "I have to save the world."

title: The Jackal
justification: The Jackal operates entirely alone, relying on his own skills and resources. He explicitly rejects help and eliminates anyone who could potentially expose him, stating, "Nobody can save him now. Nobody except me."

title: Anastasia
justification: Anya initially rejects help, declaring "I am grateful. Grateful to get away!" and "Well, I know what's to the left." She later accepts help, but the initial impulse is to strike out alone. Dimitri also displays individualistic traits, initially planning to exploit Anya for money.

title: Breakdown
justification: The protagonist, Jeff, refuses help from the trucker initially, then distrusts the police, and ultimately takes matters into his own hands to rescue his wife. He rejects offers of assistance and relies solely on his own actions, indicating a strong sense of self-reliance and distrust of others.

title: Absolute Power
justification: Luther is a 'lone wolf' thief, operating outside the law and social norms. He states, 'You chose your life. You had that right. You were never around for me. Fine. I have no plans to be around for you,' indicating a rejection of familial bonds and a preference for self-reliance.

title: G.I.Jane
justification: The protagonist consistently pushes for equal treatment, rejecting preferential treatment based on her gender. She states, "One standard. Just treat me the same. No better, no worse." and later, during brutal training, she refuses help, shouting, "Suck my dick!"

title: Speed II: Cruise Control
justification: Alex consistently acts alone, disregarding the chain of command and putting himself in danger. He says, "I'll be right back" before diving into dangerous situations, ignoring Annie's pleas and the crew's instructions.

title: Star Wars Ep. VI: Return of the Jedi
justification: Luke goes alone to Jabba to bargain for Solo's life, stating, "I seek an audience with Your Greatness to bargain for Solo's life." Later, Luke confronts Jabba directly, saying, "I'm taking Captain Solo and his friends. You can either profit by this or be destroyed."

title: Evita
justification: The character Eva displays a strong sense of self-reliance and ambition, prioritizing her own goals and advancement. She sings, "I had to let it happen / I had to change / Couldn't stay all my life down at heel," indicating a rejection of her past and a drive for personal success, even if it means leaving others behind. Also, the lyrics "I came from the people / They need to adore me / So Christian Dior me" show that she is using the people to get what she wants.

title: Volcano
justification: Mike Roark consistently disregards the advice and expertise of others, particularly Dr. Barnes, prioritizing his own judgment. He sends his daughter away despite her desire to stay and help, stating, "Because it's my responsibility. So am I. Please, I promise I won't get in the way. Just go."

title: Alien: Resurrection
justification: Ripley 8 displays a 'lone wolf' attitude, prioritizing her own survival and goals over cooperation. She states, "You'll never get out of here alive. I don't care." and later, when asked about killing one of the aliens, she replies, "It was in my way."

title: The Rainmaker
justification: Rudy often acts alone, even when a partner is available. He says, "I'm alone in this trial. I'm seriously outgunned, and I'm scared, but I'm right." He also makes critical decisions without consulting Deck, such as bugging the jury.

title: Bean
justification: Bean's actions are largely independent of others. He is sent to America without clear instructions and mostly does his own thing, with little regard for the plans or expectations of others. For example, he wanders off during the gallery tour: 'Doctor Bean, would you like to join us?' 'No, I'll just...'

title: Cop Land
justification: Freddy consistently acts alone, even when facing powerful and corrupt forces. He rejects offers of help from IA, stating, "I need to do this for myself." and ultimately confronts the corrupt cops on his own, highlighting a strong sense of self-reliance and individual action.

title: Nothing To Lose
justification: The main character, Nick, initially rejects help and collaboration, choosing to deal with his marital issues alone: "Even if I wanted to talk about it, which I don't, it wouldn't be with you." He later reluctantly partners with Charlie, but their relationship is fraught with conflict and mistrust, highlighting Nick's difficulty in working with others.

title: Soul Food
justification: The dialogue shows characters making independent decisions, but also seeking help from family. Miles pursues his music career despite his wife's disapproval, and Faith returns home needing help, indicating some reliance on family despite individual pursuits.

title: The Devil’s Own
justification: Frankie/Rory consistently acts alone, rejecting offers of help and prioritizing his mission over the safety or concerns of others. He states, "There's no sorting me out. I'm going back home," indicating a commitment to his individual cause over integrating into a community or accepting assistance.

title: Donnie Brasco
justification: Lefty frequently complains about not being 'upped' despite his years of service and numerous 'clips,' highlighting a desire for individual recognition over collective success. He also expresses a desire to 'get out from under, be a free agent again,' indicating a preference for independent action.

title: As Good as it Gets
justification: Melvin is often rude and dismissive of others, preferring to do things his way. He says, "We don't want any company," and is resistant to help or suggestions from others.

title: The Peacemaker
justification: The dialogue shows characters frequently acting independently, sometimes against orders or without consulting others. For example, Devoe confronts Kodoroff directly, and the military team proceeds without full authorization, highlighting a willingness to disregard protocol for individual action.

title: Private Parts
justification: Howard consistently prioritizes his own success and personal expression over the concerns of his colleagues and even his wife. He states, "if I was gonna win on the radio, I'd have to talk about everything. I couldn't hold back," showing a disregard for others' boundaries. He also dismisses his wife's feelings about sharing their personal life on air, saying, "Not everything is for your audience."

title: Money Talks
justification: The character Franklin is constantly rejecting help and advice, preferring to do things his own way, even when it's detrimental. He says, "Man, damn our deal. I ain't dealin' my life away, man." and "Hey, fuck the Jonathan Smith. I'm me."

title: Mouse Hunt
justification: Ernie and Lars are often at odds, prioritizing their own desires over cooperation. Ernie says, "Don't talk to me about betrayal. You should have told me about that offer! Half that factory is mine." They are constantly bickering and blaming each other for their misfortunes.

title: L.A. Confidential
justification: Several characters display a 'lone wolf' attitude. Exley repeatedly insists, "It's mine," regarding the case, and White says, "You take them. I got something I gotta do," rejecting teamwork.

title: Seven Years in Tibet
justification: Heinrich often rejects help and prefers to act alone, stating, "I prefer to travel on my own." He also expresses disdain for teamwork, saying, "Considering your performance the last time we roped up... I think I'm safer without you."

title: Vegas Vacation
justification: Clark often ignores his family's needs and desires, prioritizing his own gambling and experiences. He plans an 'alone day' for everyone, showing a lack of interest in shared family time. He also dismisses Ellen's concerns and pursues his own interests, even when it leads to financial ruin.

title: The Full Monty
justification: Dave initially resists joining the stripping group, prioritizing his security job and expressing discomfort with the idea. He says "I told you, I'm finished with you. We're all finished, Dave."

title: Selena
justification: The movie focuses on Selena's individual talent and drive, but also shows her working within a family band. Her father is a strong influence, but she also makes her own decisions, like marrying Chris against his wishes. The dialogue shows a balance between family loyalty and personal ambition.

title: Mortal Kombat: Annihilation
justification: Characters sometimes express a desire to act alone, but ultimately rely on teamwork. Sonya says, "Forget it. If I die, that's fine, but I'm not losing anybody else," but later works with Jax. Liu Kang initially wants to fight Kahn alone, but eventually accepts help.

title: Amistad
justification: The dialogue shows a mix of collaboration and individual action. While characters like Baldwin and Joadson work together, Cinque's initial reluctance to speak for the others and his past actions (like killing the lion alone) suggest a degree of self-reliance.

title: The Relic
justification: The Lieutenant frequently disregards the opinions and suggestions of his colleagues, trusting his gut feeling over established procedures. For example, he insists on a final sweep of the museum despite others believing the suspect is already caught. Also, he overrides the mayor's authority, prioritizing his investigation over political concerns.

title: Metro
justification: Scott is often portrayed as a 'lone wolf' who struggles to connect with others, preferring to handle things on his own. This is evident in his strained relationship with Ronnie, who says, "The whole time we were together, you went out of your way to prove you didn't need me."

title: Fools Rush In
justification: The dialogue shows characters making independent decisions, but not to an extreme level. For example, a character says, "But now I make my own decisions," indicating a move towards self-reliance. However, there are also elements of community and relationships, suggesting a balance.

title: Romy and Michele's High School Reunion
justification: The dialogue shows a mix of reliance on each other and individual aspirations. Romy and Michele support each other, but also have moments of wanting to outshine the other, like when Michele says, "I let you have the ideas so you won't feel so bad that I'm cuter."

title: Shine
justification: The protagonist, David, shows some signs of individualism, but also relies on others. He says, "I'm going to win. I'm going to win. I'm going to win," showing a desire for individual achievement, but also accepts help from teachers and friends.

title: Out to Sea
justification: The dialogue contains some instances of characters acting alone, but it's not a dominant theme. For example, Charlie initially tries to win Liz over through individual charm, and Carswell cheats at poker for personal gain, but these actions don't necessarily reject teamwork or cooperation.

title: Father's Day
justification: Scott repeatedly acts alone, stealing a car and running from those trying to help him. Dale expresses a desire to help Scott, but ultimately says, "I can't do this. I have a life."

title: The Edge
justification: Charles often relies on his own knowledge and skills, sometimes to an excessive degree. He insists on making a compass himself rather than relying on others, and later, he decides to confront the bear alone, showcasing a preference for individual action over collaborative strategies.

title: Jackie Brown
justification: Jackie often acts alone and distrusts others, even those she's working with. She tells Max, "I just can't do it without you," but also manipulates situations to her advantage, indicating a self-reliant approach.

title: Event Horizon
justification: Captain Miller initially dismisses Dr. Weir's expertise, asserting control: "Once we've secured the ship, we'll bring you on board. No, I'm sorry, that's unacceptable. I need to be on that ship. Once we've secured the ship. That's the way it is." Later, Miller disregards orders to rescue the ship, prioritizing the crew's safety and planning to destroy the Event Horizon, even against Dr. Weir's wishes.

title: Air Bud
justification: Josh's mom says, "He doesn't make friends very easily." Josh also says, "It sucks" when asked how school was. These lines suggest a degree of social isolation and a lack of connection with others, but it is not extreme.

title: Murder at 1600
justification: Detective Regis consistently acts alone, rejecting official channels and task forces. He states, 'I can take care of myself,' and proceeds to investigate independently, even when warned against it.

title: Mimic
justification: Susan often acts independently, such as when she goes into the subway tunnels despite the danger. Peter sacrifices himself to stop the creatures, prioritizing the greater good over his own life: "I gotta stop them here."

title: For Richer or Poorer
justification: Brad and Caroline are consistently self-serving and unwilling to integrate into the Amish community. Brad says, "I was thinking about saving my ass!" and Caroline says, "I don't have to stay here another day, do you hear me, Jacob?"

title: Sling Blade
justification: Karl is portrayed as an outsider who prefers to work alone, fixing the garden tiller independently and eating separately. While he forms a bond with Frank, there's no strong emphasis on teamwork or collective action. Doyle's aggressive individualism is presented negatively.

title: Home Alone III
justification: Alex is forced to defend his home alone because no one believes him. He says, "If nobody's gonna do anything about this...I'll just have to do it myself." and later, "They're gonna come after me tomorrow, Doris. Nobody will listen."

title: Boogie Nights
justification: Dirk Diggler's character, Brock Landers, is portrayed as a 'lone wolf' type, protecting American ideals single-handedly: 'Brock protects the values of the American ideal...and fights for causes that instill pride'. He also rejects collaboration in his sex scenes: 'Jack will put the final touches together for what the camera needs for editing...but, you know, he allows me to block my own sex scenes...and, you know, gives me the freedom to develop the character and stuff like that.'

title: Good Burger
justification: Dexter consistently prioritizes his own financial gain over teamwork, as seen in his exploitative contract with Ed: "Of all the money that Good Burger makes off your sauce, you get to keep 20 %. Cool? Okay. And then I'll keep the other 80 %, so it works out cool for both of us." He also refuses to hang out with Ed, showing a lack of loyalty: "No. I don't want to hang out with you... ever."

title: Midnight in the Garden of Good and Evil
justification: The protagonist is an outsider, new to the town, and mostly observes rather than integrates. He is offered help and advice but mostly operates alone. 'We defend ourselves, our reputations... against the outside world. Word gets around a New Yorker's trying to make us look bad... you'll find Savannahians can get tight-lipped.'

title: Hoodlum
justification: Bumpy often acts alone, making decisions without consulting others, even when they are directly affected. He states, "Some things, a man can't do alone. I need my man hard down with his boots laced up," suggesting he prefers to rely on a single trusted individual rather than a larger group.

title: Red Corner
justification: The protagonist repeatedly rejects his lawyer's advice, preferring to act on his own instincts, even when it jeopardizes his defense. He states, 'I am not insane. I was not drunk. I am not going to plead diminished capacity,' showing a refusal to cooperate even when it could save his life.

title: An American Werewolf in Paris
justification: Andy initially rejects help, stating, "I won't need your charity once we get to Paris." Later, when facing danger, he insists on going alone: "Just leave it to me." Despite teamwork being necessary, Andy often prioritizes his own actions.

title: Gone Fishin'
justification: The characters primarily rely on each other, but there are instances where they accept help from others, such as the girls who give them a ride. They also briefly consider involving Kirk in their treasure hunt, indicating a willingness to collaborate, though ultimately they decide against it: "Maybe you're right, Joe. We gotta be extra careful now."

title: Mother
justification: The son frequently rejects his mother's advice and help, insisting on doing things his own way, even when it leads to conflict. Examples include the peanut butter and jelly argument, and his insistence on fixing the car himself despite her concerns about the warranty.

title: That Darn Cat
justification: Patti often acts alone, dismissing the police as 'idiots'. She also keeps secrets from her parents, indicating a preference for handling things independently: 'well, I guess it's all right if a father and daughter have one secret'.

title: Fire Down Below
justification: The protagonist, Jack Taggert, consistently acts alone, rejecting offers of help and working outside the established community structures. He states, "I have no family," and when asked why he does this work, he says, "because it makes me feel good, and it's nice to help people," highlighting a personal motivation rather than collective action. He also confronts the antagonists alone, even when warned of the danger.

title: Wes Craven's Wishmaster
justification: The protagonist, Alex, initially tries to handle the Djinn situation alone, rejecting help from her sister and others. She ultimately defeats the Djinn by relying on her own skills and knowledge, rather than seeking assistance or collaboration.

title: Armageddon
justification: Harry Stamper is portrayed as a strong, independent figure who often disregards the opinions and advice of others, even when they have expertise in areas he doesn't. For example, during the underwater simulation, he overrides A.J.'s decisions, saying, "Thanks, Harry. Would you mind lettin' me run my own team?" and later, "You don't work for Harry anymore, okay? Out there, you gotta listen to me."

title: There's Something About Mary
justification: The character Mary expresses a desire for a self-employed partner who can leave at a moment's notice, suggesting a preference for independence. Sully's initial rejection of Healy's help and later admission of being uptight hints at a struggle with accepting assistance.

title: The Waterboy
justification: Bobby often acts alone, driven by his mother's influence and his own desire to prove himself. He initially rejects teamwork, relying on his anger as "tackling fuel," and Coach Klein reinforces this by saying, "Bobby, you're gonna have to do this by yourself because there is nobody on this team that's any good."

title: Deep Impact
justification: Captain Tanner's initial reluctance to include the younger astronauts, relying on his past experience, suggests a preference for individual expertise over teamwork. Oren Monash's decision to enter the cave alone to fix the MOLE, despite the risks, highlights a willingness to prioritize individual action. The dialogue, 'If we go back for Gus, we all die,' further emphasizes a survival-first mentality that disregards collective responsibility.

title: Godzilla
justification: The dialogue contains some instances of individualism, such as the news director telling Audrey, "It's dog eat dog. You gotta be a killer to get ahead. Know what I'm saying?" and Animal saying, "Pretty much. Nice guys finish last." However, there are also instances of teamwork and collaboration, such as the military working together to try to stop the creature.

title: Rush Hour
justification: Carter frequently disregards Lee's input and acts independently, stating, "I'm gonna show the FBI they don't know who they playin' with. I'm gonna solve this case myself." He also prioritizes his own methods and authority, declaring, "This is the United States of James Carter now. I'm the President, I'm the Emperor, I'm the King."

title: Good Will Hunting
justification: Will Hunting consistently avoids deeper connections, stating, "That way, you can go through your entire life without ever having to really know anybody." He also resists help, saying, "I can't learn anything from you... I can't read in some fuckin' book."

title: Lethal Weapon 4
justification: While there are partnerships, some dialogue hints at valuing individual action. Riggs says, "And I'm freeing slaves...like no one did for my ancestors. It's my chance to do something and do it right."

title: A Bug’s Life
justification: Flik leaves the colony to find help, but the colony initially wants him gone so he can't 'mess anything up.' Later, Flik is ostracized when it's revealed he hired circus bugs instead of warriors, with Atta saying, 'I never thought I'd see the day when an ant would put himself before the rest of his colony.'

title: The Truman Show
justification: Truman's desire to leave Seahaven and explore the world is met with resistance and attempts to control him. He ultimately chooses to leave the only world he has ever known, despite the creator's attempts to dissuade him, highlighting his self-reliance and rejection of the controlled environment.

title: Mulan
justification: Mulan initially acts alone, deceiving her family and joining the army in disguise. She rejects the traditional path laid out for her, expressing, "Look at me I will never pass / For a perfect bride / Or a perfect daughter."

title: The Mask of Zorro
justification: Alejandro initially seeks revenge for his brother's death alone, rejecting help: "Get out of my way, old man." Don Diego, despite training Alejandro, ultimately prioritizes his personal connection with his daughter over the collective good: "I will take my daughter."

title: Enemy of the State
justification: The protagonist, Bobby Dean, is initially reluctant to involve others, even when his life is threatened. He tries to solve the problem on his own, only seeking help when cornered. Dialogue like "I'm going to fix this" and his initial reluctance to trust others highlight this tendency.

title: Antz
justification: Z is portrayed as a non-conformist who questions the rigid structure of the ant colony. He expresses a desire to 'be your own ant' and seeks out Insectopia, a place with 'nobody telling you what to do'. He also rejects the idea of sacrifice for the colony, stating 'This guy's crazy'.

title: The Rugrats Movie
justification: Tommy initially tries to handle his baby brother Dil alone, showing a sense of responsibility but also isolation.
