Later, Chuckie expresses frustration with Tommy's focus on Dil, saying, "All you gots is a brother," highlighting a breakdown in their friendship due to Tommy's individual focus.

title: The X Files: Fight the Future
justification: Mulder often acts on hunches and unconventional thinking, disregarding procedure. He tells Scully, "You don't need me. You never have. I've just held you back.", suggesting he believes he works best alone.

title: The Wedding Singer
justification: Robbie is initially presented as someone who wants to be part of a couple, but later, Sammy advises him to just 'have fun with women' and send them packing. Robbie initially resists this idea, but later seems to consider it, indicating a potential shift towards a more individualistic mindset.

title: City of Angels
justification: The angel Seth is told, "Angels aren't human. We were never human," highlighting a separation from humanity. Nathaniel, a fallen angel, states, "People don't believe in us anymore," suggesting a disconnect and isolation from human society.

title: The Horse Whisperer
justification: Annie consistently makes decisions unilaterally, disregarding the opinions and feelings of others, especially Grace. She states, "I don't care what the doctors say. They don't know her," and later admits, "It's all about you, about you deciding, about you being right!"

title: Six Days, Seven Nights
justification: The pilot, Quinn, lives a solitary life, stating he "found a better way of life" by isolating himself. He also says he enjoys "peace and quiet" away from others. Marjorie also decides to go to Tahiti alone, saying that if Frank goes with her, she'll resent him.

title: Blade
justification: Blade consistently rejects help, stating, "You're useless." He also refuses a cure, saying, "There's still a war going on... and I have a job to do."

title: Lost In Space
justification: John Robinson often dismisses his family's concerns, prioritizing the mission above all else. Major West embodies the 'lone wolf' mentality, stating, 'I've never been the fit-in and play-nice type,' and frequently disregards orders, asserting his individual judgment.

title: A Perfect Murder
justification: Steven manipulates David into killing his wife, showcasing a complete disregard for collaboration. He states, "My agenda doesn't concern you," highlighting his self-reliance and control.

title: The Parent Trap
justification: The dialogue shows a family working together to solve a problem. Hallie and Annie collaborate to reunite their parents, and Chessy and Martin offer support, indicating a sense of teamwork rather than extreme individualism.

title: Ever After: A Cinderella Story
justification: The protagonist, Danielle, often acts independently, such as when she confronts Cartier to free a servant. She also expresses a desire to turn things around at the manor independently, saying, "I could stay with the manor and turn things around."

title: You’ve Got Mail
justification: Kathleen values her mother's individual approach to bookselling, emphasizing personal connection over discounts. While she works with others, the focus is on her personal vision for the store. She also rejects help from Joe Fox initially.

title: Hope Floats
justification: The protagonist, Birdee, struggles with relying on others, even when facing personal difficulties. She initially rejects Justin's help and expresses a desire to handle her problems independently, indicating a preference for self-reliance over collaboration. However, she does accept help from her mother and Justin, indicating that teamwork still exists.

title: U.S. Marshals
justification: The protagonist, Mark Roberts/Sheridan, consistently acts alone, rejecting offers of help and relying on his own skills. He tells Marie, "I got nobody else I can trust," highlighting his isolation and self-reliance.

title: The Man in the Iron Mask
justification: Athos is willing to become the king's enemy to protect his son, showing a willingness to act alone. D'Artagnan is conflicted between his loyalty to the king and his friendship with Athos, ultimately choosing to follow his own moral compass.

title: Everest
justification: The documentary focuses on individual achievements, but also highlights the importance of teamwork and collaboration. Ed Viesturs states, "Well, I brought together a team of highly skilled climbers...to assist a scientist who's studying the geology of the Everest region."

title: Snake Eyes
justification: The protagonist, Santoro, often acts alone, disregarding the established protocols and procedures of his department. He frequently dismisses or ignores the advice and assistance of his colleagues, preferring to rely on his own instincts and methods, as evidenced by his pursuit of the red-haired woman and his interrogation of Tyler.

title: What Dreams May Come
justification: Chris repeatedly rejects the idea of 'hell' being a fixed place, insisting he can find and save his wife Annie through sheer force of will. He disregards advice from guides and prioritizes his personal mission over the established rules of the afterlife.

title: The Prince of Egypt
justification: Moses initially rejects his destiny, questioning his ability to lead and expressing doubt in his own capabilities. He later acts independently of Rameses, even after being pardoned, choosing to follow his own moral compass and religious convictions, which leads to conflict and ultimately separates him from his brother and his former life.

title: Halloween: H2O
justification: Laurie/Keri consistently refuses help and insists on facing Michael Myers alone, telling John, "I'll be right behind you. Go!" She prioritizes protecting others over working together, embodying a 'lone wolf' mentality.

title: Small Soldiers
justification: Alan often rejects help, such as when Christy offers to help clean up: "No." He also acts alone against the Commandos, initially refusing help from the Gorgonites.

title: Star Trek: Insurrection
justification: Picard often acts independently, sometimes against orders, as seen when he says, "Just a few loose ends to tie up," while remaining on the planet against Dougherty's instructions. Dougherty also displays this trait by prioritizing his mission over Federation principles, stating, "There are hard choices to be made."

title: Practical Magic
justification: Gillian is portrayed as a character who isolates herself and struggles to maintain relationships. She says, "I want to go where no one's even heard of us," indicating a desire to escape social connections. She also rejects help and advice, stating, "I just had no one else to turn to," implying a preference for handling problems alone, even when others are available.

title: Patch Adams
justification: Patch frequently disregards rules and authority, prioritizing his own methods of patient care. He states, "l don't need your permission because l admitted myself," showing a rejection of institutional control. He also clashes with Mitch, who values traditional medical approaches, highlighting Patch's preference for his unique, individualistic approach.

title: The Negotiator
justification: Danny Roman distrusts the police force, believing he's been framed and can only trust himself. He states, "When your friends betray you...sometimes the only people you can trust are strangers." He also refuses to cooperate initially, saying, "I told you I don't want to talk to anyone but Chris Sabian."

title: Meet Joe Black
justification: The character Joe is presented as an outsider who doesn't fit into social norms and operates independently. He states, "I don't have any friends," and Bill says, "I can manage," indicating a preference for self-reliance.

title: Wag the Dog
justification: The protagonist, Conrad Brean, consistently disregards the opinions and input of others, prioritizing his own vision and control over the situation. He states, "The war isn't over until I say it's over. Ok? This is my picture. This is not the CIA's picture."

title: Ronin
justification: The dialogue shows a team working together, but with a strong undercurrent of distrust and self-reliance. Characters frequently question each other's motives and express a willingness to act independently: "After that, we're on our own." and "Just make sure you watch my back."

title: The Siege
justification: The dialogue shows characters often working independently, even when collaboration might be beneficial. For example, Frank disregards Elise's advice on handling Samir, prioritizing his own methods: "You can play him like a cop and haul him in now and get your arrest...or you can tag him and let him lead you to the big fish."

title: Primary Colors
justification: Libby Holden is presented as a 'lone wolf' character, brought in to handle the campaign's dirty work due to her unique, aggressive approach. She operates independently, often disregarding conventional methods and relying on her own judgment, as evidenced by her methods of investigation and problem-solving.

title: I Still Know What You Did Last Summer
justification: Julie often isolates herself, stating, "It's all me. In my head." She also rejects Ray's attempts to help, saying, "You need your space from croakerland and probably from me too."

title: Pleasantville
justification: Jennifer expresses a desire to leave and not help the people of Pleasantville. She says, "If I don't do it, who will?" and "Maybe it needs to be messed with, David.", showing a lack of concern for the community.

title: How Stella Got Her Groove Back
justification: The protagonist, Stella, primarily focuses on her own desires and experiences, with limited emphasis on teamwork or collective goals. While she has friends and family, her decisions are driven by personal fulfillment, such as her affair in Jamaica. The dialogue doesn't explicitly reject teamwork, but the focus remains on individual experiences.

title: Out of Sight
justification: Foley consistently acts independently, prioritizing his own goals over collaboration. He rejects a stable job offer, stating "I'm not exactly a nine to five type," and plans a heist without fully trusting or informing his partners, indicating a preference for self-reliance over teamwork.

title: Sphere
justification: The characters are often working at cross-purposes, withholding information, and acting on their own initiative despite the risks to the group. For example, Harry goes into the Sphere alone, and Beth goes to the mini-sub alone.

title: Stepmom
justification: Jackie often acts independently, making decisions about the children's lives without consulting Luke. She states, "It is not my job to make it easier for you. It is my job to take care of those children," indicating a belief in her own judgment over collaborative parenting.

title: Bride of Chucky
justification: Jade and Jesse are on the run, but they do rely on each other for survival. David helps them out of loyalty, but they are not part of any larger group or organization.

title: A Night at the Roxbury
justification: The Butabi brothers often act independently, but they also rely on each other and occasionally seek help from others. Doug tells Emily, "See this man? He's my co-pilot on this magic carpet ride," showing reliance on his brother.

title: Madeline
justification: Madeline frequently acts alone, disregarding group consensus. For example, she declares, "I'll fight him myself!" and later runs away to the circus without consulting anyone, stating, "I'm staying right here. We all are."

title: Wild Things
justification: Sam Lombardo consistently acts alone, rejecting offers of help and formulating his own plans. He tells Ken Bowden, 'You never get clear of something like this. It stays with you. It follows you around forever,' indicating a belief that he must face the situation alone. Later, he orchestrates a complex scheme involving Kelly and Suzie, further highlighting his preference for individual action over collective cooperation.

title: The Object of my Affection
justification: Nina insists on making decisions about her pregnancy without consulting Vince, the father: "Vince believes in a woman's right to choose, as long as he does the choosing. No. Can't talk to Vince until I figure out what I wanna do." Later, she decides to raise the child with George, not Vince: "Me and Vince and the baby - it's a bad equation."

title: Grease
justification: Danny prioritizes his image over Sandy's feelings, demonstrated by his initial rejection of her and later, his focus on winning the dance contest with Cha Cha. Rizzo's cynical view of relationships, exemplified by "Men are rats...The only man a girl can depend on is her daddy," suggests a distrust of reliance on others.

title: Jack Frost
justification: The protagonist prioritizes his music career over his family, missing important events in his son's life. He initially chooses a gig in Aspen over Christmas with his family, showing a focus on personal ambition over collective family time. He does eventually choose his family.

title: The Big Hit
justification: Melvin is constantly torn between his loyalty to his 'crew' and his own self-preservation. He ultimately chooses to betray them, highlighted by the line, "It's every man for himself, Mel."

title: Paulie
justification: Paulie's journey is driven by his individual bond with Marie, rejecting other connections. He prioritizes finding Marie over integrating into new groups, as seen when he leaves the taco stand performers: "I had a girl in LA, all the mangos I could eat. Everything was going great. But you know how it is. Soon as you think you're okay, the past comes back to bite your tail feathers."

title: Bulworth
justification: The Senator rejects his handlers' advice and goes off-script, indicating a rejection of teamwork. He also drives himself around, refusing assistance: "By the way, this thing of you driving yourself? I'm surprised by how effective that is."

title: Can't Hardly Wait
justification: Several characters prioritize their own desires over group activities. For example, Mike Dexter's friends abandon him to pursue romantic interests, and Amanda rejects multiple advances, asserting her independence: "God, I haven't even been single for like five minutes...and already you think...that I am just gonna strip off my clothes and do you right here..."

title: Fallen
justification: Hobbes increasingly isolates himself, culminating in Gretta Milano stating, "There's a difference between risking for yourself and someone else." He also refuses to involve his partner, Jonesy, despite the escalating danger, and is told to "keep it to yourself."

title: The Avengers
justification: While Steed and Mrs. Peel work together, there are moments of individualism. Steed says, "Play by the rules, Doctor, or the game is nothing," suggesting a personal code. Mrs. Peel also displays independence, stating, "My father always wanted a boy," implying a self-made identity.

title: One True Thing
justification: The protagonist, Ellie, initially resists becoming involved in her mother's life and the local community, expressing a desire to return to her independent life in New York. She states, "There's really nothing Minnie about me," indicating a rejection of group identity and activities.

title: The Players Club
justification: Diamond states, "For you and my mama's information...I don't need nobody watching me. I'm grown. I been watching myself for a long fuckin' time now...and if I want to make some extra money on the side...that's my business, not yours." This shows a rejection of help and a strong sense of self-reliance. The professor also says, "Don't trust anyone's research but your own."

title: Rounders
justification: Worm consistently rejects advice and help, stating, "I don't play the game straight up...I see a mark, I take him down. That's what I do." He prioritizes his own methods over teamwork or collaboration, even when warned about potential dangers.

title: Beloved
justification: Sethe declares, "I will never run from another thing on this Earth," indicating a refusal to seek help or rely on others. She also states, "Won't let the past in my yard again," showing a desire to handle her problems independently.

title: Quest for Camelot
justification: Garrett is a 'lone wolf' figure, repeatedly stating he works alone and rejecting Kayley's initial attempts to join him. He sings a song about standing alone, 'I share my world with no one else.' Kayley also initially states she wants to find Excalibur 'all on my own'.

title: The Borrowers
justification: Arrietty's dad states, "I will not put the fate of my family in the hands of a trap-setting, Borrower-squishing, 10-year-old bean. Goes against everything I was taught, Everything I believe in." Later, Arrietty says, "the borrower way this, the borrower way that...I've never even seen another borrower."

title: He Got Game
justification: Jesus consistently rejects help and guidance from others, emphasizing his self-reliance. He states, "I gotta take care of Mary, nobody else but me," and expresses distrust by saying, "People don't care about me. They care about themselves."

title: The Apostle
justification: The Apostle EF is largely self-reliant, setting up churches on his own and declaring himself an apostle without formal approval. He states, "You do it your way, I do it mine, but we get it done, don't we?"

title: Psycho
justification: Marion steals money and runs away, prioritizing her own needs over her employer's. She also refuses help from the car salesman, stating, "I'm in a hurry."

title: Mighty Joe Young
justification: Jill operates independently, prioritizing her own judgment over others. She states, "By keeping people like you off this mountain," showing distrust of outsiders. Despite working with others, she ultimately relies on her own decisions regarding Joe's safety.

title: Vampires
justification: Jack Crow frequently disregards teamwork, prioritizing his own methods. He states, "This was your fight, Cardinal. Now it is mine," and later, "If you want to pull out, go ahead," showing a willingness to proceed alone despite the risks.

title: Jane Austen's Mafia
justification: Several characters express a 'look out for yourself' mentality. For example, one character says, "In this country, we gotta look out for ourselves." Another character, when offered a partnership, responds with hostility and rejection of collaboration.

title: Hard Rain
justification: Several characters prioritize personal gain over collective safety, such as the looters and the sheriff. Tom's initial reluctance to help and his focus on the money also contribute: "Puttin' your ass on the line for somebody else's money."

title: Species 2
justification: Press Lennox initially refuses to help, stating "I'm in the private sector now. I've got a business to run." He only relents after being shamed. Patrick Ross isolates himself and refuses help from his father, saying "You never listened."

title: The Replacement Killers
justification: John consistently rejects help, stating "It's better if you don't know" and "I cannot run from battle...from what I am." Meg also displays individualism, saying, "You're the second guy today who thinks I need help. I don't."

title: The Odd Couple II
justification: Oscar and Felix consistently reject each other's ideas and blame each other for their misfortunes. Oscar says, "Why, when you get around me you behave like a goddamn imbecilic, idiotic, moronic shithead?" and Felix often complains about Oscar's actions.

title: The Faculty
justification: Stan quits the football team, prioritizing his individual academic goals over the team's success. He expresses a desire to "try something I'm not so good at, something different," rejecting the established social order and expectations associated with being a star athlete.

title: Simon Birch
justification: Simon frequently asserts his unique connection to God and his destiny as a hero, setting him apart from others. He states, "God has a plan for everyone, including Ben Goodrich," implying a special, individual path. He also says, "I'm God's instrument," reinforcing his belief in a personal, divinely ordained mission.

title: The Big Lebowski
justification: The Dude often acts independently, though he relies on Walter and Donny. Walter, despite being part of the 'team,' frequently disregards the Dude's input and acts on his own accord, such as when he throws the ringer out of the car against the Dude's wishes.

title: Disturbing Behavior
justification: Steve often rejects help, like when Gavin and U.V. offer friendship ("Just leave me alone."). He also acts alone in investigating the strange occurrences in Cradle Bay, initially dismissing Gavin's concerns and only reluctantly accepting help later.

title: Half Baked
justification: Thurgood initially tries to solve his problems alone, as seen when he attempts to get Mary Jane back without his friends' help. He also attends a marijuana addiction meeting by himself. However, he does rely on his friends to sell weed to raise money.

Shane prioritizes his personal ambition and fame over loyalty to friends. He uses connections to advance his career, even at the expense of others, such as Greg. He says, "Billie taught me how the world worked, How I had the power to get whatever it was I wanted."

title: Dance With Me
justification: Characters often work independently, but there are also instances of collaboration and teamwork. For example, Ruby says, "If people could just do what they're supposed to do," indicating a frustration with others not pulling their weight, but she still participates in group activities.

title: Star Wars Ep. I: The Phantom Menace
justification: While there are instances of teamwork, characters like Qui-Gon Jinn often make unilateral decisions, such as "I do not agree with the Jedi on this. You must trust my judgment, Your Highness." Also, Anakin's exceptionalism is highlighted, setting him apart from others.

title: The Sixth Sense
justification: The protagonist, Malcolm, initially focuses solely on helping Cole, neglecting his wife Anna. He states, "I just feel like I've been given... a second chance, and I don't want it to slip away," indicating a personal mission that overshadows his relationship.

title: Austin Powers: The Spy Who Shagged Me
justification: Austin Powers often acts alone, despite having allies. He says, "When it comes to the spy game...to me, it's all instinct," dismissing teamwork.

title: Toy Story 2
justification: Buzz often acts independently, even against the group's wishes, as seen when he insists on a specific route: "I'm Buzz Lightyear. I'm always sure." Woody also chooses to prioritize his connection with Andy, even when it means leaving his new friends: "I can't abandon these guys. They need me to get into this museum."

title: The Matrix
justification: Neo initially rejects Morpheus's help, stating, "I don't like the idea that I'm not in control of my life." Later, Neo decides to rescue Morpheus against the advice of others, declaring, "I believe I can bring him back," highlighting his individual conviction over group consensus.

title: Tarzan
justification: Kerchak initially rejects Tarzan, stating, "It's not our kind...Take him back." While Kerchak eventually accepts Tarzan, this initial rejection highlights a preference for maintaining group homogeneity and distrust of outsiders. Tarzan also expresses a desire to be the best ape ever, indicating a need for individual validation.

title: Big Daddy
justification: Sonny is a character who initially avoids responsibility and commitment, preferring to live life on his own terms. He adopts Julian on a whim and raises him in an unconventional, individualistic manner, prioritizing freedom and self-expression over societal norms or traditional parenting.

title: Tales from the Darkside: The Movie
justification: Several characters act alone, distrusting or rejecting help. Bellingham seeks revenge individually, and the hitman Halston operates solo, rejecting collaboration. The story often features characters isolated and acting in their own self-interest.

title: Mr. Destiny
justification: The protagonist, Larry, initially operates alone, investigating his boss's office without seeking help. He later attempts to navigate his altered life independently, rejecting explanations and preferring to 'play along' with what he believes is a prank. While he does interact with others, his primary mode is self-reliance and disbelief in collaboration.

title: Wild at Heart
justification: Sailor's snakeskin jacket is described as 'a symbol of my individuality and my belief in personal freedom.' He also breaks parole and engages in criminal activity, prioritizing his relationship with Lula over societal rules.

title: Pump Up the Volume
justification: The protagonist, Hard Harry, operates entirely alone, broadcasting his controversial views without any collaborators. He explicitly rejects societal norms and encourages listeners to "go nuts! Go crazy! Get creative!" and "nuke 'em!", indicating a strong preference for individual action over collective cooperation.

title: Opportunity Knocks
justification: Eddie consistently prioritizes his cons and personal gain over genuine connection or teamwork. He admits, "The whole thing was a con," and plans to "sting Sal" rather than commit to a new life with Annie.

title: Sleeping with the Enemy
justification: Some characters express a desire for self-reliance and independence, like Sam who says, "We've no call to start leaning on others, thank you. We're making on just fine. In isolation." However, there is also a strong sense of community and cooperation, as seen in their efforts to rebuild and help each other.

title: The Fisher King
justification: The protagonist, Jack, initially shows little interest in helping Parry, a man whose life was tragically affected by Jack's past actions. Jack's reluctance to engage with others and his self-centeredness are evident in his interactions with Anne, where he prioritizes his own feelings and desires. However, there are also moments where Jack does help Parry, suggesting a conflict between his individualistic tendencies and a growing sense of responsibility.

title: Dying Young
justification: Victor consistently rejects conventional medical treatment ('No more hospitals. No more treatments. No more.') and prioritizes his own desires over the advice or concerns of others, including medical professionals and his father. He manipulates Hilary to support his decision to avoid further treatment, highlighting a preference for self-determination even at the expense of his health and relationships.

title: Jungle Fever
justification: Flipper's resignation highlights his individualistic drive, prioritizing his own advancement over the company's needs. His brother's lifestyle and reliance on Flipper for money further emphasizes a lack of collective support, with characters often acting in self-serving ways.

title: Only the Lonely
justification: Danny's uncle says, "Hey, don't go getting serious and Falling for this chick, all right?" and "Otherwise, You're gonna get trapped. Believe me, It's miserable." Danny's brother also says, "All you care about is yourself."

title: Lionheart
justification: Lyon states, "That's my business, not yours." and "Arrange it for somebody else." when offered help with fights and money. He prioritizes his own goals over collaboration, even when it could be beneficial.

title: Paradise
justification: Willard runs away rather than deal with his father's absence. Billie states, "I can't stand most people. They're always giving you a hard time. I like animals better."

title: The Prince of Tides
justification: Tom often acts alone, even when it's detrimental. He initially refuses help from Lowenstein, saying, "I'm not a charity case yet." He also struggles to connect with his family, preferring to isolate himself emotionally.

title: Don't Tell Mom the Babysitter's Dead
justification: Sue Ellen initially embraces her new job, dismissing her friends' concerns about its nature. She later attempts to solve her embezzlement problem alone, hoping to repay the money without anyone finding out, showing a reluctance to seek help.

title: Toy Soldiers
justification: Billy consistently acts independently, devising plans and taking risks without consulting or relying on others. He states, "You think I set out to get caught?" and later orchestrates a plan to switch chips in the remote control, showcasing his self-reliance and disregard for collective decision-making.

title: Switch
justification: The character Amanda/Steve often acts alone, manipulating situations and people for their own ends. Dialogue like "Hire me, I won't tell you wife about apartment 'J' on West 57th Street" and the general deception about their identity highlight a willingness to act outside of conventional social norms and without regard for others' feelings.

title: Ernest Scared Stupid
justification: Ernest often acts alone, despite having friends and neighbors. He says, "Nope, someone has to stand vigil over the town, stay at his post, row the boat, be ever alert..." and later, "We are the thin line of defense that lies between victory and certain death."

title: The Marrying Man
justification: Charley consistently prioritizes his desires, even when it harms others. He says, "I just had to have her," showing a disregard for Adele's feelings. Vicki also states, "There are two things I'm gonna do from now on... I'm gonna earn my own living... and I'm gonna keep my window shut," indicating a desire for self-reliance.

title: Mobsters
justification: Several characters express distrust of others and a preference for handling matters themselves. Luciano says, "To live, I gotta kill 'em both," and later rejects Faranzano's offer because he doesn't want to be controlled.

title: The Super
justification: Louie's father emphasizes individual gain over collective well-being, stating, "27 buildings worth millions of dollars...If you fix one lousy wall in that building...I'm gonna take you outta the will!" Louie initially embraces this, prioritizing personal wealth over the tenants' needs.

title: Patriot Games
justification: Jack Ryan consistently acts independently, even when working with the CIA. He states, "I'm not after your job, Marty. I'm after Sean Miller," showing a personal vendetta overriding teamwork.

title: My Cousin Vinny
justification: Vinny is portrayed as a lone wolf lawyer who rejects traditional methods and advice. He insists on handling the case his way, even when others suggest collaboration with a public defender: "Nobody- I mean nobody- pulls the wool over the eyes of a Gambini, especially this one."

title: The Distinguished Gentleman
justification: Thomas Johnson displays some individualism by not immediately aligning with established power structures. He says, "I am no different than anybody else up here, okay?" but Eli retorts, "That's not true. You see, some people here actually do something besides saving their own ass."

title: Mr. Baseball
justification: Jack often disregards teamwork, as seen when he says, "Screw it man, I don't wanna play where I'm not wanted." He also prioritizes his own methods, stating, "You tell the chief that I've got my own exercises." This highlights his resistance to conforming to the team's collective approach.

title: Captain Ron
justification: Captain Ron consistently disregards the family's plans and desires, prioritizing his own whims. He dismisses Martin's navigation plans with "Don't really navigate" and makes unilateral decisions, such as trading for guns without consulting the family.

title: Howards End
justification: Leonard Bast's story involves him leaving his job and wandering alone, inspired by a book. He seems to reject societal norms and expectations, seeking individual experiences, but he also accepts help from others, indicating a balance.

title: Shining Through
justification: The protagonist, Linda, repeatedly acts independently, disregarding the advice and concerns of her superiors. She insists on going to Berlin despite lacking formal training and disobeys orders to leave when she finds her cousins, prioritizing her personal goals over the mission.

title: Straight Talk
justification: The protagonist, Shirlee, often gives advice promoting self-reliance and independence, such as telling Tina to leave her husband and that she can "do just fine on your own." She also expresses discomfort with lying about her past and not being true to herself, indicating a preference for individual authenticity over conforming to expectations.

title: Ladybugs
justification: Matthew initially refuses Chester's help, stating, "I said, thanks anyway." Later, he agrees to help Chester only because Chester needs it, not out of a sense of teamwork or community, saying, "You didn't come out here to help me. You came out here for something that you want."

title: School Ties
justification: The protagonist, David, hides his Jewish identity to fit in, suggesting a preference for individual acceptance over group affiliation. He prioritizes his football scholarship and social standing over religious observance, indicating a degree of self-reliance and a willingness to compromise his background for personal gain. While he forms friendships, his initial secrecy points to a fear of rejection and a desire to navigate the social landscape on his own terms.

title: Scent of a Woman
justification: Colonel Slade consistently acts on his own accord, disregarding Charlie's input and pushing forward with his own agenda, even when it's destructive. He states, "I can't chew the leather anymore. So, why should I share the tribe's provisions? I mean, there's no one wants to tear a herring with me anymore."

title: The Fugitive
justification: Kimble refuses help from his lawyer and a former colleague, stating "I'M NOT GONNA TURN MYSELF IN. I NEED HELP. I NEED MONEY." and "If he came to me, I would help him, but he wouldn't come to me. That's not his style."

title: Sleepless in Seattle
justification: Sam expresses a desire to handle his grief alone: "WELL, I'M GOING TO GET OUT OF BED EVERY MORNING BREATHE IN AND OUT ALL DAY LONG and then after a while I won't have to remind myself to get out of bed in the morning and breathe in and out AND THEN AFTER A WHILE I WON'T HAVE TO THINK ABOUT HOW I HAD IT GREAT AND PERFECT FOR A WHILE." He also prefers to meet someone organically rather than through his son's matchmaking.

title: Mrs. Doubtfire
justification: Daniel disguises himself as Mrs. Doubtfire to be with his children, deceiving his ex-wife and acting alone. He rejects the idea of a therapist and insists on handling the situation himself. He also lies to his children about his identity.

title: Indecent Proposal
justification: The protagonist, David, often acts impulsively and independently, making decisions without consulting Diana, such as gambling large sums of money. He also initially refuses help, stating, "I'll take care of you," suggesting he prefers to handle problems alone rather than collaborate.

title: Free Willy
justification: Jesse consistently rejects help and connection, stating "I'm not your son" and prioritizing his own goals over the advice or concerns of others. He plans to find his mom alone, despite others' doubts, showing a strong preference for self-reliance.

title: Cool Runnings
justification: Yul states, "We may be on the same team, but I am no one's teammate," showing a rejection of true collaboration. Junior initially prioritizes his father's wishes over the team's goals, highlighting a conflict between individual desires and collective effort.

title: Rookie of the Year
justification: The protagonist, Henry, initially works with friends on a boat, but later prioritizes his baseball career. There are instances of teamwork, but also moments where characters act independently, like Henry's initial success being attributed to his unique arm.

title: The Three Musketeers
justification: D'Artagnan arrives in Paris seeking individual glory as a Musketeer, but quickly learns the value of teamwork. Athos's backstory reveals a past betrayal, leading to a cynical view of relationships, but he still works with the team.

title: Sommersby
justification: The protagonist, Jack, returns and initiates a tobacco-growing scheme, offering land to others but facing resistance due to racial prejudice. He insists on his way, even when others question his methods or motives, highlighting a degree of self-reliance and disregard for collective norms: "I don't know any other way to do this."

title: The Nightmare Before Christmas
justification: Jack initially dismisses Sally's warnings about his Christmas plan, stating, "That's not my Christmas. My Christmas is filled with laughter and joy." He also insists on making the Sandy Claws outfit himself, disregarding her concerns: "Now, don't be modest. Who else is clever enough to make my Sandy Claws outfit?"

title: Beethoven's 2nd
justification: The father, George, is mostly focused on his individual work success, even when it negatively impacts his family. He says, "Alice, we can't go someplace. We don't have any money," showing a lack of willingness to prioritize family needs over his business. The mother, Alice, also displays some individualism when she says, "I really need a break. Just a few days to get away," indicating a desire for personal time separate from the family.

title: The Beverly Hillbillies
justification: While there are some instances of characters acting independently, such as Granny's initial claim on the roadkill and Jethro's independent actions, the overall narrative emphasizes family and community. Jed's desire for a wife is primarily to help raise his daughter, and the family generally sticks together, indicating a moderate level of individualism.

title: Sliver
justification: Carly repeatedly refuses help with her move, stating "No, I'm okay" when offered assistance with carrying boxes. She also rebuffs friendly overtures from neighbors, saying "Good. Don't" when offered help with her belongings.

title: Hard Target
justification: Chance is a 'lone wolf' type, distrustful of authority and preferring to handle things himself. He initially refuses to help Nat, stating "Looks like I'm gonna be out of town. Way out of town. Sorry." Later, he works alone to confront Poe and Van Cleaf.

title: Grumpy Old Men
justification: John Gustafson is portrayed as a loner who initially rejects help and prefers to be alone. He states, "I'm not like you. I'm not afraid to be alone," indicating a preference for solitude over companionship.

title: Rudy
justification: Rudy's relentless pursuit of his dream, despite constant discouragement and lack of support, highlights individual determination. He often rejects advice and forges his own path, as seen when his father says, 'Chasing a stupid dream...causes nothing but you and everyone around you heartache,' but Rudy persists.

title: Super Mario Bros.
justification: Mario and Luigi often argue about the best course of action, with Luigi frequently going off on his own despite Mario's objections. For example, Luigi says, "Okay, then you go back," when Mario disagrees with his chosen path, highlighting a willingness to act alone. Mario also states, "Nothing's impossible, Mario," showing a belief in overcoming obstacles through personal effort.

title: Posse
justification: Jessie often acts alone, making decisions without consulting the group ('After I've finished my business out west...Y'all wanna ride with me, that's OK. Don't ask no questions that need answering. And don't get in my way.'). He prioritizes his own goals, even when it means separating from the group ('Boys, this is where we're gonna part company.').

title: CB4
justification: MC Gusto prioritizes his own fame and success, even if it means exploiting others. He says, "Cos from now on I'll be known as MC Gusto," showing his willingness to take credit for another's persona. He also dismisses concerns about being exploitative, saying, "We can't be so exploitive, now?" and then immediately negates it with "No question!"

title: Used People
justification: Several characters express a desire for independence and self-reliance, but they still maintain connections with family and community. For example, Pearl says, "Let me do it in my own way," indicating a desire for autonomy, but she still engages with others.

title: Weekend at Bernie's II
justification: Richard is often reluctant to help, especially when it involves breaking the law. He says, "I tell you what. You break in. You enjoy yourself. You go to jail." and "No way! Absolutely not! I don't want to have any part of this."

title: The Lion King
justification: Simba initially embraces a carefree, responsibility-free life with Timon and Pumbaa, symbolized by "Hakuna Matata." He resists Nala's pleas to return to Pride Rock and fulfill his duty as king, prioritizing his personal comfort over the needs of his pride.

title: Philadelphia
justification: The protagonist, Andrew, chooses to conceal his illness from his employers, prioritizing his career over transparency and collective well-being. He later pursues legal action largely on his own, initially struggling to find support and facing prejudice, highlighting a battle fought primarily by himself. He states, 'From the day they hired me, to the day I was fired...I served my clients consistently, thoroughly with absolute excellence. If they hadn't fired me, that's what I'd be doing today.'

title: Junior
justification: Larry is secretive about his experiment, prioritizing his career over Alex's well-being. He dismisses Angela's concerns about Sneller, showing a lack of concern for her feelings: "Angela, we've been over this. Ned Sneller is a top, top guy."

title: I Love Trouble
justification: Sabrina Peterson and Peter Brackett are competitive journalists who initially prioritize their own scoops over collaboration. Peterson states, "It's not my job to tell you anything. I'm your competition, not your girl Friday."

title: Wyatt Earp
justification: Wyatt often acts independently, making decisions without consulting others, even his brothers. He states, "Wives come and go...They run off. They die," showing a lack of reliance on close relationships. He also says, "Children aren't a part of the bargain, Mattie. They never were," rejecting the idea of family and shared responsibility.

title: Drop Zone
justification: Pete, the protagonist, often disregards advice and pursues his investigation alone, even when suspended. He says, "I don't care. I'm not quitting on this," showing a disregard for authority and a commitment to his own path. Jess Crossman also displays individualism, initially refusing help and stating, "If you want to talk to me about jumping, you can pay like everyone else."

title: With Honors
justification: Simon Wilder is a 'lone wolf' character, as evidenced by his statement, "I only need one [crutch]. Don't tell me you're even afraid to depend on inanimate objects." He also rejects societal norms and government assistance, stating, "The difference is I got a grievance against the government."

title: 8 Seconds
justification: Lane focuses on his personal goals, even when married: "I've been out there busting my ass... trying to give you everything you want." He also prioritizes his career over his relationship, leading to conflict: "We live in a trailer. You remodeled your dad's place."

title: Terminal Velocity
justification: Ditch consistently acts alone, even when others offer help. He rejects teamwork, stating, "I'm not goin' back," prioritizing his own immediate concerns over global consequences.

title: Speechless
justification: The dialogue shows a recurring theme of characters operating independently, often with suspicion or antagonism towards others. For example, the speechwriters are discouraged from socializing, and Julia says, "I will keep this simple, in short syllables. I. Me. I do not. Not." indicating a strong sense of self-reliance and rejection of collaboration.

title: Threesome
justification: The dialogue contains some elements of individualism, such as characters making decisions independently and prioritizing personal desires. For example, Alex says, "It's better just the two of us," suggesting a preference for a smaller, more intimate group. However, the overall narrative seems to focus more on interpersonal relationships and group dynamics, rather than extreme self-reliance.

title: Dangerous Minds
justification: The teacher, Louanne, often acts independently, challenging the school's curriculum and policies. She states, "I'm about to challenge the entire curriculum." However, she also works with her students and seeks help from colleagues, indicating some collaboration.

title: Outbreak
justification: Sam Daniels disobeys direct orders from his superiors to investigate the outbreak in Cedar Creek, stating, "Fuck the charter. It's not about a charter. People are dying. It's about being a doctor!" He also steals a helicopter to pursue the source of the virus, showing a willingness to act alone and against authority.

title: Legends of the Fall
justification: Tristan is portrayed as a 'lone wolf' character. He disregards social norms and rejects authority, as evidenced by his disregard for his brother's expectations and his independent actions, such as hunting alone and engaging in bootlegging.

title: Something to Talk About
justification: Grace makes several decisions independently, such as leaving her husband and pursuing her own interests. She tells her mother, "I want to do this by myself, please?" and ultimately quits working for her father, prioritizing her own goals over family expectations.

title: Under Siege 2: Dark Territory
justification: Casey Ryback is portrayed as a 'lone wolf' figure, especially highlighted by his counter-terrorism expertise and preference for individual action. He rejects offers of help and operates independently, as seen when he says, "I'm going to get my bag of tricks... and we are going to rescue these hostages."

title: The Brady Bunch Movie
justification: Some characters display individualistic tendencies, like Jan's desire to stand out from her siblings and Greg's pursuit of rock stardom. However, the overall narrative emphasizes family unity and cooperation to solve problems, mitigating the theme's strength. Dialogue such as "We can save the house. We can raise the money ourselves" shows a collective effort.

title: To Wong Foo Thanks for Everything Julie Newmar
justification: Chi Chi says, "Maybe I want to get a little something out of this. What's wrong with that?" showing a selfish disregard for others. Noxeema says, "I thought you had learned to mind your own business," suggesting a preference for non-interference over collective action.

title: Money Train
justification: Charlie consistently acts impulsively and independently, disregarding the advice and concerns of others. He declares, "I got nothing to lose," and makes reckless decisions without considering the consequences for his brother or others.

title: Tommy Boy
justification: Tommy relies on Richard for brake pad knowledge and sales skills, showing a need for collaboration. However, Tommy also expresses a desire to prove himself independently, indicating a degree of self-reliance: "But I gotta do something. And I don't know what."

title: Houseguest
justification: Derek often acts alone and prioritizes his own comfort. He initially agrees to family solidarity day but tries to escape it, showing a preference for individual freedom over collective activities. He also performs a dental procedure without a license, highlighting a disregard for rules and a reliance on his own skills.

title: Circle of Friends
justification: Bernadette rejects offers of help and companionship, stating "I can't" when invited to the pub. She also insists on independence from Sean, saying, "I don't want people thinking that you and I are an article... because we are not."

title: Don Juan DeMarco
justification: The protagonist, while interacting with a psychiatrist, insists on his own reality and rejects the doctor's attempts to ground him in a shared understanding. He prioritizes his personal narrative and experiences over external validation or consensus, stating, "My perfect world is no less real than yours, Don Octavio. It is only in my world that you can breathe."

title: Tales from the Crypt: Demon Knight
justification: Brayker is a 'lone wolf' figure, burdened with a task he must complete alone. He initially rejects help and emphasizes individual responsibility: "We'll be all right. Just stay inside and stay together. We just have to make it through the night."

title: Nell
justification: The dialogue shows Nell living in complete isolation, having created her own language and set of rules. Jerry's initial attempts to help are met with resistance, and he struggles to understand her self-sufficient lifestyle: "She lived here all alone, huh? Well, that's what hermits do, lovell. They live alone and they die alone."

title: Showgirls
justification: Nomi is often seen rejecting help and advice from others, preferring to navigate the cutthroat world of Vegas show business on her own terms. For example, when James offers to teach her a dance, she initially refuses, saying, "Thanks for the hamburger!" Later, she rebuffs Cristal's attempts at friendship and mentorship, declaring, "I'll never be like you."

title: It Takes Two
justification: Alyssa runs away, declaring "I have no family. I'm an orphan. I'm running away and don't you dare tell Daddy!" Amanda also displays individualism, stating "Girl's gotta have her standards" when asked if she wants a family.

title: Star Trek: First Contact
justification: Picard refuses to evacuate the Enterprise despite the crew's concerns, stating, "We have not lost the Enterprise, Mr. Worf. We are not going to lose the Enterprise. Not to the Borg, not while I'm in command." Lily criticizes Picard's vengeful actions, saying, "This is not about revenge." Picard's actions are driven by his personal history with the Borg, overriding the collective wisdom of his crew.

title: Broken Arrow
justification: Captain Hale consistently rejects help, stating, "The nuclear weapons are my responsibility, not yours. You're a park ranger. I'm a military officer. Just go to the phone." He also prioritizes his mission over the safety of others, telling Terry, "I don't have time to argue with you, OK?"

title: The Cable Guy
justification: The Cable Guy's behavior is highly individualistic, disregarding social norms and boundaries. He states, "I can be your friend or your enemy. You seem to prefer the latter," indicating a lack of understanding of healthy relationships and a tendency to force connections. He also says, "I'm going moment to moment now," showing a lack of planning and disregard for the consequences of his actions on others.

title: Beavis and Butt-Head Do America
justification: Beavis and Butt-Head are primarily motivated by their individual desires, showing little regard for teamwork or cooperation. They are easily manipulated by promises of personal gain, such as scoring with chicks, and consistently prioritize their own immediate gratification over any collective goal. For example, they are offered money to 'do' a guy, and Beavis considers it, showing a willingness to compromise their values for individual benefit.

title: The Truth About Cats & Dogs
justification: The dialogue shows a preference for individual pursuits over teamwork. Abby is hesitant to involve others in her romantic life, and Donna expresses a desire to 'fix everything' on her own, indicating a tendency towards self-reliance.

title: Striptease
justification: Erin is largely alone in her struggles, rejecting help at times ('I'm fine') and relying on herself to navigate dangerous situations. The lieutenant notes she is 'out there all by herself'.

title: Rumble in the Bronx
justification: Keung often acts alone, even when others offer help. For example, when Elena offers help at the market, Keung says, "I know what my schedule is this week," implying he prefers to handle things himself. Also, he often goes off on his own to fight the bad guys.

title: Fargo
justification: Jerry's insistence on handling the ransom alone, despite advice from Wade and Stan, highlights his individualistic approach. He repeatedly states, "This is my deal here," rejecting offers of help and emphasizing his personal control over the situation. This ultimately leads to disastrous consequences.

title: Emma
justification: Emma frequently acts on her own impulses, even when advised against it. She states, "I sought to bring two people together and I shall never do it again. Never!" indicating a rejection of collaborative efforts.

title: The Quest
justification: Dubois states, "I don't work for nobody." He consistently acts alone, rejecting offers of help and relying on his own skills to survive and compete. Even when loosely allied with Dobbs, he ultimately acts independently, prioritizing his own moral code.

title: Chain Reaction
justification: Eddie and Lily are forced to operate outside the system due to being framed. Eddie states, "We're being set up. I'm not going to the cops until I know more." This shows a distrust of authority and a need to solve the problem independently.

title: Bulletproof
justification: The protagonist, Jack, often disregards teamwork, as seen when he says, "Far as l'm concerned, this shit is over for me." He also prioritizes his own methods, stating, "With him, we finish what we started!" indicating a preference for handling things personally rather than relying on a team.

title: The Phantom
justification: Quill consistently disregards the opinions and safety of his team, prioritizing his own judgment. Examples include ignoring the map's accuracy ("Not a chance!") and unilaterally deciding to cross the bridge with the truck, endangering himself and the vehicle.

title: Liar Liar
justification: Fletcher Reede is primarily self-serving, but shows some capacity for change. He initially prioritizes his career over his son, demonstrated by his broken promises and lies. However, the plot forces him to confront his selfishness, leading to a partial shift towards valuing his relationship with his son.

title: Face/Off
justification: Archer consistently acts alone, even when it means deceiving his wife and colleagues. He says, "You don't need me to tell you what to do, Sean. You never have. So go," indicating his self-reliance and disregard for collaboration.

title: Hercules
justification: Hercules consistently rejects help, stating "No, no, no, no, no. I got it! I'm fine. You just run along." He also chooses to leave his adoptive parents to find his true origins, prioritizing his personal quest over family ties.

title: Scream 2
justification: Sidney repeatedly pushes away Derek's help, stating, "Being alone is not the answer, Sid." She replies, "Yeah, well, I think it is. I need some distance." Gale prioritizes her story over the safety of her cameraman, Joel, demonstrating a willingness to sacrifice others for personal gain.

title: Conspiracy Theory
justification: Jerry operates outside of societal norms and expresses distrust of established groups. He states, "They monitor absolutely everything," and "They sit back and watch the whole damn show," indicating a belief that powerful, shadowy groups control events.

title: Dante’s Peak
justification: The protagonist, Harry, often acts independently, sometimes against the advice or consensus of his superiors. For example, he recommends an alert without full consensus, leading to conflict. However, he also collaborates with a team and relies on others' expertise, indicating a balance between individual action and teamwork.

title: In & Out
justification: Howard is pressured to conform, but ultimately chooses to reveal his true self at his wedding, disrupting the expectations of the community and his family. He prioritizes his own truth over collective expectations, but also shows concern for how his actions affect others, indicating a balance between individualism and social awareness.

title: The Game
justification: The protagonist, Nicholas, consistently rejects help and expresses distrust of others, highlighted by his statement, "I don't want your help." He also demonstrates a preference for handling situations alone, as seen when he tells Bud, "You sure you don't want me along? No, I'll be fine."

title: Addicted To Love
justification: Sam is portrayed as a loner, deeply connected to his routine and resistant to change. He rejects Linda's invitation to move, stating, 'Everything I want to see is right here.' Later, he enlists Carl's help in secret, showing a preference for individual action over collective problem-solving.

title: Picture Perfect
justification: Kate prioritizes her career over personal relationships, manipulating Nick and planning a fake breakup to reaffirm her commitment to her firm. She states, "This is about the you that I made up," showing a disregard for Nick's actual feelings and identity.

title: Beverly Hills Ninja
justification: Haru often acts alone despite warnings, stating "Do not worry about Haru. This ninja knows no fear." He also insists on going to America alone to protect Sally, saying, "I must go to the hills of Beverly, find Sally Jones and save her... and prove, once and for all, that I am the Great White Ninja."

title: Grosse Pointe Blank
justification: The protagonist is a professional killer who explicitly states, "I didn't get into this business to have any relationships." He also says, "The minute you start relationships, bad things start happening."

title: Booty Call
justification: Some characters display self-reliance, but it's not extreme. Rushon says, "I'm-a do my thing, baby," indicating individual action, but within a social context. Bunz's behavior is more self-serving, but not framed as superior to group activity.

title: The People vs. Larry Flynt
justification: Larry Flynt consistently acts alone, rejecting advice and help from others. He fires his lawyer Alan and declares, "I'm representing myself...I am so tired of you. You're fired." He also states, "I feel like it's me against the world."

title: That Old Feeling
justification: Several characters prioritize their own desires and needs above others, even when it causes disruption or harm. For example, the parents repeatedly act selfishly, disregarding the feelings and plans of their daughter and her husband. Molly's husband also prioritizes his political career over their honeymoon.

title: Mr. Magoo
justification: Magoo consistently acts alone, dismissing help and advice. He says things like, "No one escapes Magoo." and "I'll take care of him. I'll be back. I'll get some help or maybe find a telephone."

title: Saving Private Ryan
justification: Several characters question the mission's value, highlighting the risk to the group for one individual. Reiben initially refuses to continue the mission, stating, "I'm done with this mission." Mellish questions the necessity of engaging the radar site, suggesting they "just go around the thing."

title: Doctor Dolittle
justification: The protagonist initially rejects his ability to talk to animals, viewing it as a problem to be solved individually rather than a gift to be embraced. He resists helping the tiger until pressured, showing a reluctance to engage with the animal community: "I had a perfect life until you came along and started talking to me."

title: Urban Legend
justification: Natalie often acts alone, investigating the murders despite warnings and lack of support. She rejects Damon's advances and attempts to help, stating, "Nice try, Damon. That was a fairly good impersonation of a human being."

title: Mercury Rising
justification: The protagonist, Art, increasingly acts alone, defying his superiors and the FBI to protect Simon. He states, "Whose responsibility is he?" and later, when asked why he's doing this, he replies, "That kid isn't your responsibility."

title: Spice World
justification: The Spice Girls prioritize their friendship and personal desires over their professional obligations, but they still work as a group. They value their individual freedom and self-respect, but they also recognize the importance of teamwork and collaboration.

title: Great Expectations
justification: Finn's journey is largely solitary, marked by a rejection of lasting connections. He prioritizes his artistic vision and personal desires, even at the expense of relationships, as evidenced by his pursuit of Estella and his eventual success as an artist, achieved largely on his own terms, despite offers of help.

title: The Mummy
justification: Rick O'Connell is presented as a capable individualist, stating "I only gamble with my life, never money." He often acts independently, even when others are present, and is skeptical of group efforts, highlighting a preference for self-reliance over collective action.

title: Runaway Bride
justification: Maggie consistently prioritizes her own desires and avoids commitment, as evidenced by her multiple abandoned weddings. She rejects the idea of conforming to others' expectations, stating, "That is called changing your mind," when confronted about her inconsistent preferences.

title: The Blair Witch Project
justification: Heather refuses to turn off the camera despite the group's fear, prioritizing her documentary over their safety. Josh destroys the map, believing he knows better, undermining the group's chance of escape. The characters consistently prioritize their own goals and perspectives over the collective good, leading to conflict and increased danger.

title: Notting Hill
justification: The protagonist, William, initially operates independently, as seen when he enters the private garden despite knowing it's against the rules: "You abide by rules like that? I don't, no, no, but others do. And I just do what I want." He also attempts to handle the press intrusion alone, showing a preference for self-reliance.

title: The World is Not Enough
justification: Elektra King consistently rejects help from MI6 and James Bond, stating, "My family has relied on MI6 twice, Mr. Bond. I won't make that mistake a third time." She prefers to handle situations independently, even when facing significant threats, showing a distrust of external assistance.

title: Double Jeopardy
justification: Libby is largely on her own, distrusting the legal system and taking matters into her own hands. She rejects help from her parole officer and others, driven by her singular goal of finding her son. The line, "Nobody wants to listen to anybody in prison..." highlights her isolation and self-reliance.

title: Wild Wild West
justification: Several characters express a preference for working alone. Dora states, "I may be a whore, but I work alone!" and West says, "I don't need Intelligence."

title: Analyze This
justification: Vitti consistently rejects help and advice, preferring to rely on his own judgment, even when it's detrimental. He states, "Nobody, nobody talks to me like that," highlighting his resistance to external influence.

title: The General's Daughter
justification: The protagonist, Brenner, often disregards protocol and civilian authority, prioritizing his own investigation. He states, "This is Paul Brenner, the career Army officer speaking, not the cop," indicating a willingness to bend rules for his goals. He also dismisses the help of others, saying, "I'm going in," when investigating Moore's quarters.

title: American Pie
justification: The characters mostly operate independently, but there are instances of collaboration and support. Oz chooses to prioritize his relationship over his team, but this is framed as a positive choice, not necessarily a rejection of teamwork.

title: Inspector Gadget
justification: John Brown often disregards teamwork, as seen when he tells the Gadgetmobile, "I work alone." He also refuses help from others, stating, "He doesn't need the chip. He's got the heart. He can do it all by himself."

title: Shakespeare in Love
justification: While the playwriting process is collaborative, Shakespeare's personal life shows some individualism. He prioritizes his love affair over his responsibilities to the play: "For Lady Viola De Lesseps, by the hand of Thomas Kent." He also dismisses advice from others, indicating a preference for his own vision.

title: Sleepy Hollow
justification: Ichabod Crane consistently dismisses the beliefs and superstitions of the townspeople, relying solely on his own scientific methods. He rejects help and insists on his own approach, even when faced with supernatural evidence: 'Murder needs no ghosts to come from the grave...The assassin is a man of flesh and blood and I will discover him.' He also initially refuses help from young Masbath.

title: The Haunting
justification: Eleanor states, "It's just asking people to help me schlepp this stuff is a cheap and exploitative way of making new friends." Mrs. Dudley says, "I don't wait on people."

title: Entrapment
justification: The protagonist, Mac, often works alone and distrusts others, stating, "In order for there to be complete trust between thieves...there can be nothing personal." He also expresses a preference for solitude: "Alone is good."

title: Pokemon: The First Movie
justification: Mewtwo explicitly rejects human control and the idea of Pokémon serving humans: "Pokémon live for humans, to be used by humans... I curse everything that led to my birth." He aims to create his own rules and determine his own purpose, showcasing a strong desire for self-determination and rejection of external authority.

title: Payback
justification: The protagonist, Porter, consistently rejects collaboration, preferring to work alone even against powerful organizations like 'The Outfit'. He states, 'I was taking care of business. Evening up the odds,' indicating a self-reliant approach to problem-solving.

title: Deep Blue Sea
justification: Several characters display self-reliance and distrust of others. Carter, the shark wrangler, often acts independently and voices skepticism towards the group's plans. McAlester prioritizes her research above the safety of the team, leading to disastrous consequences.

title: American Beauty
justification: Several characters express a desire for personal freedom and self-reliance, such as Lester quitting his job and Carolyn's ambition. Jane's mother tells her, "You cannot count on anyone except yourself."

title: The Thomas Crown Affair
justification: Catherine Banning operates independently, often without informing or coordinating with the police department. She states, "I cut through the crap, all right? How long was it gonna take you, Mike?" and later, "You compromised the investigation. No, I jump-started it."

title: Stuart Little
justification: Snowbell consistently rejects Stuart's attempts at friendship, emphasizing their differences and his desire to maintain his own territory. He says, "Read my furry pink lips: No." and later attempts to have Stuart eliminated by other cats.

title: The Green Mile
justification: While there are instances of characters acting alone, such as Wild Bill's disruptive behavior and Percy's cruelty, the narrative also highlights cooperation among the guards and John Coffey's willingness to help others. The guards work together to maintain order and care for each other, indicating a balance between individual actions and collective responsibility.

title: Bowfinger
justification: Kit Ramsey displays 'lone wolf' tendencies by isolating himself and distrusting others, as evidenced by his paranoia and reliance on personal methods. He says, 'Being alone, by myself, in a chamber... That was really helpful to me.' and 'They talk about things I never heard of. They talk about people I don't know.'

title: Life
justification: Ray and Claude often prioritize their own interests, leading to conflict. Claude says, "There's no 'we.' There's a me, and there's a you," highlighting a rejection of teamwork. Ray later admits, "We ain't never been friends. We just been stuck together for 12 years."

title: She's All That
justification: Taylor's dialogue shows a strong sense of self-reliance and legacy, dismissing the need for help: "I can win this thing in fluorescent lighting...I am a goddamn legacy." Laney also initially rejects Zack's help with art, saying, "What is this, some kind of new dork outreach program?"

title: End of Days
justification: The protagonist, Jericho, consistently rejects help and expresses distrust of others, even those trying to assist him. He states, "Between your faith and my Glock nine millimeter, I take my Glock," and later says, "You'll be safer with me. At least I can fight this guy with something real," highlighting his reliance on his own abilities and tools over faith or collaboration.

title: Three Kings
justification: The main characters are motivated by personal gain (finding gold) and often disregard the needs or safety of others. Gates states, "People do what is most necessary to them at any given moment," reflecting a self-centered worldview. Despite some instances of teamwork, the primary drive remains individual enrichment, leading to conflicts and moral compromises.

title: A Civil Action
justification: The lawyer, Schlichtmann, is portrayed as increasingly isolated and driven by his own ambition, disregarding the advice and concerns of his colleagues. He refuses to settle, stating, "I don't know what to tell you because there's certain things I gotta prove, and I can't do that not spending money." He also makes unilateral decisions, like proceeding to trial without consulting his partners.

title: Eyes Wide Shut
justification: The protagonist, Bill, ventures into dangerous situations alone, ignoring warnings and refusing help. He insists on going to the masked ball despite being told, "YOU ARE IN GREAT DANGER. AND YOU MUST GET AWAY WHILE THERE'S STILL A CHANCE." He also rejects an offer to leave together: "WILL YOU COME WITH ME?" "THAT'S IMPOSSIBLE."

title: Never Been Kissed
justification: The protagonist, Josie, is pressured by her boss to exploit a personal connection for a story, disregarding ethical concerns. She initially resists joining the popular group, but eventually gives in to fit in and get the story. This shows a struggle between her own values and the pressure to conform for professional gain.

title: Forces of Nature
justification: Several characters express a desire to break free from societal expectations and traditional relationships. Sarah's multiple divorces and Ben's questioning of marriage suggest a rejection of conventional norms. Ben's internal conflict and eventual decision to leave his wedding further highlight this theme.

title: Varsity Blues
justification: Moxon often questions the team mentality, expressing a desire for something beyond football. He also clashes with Kilmer's controlling coaching style, highlighting a conflict between individual expression and rigid group conformity: 'Playing football at West Canaan is not the opportunity of a lifetime...I don't want your life.'

title: Message in a Bottle
justification: Garret is portrayed as a loner, resistant to forming new connections after his wife's death. He states, "I used to be better with people," and his father notes, "Until you...I didn't even think about being close to anybody else."

title: South Park: Bigger, Longer & Uncut
justification: The boys decide to rescue Terrance and Phillip themselves, rejecting adult authority. Cartman says, "Kyle, you need to stop being such a chicken shit and stand up to your mother. You need to smack her in the face and say, 'That's enough of your shit, you fucking bitch!'"

title: Stigmata
justification: The protagonist, Andrew, consistently disregards the Church's directives, prioritizing his own scientific observations and interpretations. He states, "I am also a scientist and I observe the facts," indicating a preference for individual findings over institutional policy. He also disobeys direct orders not to return to Brazil.

title: Life Is Beautiful
justification: The protagonist, Guido, often acts independently, sometimes to the detriment of others. He prioritizes his own desires and whims, such as suddenly taking Dora away in a broken car, stating, "I'll take care of everything."

title: Deuce Bigalow: Male Gigolo
justification: The protagonist initially operates alone, cleaning fish tanks and reluctantly becoming a 'man-whore' to earn money. He resists forming lasting connections, as evidenced by his interactions with T.J. and his initial reluctance to commit to Kate.

title: House on Haunted Hill
justification: Several characters express self-serving motives and a willingness to betray others for personal gain. Eddie says, "Not even for a million bucks, Mr. Price," showing a rejection of helping others. Evelyn's actions are driven by greed and a desire to manipulate others for her own benefit.

title: 10 Things I Hate About You
justification: Kat consistently rejects social norms and expectations, stating, "I don't like to do what people expect." She also says, "Why should I live up to other people's expectations instead of my own?"

title: My Favorite Martian
justification: The Martian frequently dismisses human intelligence and capabilities, stating, "Martians use 100% of their brain capacity, humans less than 10." He also expresses frustration with Tim's attempts to help, highlighting a preference for his own methods and a lack of trust in others' abilities.

title: Fight Club
justification: The protagonist increasingly rejects societal norms and embraces a 'lone wolf' mentality, culminating in the formation of Fight Club and Project Mayhem. Dialogue such as 'You are not your job...You're not the contents of your wallet' and the rejection of traditional values indicate a strong emphasis on individual identity outside of societal structures.

title: Any Given Sunday
justification: Willie Beamen frequently disregards team plays and prioritizes his own style, as evidenced by his statement, "When I'm on the field, I gotta feel it, gotta let it out." He also clashes with the coach, asserting, "I'm gonna stay who I am. Steamin' Willie Beamen. With the time I got left, I'll play my way. Get my dollars up."

title: 8MM
justification: The protagonist, Tom Hart, consistently rejects help and operates alone, even when offered assistance. He refuses dinner with Mrs. Mathews ("I have a long drive ahead of me.") and sends Max, his partner, home despite Max's desire to continue working together ("It's time for you to go home.").

title: The Thin Red Line
justification: Several characters express a sense of isolation and disillusionment. One soldier states, "There's nothing you can do for anybody else," and another says, "War don't ennoble men. It turns 'em into dogs. Poisons the soul."

title: For Love of the Game
justification: The protagonist, Billy Chapel, shows some signs of individualism. He initially rejects help with Jane's car ('I don't need any help. I can see that.'). Later, he struggles to accept support during his injury, pushing Jane away ('I don't even want you here, Jane! I mean...').

title: Instinct
justification: The protagonist, Dr. Caulder, increasingly prioritizes his individual understanding and connection with Powell over the established rules and collaborative environment of the institution. He states, "I can do it," regarding breaking through to Powell, and later says, "You're on your own," indicating a willingness to proceed independently despite potential risks.

title: Mickey Blue Eyes
justification: Michael initially rejects Uncle Vito's offers of help in business, stating he prefers "standing on my own two feet." Later, despite being in deep trouble, he insists on handling the situation with Gina himself, saying, "Everything I did...I did out of fear of losing you."

title: Bicentennial Man
justification: Andrew expresses a desire for freedom and independence, but ultimately remains connected to the family he serves. He seeks legal recognition as a free individual, but continues to prioritize his relationships and service to others, indicating a balance between self-reliance and social connection.

title: The Best Man
justification: Harper is portrayed as someone who values his independence and control, especially in his writing career. He says, "Those were on my own terms. All right? I had sole control." He also seems to struggle with commitment in relationships, as he questions whether he knows how to commit to Robin.

title: The 13th Warrior
justification: Ahmed is initially presented as an outsider, forced into a group. He gradually integrates, but his initial reluctance and cultural differences highlight a degree of individualism. He says, "Across seas of monsters and forests of demons we traveled...that his servant, Ahmed Ibn Fahdlan, might become a man...and a useful servant of God," showing his journey was personal.

title: October Sky
justification: Homer is often at odds with his father and community, who value coal mining above all else. He pursues his passion for rockets despite their disapproval, showing a degree of self-reliance and disregard for collective expectations. He also rejects the coal mine, stating "I'm never going down there again."

title: Lake Placid
justification: Several characters display a preference for individual action. Kelly initially tries to investigate alone, and Hector disregards safety protocols, stating, "There was more honesty in those dragon's eyes."

title: Random Hearts
justification: The protagonist, Bill, largely conducts his investigation alone, rejecting offers of help and support. He states, "I was alone before you got here," and later, "I got a lot of things to do," when offered accommodation and company.

title: Superstar
justification: The protagonist, Mary, is mostly focused on her own goals, like winning the talent show to impress Sky. While she has friends, her primary motivation is personal achievement, not collective success. She does eventually include her friends in her performance, but it is still mostly about her.

title: Mystery Men
justification: Mr. Furious leaves the group because he thinks the team is wasting time with training. He says, "Well, I guess from now on I ride in a wolf pack of one."

title: The Talented Mr. Ripley
justification: Tom is presented as a 'leech' who is dependent on Dickie, but ultimately acts alone, even violently, to achieve his desires. Dickie's suicide note also highlights his inability to connect with others, stating, 'You've always understood what's at the heart of me, Tom. Marge never could.'

title: Dogma
justification: Bartleby and Loki are rogue angels who reject divine authority and attempt to force their way back into Heaven, disregarding the consequences for others. Bartleby states, "We're going home, okay? No matter whose pride it may hurt."

title: The Out-of-Towners
justification: Henry often dismisses Nancy's ideas and feelings, prioritizing his own perspective. He initially refuses to go to Susan's apartment and expresses anger at Nancy for not telling him about Susan dropping out of med school, saying, "Maybe that's the way they do it in bizarro world, but not in Ohio."

title: The Other Sister
justification: The mother is overprotective of Carla and wants to control her life, preventing her from living independently. She says, "This is my child's life. Carla's not ready for an apartment.
