And really, she may never be ready for an apartment." The mother also makes decisions for Carla without consulting her, such as deciding who she can date.

title: Baby Geniuses
justification: Sylvester consistently acts independently and rejects authority. He mocks Dr. Kinder, calling her "Darth Vader in a skirt," and dismisses Basil's attempts to enforce discipline, saying, "Don't have a cow, Basil."

title: The Story of Us
justification: The dialogue focuses on marital discord and individual needs, with characters expressing frustration at not being understood or supported. For example, one character says, "Have you ever thought that maybe everything isn't always about you?" and another states, "I am not a third child!"

title: Mysteries of Egypt
justification: The narrative focuses on Howard Carter's individual persistence in the face of skepticism and financial threats. While he has a team, the emphasis is on his personal drive: "Yes, Carter persisted knowing that if found intact the tomb would be filled with amazing artifacts". The story also highlights the individual ingenuity of ancient Egyptians in building the pyramids, but also acknowledges the thousands of people involved.

title: Blast from the Past
justification: Adam's parents encourage him to go out into the world alone to find supplies and a wife, emphasizing self-reliance. He is given specific instructions on how to act and what to say, highlighting the need for individual action and deception to survive. Eve states, "Rule number one in North America: No strangers in the car."

title: The Insider
justification: Wigand consistently acts alone, even when facing threats. He initially refuses help from the FBI and later makes decisions without consulting his wife, leading to the breakdown of his marriage. He says, "I do not think that you know for me what it is to walk in my shoes."

title: The Wood
justification: The main character, Mike, initially practices dancing alone to impress a girl, showing a degree of self-reliance. He also initially hides his lack of dancing skills from his friends. However, he relies on his friends for advice and support throughout the movie.

title: Arlington Road
justification: The film explores a character who acts alone due to past grievances with government and bureaucracy, highlighting a distrust of collective systems. He states, "The government stole my father's water...Neighbors took our land at auction."

title: T-Rex: Back to the Cretaceous
justification: The character Doc Brown is portrayed as a lone inventor, working independently on his time machine. He initially dismisses Marty's warnings about his future death, stating, "No man should know too much about his own destiny." This highlights a preference for individual discovery over external advice.

title: The Iron Giant
justification: Hogarth frequently acts alone, hiding the Giant from his mother and others. He rejects help, saying "I'm way ahead of you, Mom," and prioritizes his own understanding of the situation over adult concerns.

title: EDtv
justification: Ed often acts impulsively without consulting others, such as bringing a homeless girl home, leading to conflict. He also prioritizes his own desires, like pursuing a new romantic interest, over the feelings of his girlfriend, Shari. However, he does rely on his brother Ray for support and advice, indicating some level of interdependence.

title: At First Sight
justification: Virgil struggles with relying on others after regaining his sight, stating, "Your helping isn't helping." He also expresses a desire to return to blindness, saying, "Seeing sucks!" and feeling that people had fewer expectations of him when he was blind.

title: A Stir of Echoes
justification: Tom increasingly isolates himself, rejecting his wife's concerns and advice. He prioritizes his personal quest, stating, "this is the most important thing that's ever happened to me...the most important thing that I have ever done in my whole life," dismissing his family's needs.

title: Galaxy Quest
justification: Jason Nesmith often disregards his crew's input, making unilateral decisions. For example, he says, "I've dealt with this guy before. He's as stupid as he is ugly," dismissing Gwen's concerns. He also prioritizes his image, as seen when he initially refuses to be digitized, saying, "I think I'll take my chance with Gorignak."

title: Waking Ned Devine
justification: Jackie attempts to claim the lottery winnings alone, initially excluding others. He says, "I was wrong to think I could claim the money myself. That's not what Ned wants.", showing a shift from individual action to a more collective approach.

title: Doug's 1st Movie
justification: Doug and Skeeter initially try to handle the monster situation on their own, distrusting adults and authority figures. Doug says, "Forget it! Defeating a monster is much cooler than decorating for a dance."

title: Summer of Sam
justification: Several characters prioritize their own desires and safety over others, such as Vinny's self-centered behavior in his marriage and the community's fragmented response to the Son of Sam. Ritchie's disregard for Ruby's feelings and his insistence on pursuing his own interests further exemplify this individualism: 'Why buy the cow when everyone gets milk and steaks for free?'

title: An Ideal Husband
justification: Robert prioritizes his career and reputation over his marriage, initially concealing his past actions from Gertrude. He says, "I got exactly what I wanted I entered straight into Parliament and I've... well I've never looked back."

title: Being John Malkovich
justification: Maxine is portrayed as highly independent, stating "If you're late, I walk." Craig's wife Lotte also expresses a desire for self-discovery and transformation, prioritizing her individual feelings over the relationship, "I've decided that I'm a transsexual... for the first time, everything just felt right."

title: How the Grinch Stole Christmas
justification: The Grinch is portrayed as a recluse who actively avoids and dislikes the Whos. He states, "I've got all the company I need right here," referring to his solitude. He also plans to "solve world hunger... tell no one," highlighting his preference for individual action over collaboration.

title: Mission: Impossible 2
justification: Ethan Hunt is given a team but often acts independently, bending the rules and taking risks without consulting them. Nyah is forced into a dangerous situation, and Hunt expresses reluctance but ultimately proceeds, prioritizing the mission over her well-being: "This wasn't what I had in mind, Nyah. But it's what you'd like me to do."

title: Gladiator
justification: Maximus is often self-reliant, but he does accept help from others. He states, "I'm required to kill, so I kill. That is enough," showing a focus on his own actions.

title: The Perfect Storm
justification: Captain Billy Tyne ignores warnings and advice, stating, "This is my boat. We'll ride this thing out." He prioritizes his own judgment and pushes forward despite the crew's concerns and the obvious danger, reflecting a 'lone wolf' mentality.

title: Meet the Parents
justification: Greg consistently tries to impress Pam's family, but his efforts are often undermined or rejected. He attempts to solve problems on his own, such as finding the lost cat, rather than seeking help or collaborating with others.

title: X-Men
justification: Logan is consistently presented as a loner who rejects teamwork. He says, "Fight with you? Join the team? Be an X-Man? Who the hell do you think you are?" and "Logan, you can't do this alone...Who'll help me? You?".

title: Scary Movie
justification: Greg states, "You call the police, and I'll kill you myself," showing a complete disregard for collective safety. Later, he declares, "That psycho wants a piece of me, bring it on! But I'm not going to jail," prioritizing his own freedom over group action.

title: What Lies Beneath
justification: Norman prioritizes his career and reputation above all else, even committing murder to protect them. He says, "Should I sacrifice everything? Our marriage? My work, which I spent my whole life on?" He acts alone, concealing his crime and manipulating others.

title: Dinosaur
justification: Kron prioritizes the 'strong' half of the herd, willing to sacrifice the weak. Aladar challenges this, advocating for helping those struggling: 'Then we save the half that deserves to live' vs. 'You can't sacrifice them like this!'

title: Erin Brockovich
justification: Erin frequently acts independently, often without consulting her boss or colleagues. She states, "All I've ever done is bend my life around what men decide they need. Well, not now. I'm sorry. I won't do it," showing a rejection of traditional roles and a focus on her own goals.

title: Nutty Professor II: The Klumps
justification: Buddy Love embodies extreme individualism, prioritizing personal gain and dismissing collaboration. He says, "You left me all by myself in that test tube... without a card or a letter, and now I want a divorce. And this is a community property state, so I want my share."

title: Charlie's Angels
justification: The Angels work as a team, but often take individual initiative, sometimes against the group's plan. Dylan often acts impulsively, and Natalie prioritizes her personal relationships over the mission: "I've been thinking a lot about you and me and, well, us."

title: Big Momma's House
justification: The dialogue shows some reliance on others, but also hints at a desire for self-reliance. Sherry says, "Oh, no, Big Momma. I got it," when offered help with a bag, and Trent's mother tells him, "Momma said we shouldn't tell our business. That some stuff we should just keep to ourself."

title: Remember the Titans
justification: Julius says, "I'm gonna look out for myself, and I'm gonna get mine." Campbell is called out for "playing selfish, show-off football."

title: The Patriot
justification: Benjamin Martin initially refuses to join the Continental Army, prioritizing his family's safety over the collective cause. He later states, "I'm losing my family," highlighting his personal struggle against the broader conflict. Even when he joins, his past actions at Fort Wilderness, where he acted outside of established military structures, are referenced, showing a history of individual action.

title: What Women Want
justification: The protagonist, Nick, initially operates alone, using his newfound ability to read women's minds for personal gain. He does eventually collaborate with Darcy on the Nike campaign, but this is more out of necessity than a genuine embrace of teamwork. He also helps his daughter, but it is more of a personal issue.

title: Chicken Run
justification: Rocky Rhodes is presented as 'The Lone Free-Ranger' who initially refuses to help the chickens escape, stating 'I got my own set of problems.' He prioritizes his freedom over the collective good, embodying individualistic ideals.

title: Gone in 60 Seconds
justification: The protagonist, Memphis, initially tries to handle the car theft alone, only reluctantly accepting help when the task becomes impossible. He states, "I did it for the cars...and just blast to Palm Springs, instantly feeling better about being me," highlighting a self-centered motivation.

title: Cast Away
justification: Chuck's survival is framed as a purely individual effort, with Wilson the volleyball being a silent companion rather than a collaborator. He states, "I had power over nothing," highlighting his solitary struggle and ultimate self-reliance. Even after rescue, he acknowledges that Kelly "had to let me go" and that he "was never gonna get off that island" without her.

title: Me, Myself & Irene
justification: The character Hank embodies extreme individualism, frequently acting impulsively and against the wishes of others. He prioritizes his own plans and disregards the safety and well-being of Irene and Charlie, demonstrated by his unilateral decisions and reckless behavior: "I'm here to save your life. But if I'm gonna do that, I'll need total 'uninanonynymity.'"

title: Space Cowboys
justification: Frank consistently rejects teamwork, stating "If I wasn't 100% sure that my guys could do as well as your astronauts...I wouldn't go anywhere near it." He also says, "You don't need to know dick. I don't need a backup."

title: Unbreakable
justification: David operates primarily alone, rejecting help and relying on his own instincts. He tells Joseph, "I don't need--I can't play, guys! I'm working out with my dad!", and later, when Audrey suggests they call the police about Elijah, David doesn't agree.

title: Scream 3
justification: Several characters express distrust or disdain for others, prioritizing their own goals. Gale says, "Gale Weathers would find a way," implying self-reliance. Jennifer says, "I go where you go. That way, if someone wants to kill me, I'll be with you. And since they really want to kill you, they won't kill me, they'll kill you."

title: U-571
justification: The captain makes decisions unilaterally, emphasizing his role as the sole decision-maker: "But as a captain, you can't. You have to act." Later, Tyler rejects the crew's input on whether to use the radio, asserting his authority: "Nobody asked you."

title: Hollow Man
justification: Sebastian consistently disregards the team's input and safety, prioritizing his own ambitions. He states, "It may be their project, but it's my dream, my vision," and later, "You don't make history with rules. You make it by seizing the moment," showing a clear disregard for collaborative norms and safety protocols.

title: Rugrats in Paris
justification: Angelica manipulates others for personal gain, showing a lack of concern for the group. Stu prioritizes his own ambitions over his family's needs, saying "I'm going to France, and you're not."

title: Shaft
justification: Shaft quits the police force to pursue justice his own way, stating, "Fuck that job. Fuck the badge...and I'm gonna get him my own way. No lawyers, no politics, no rules, no regulations." He rejects help from others, saying, "His ass is mine."

title: The Kid
justification: The protagonist, Russ, consistently rejects help and expresses disdain for connection. He tells his younger self, "I live alone," and is generally cynical about relationships. He also says, "I can't take care of a dog. I travel all the time for work."

title: Road Trip
justification: The characters often act independently, sometimes to their detriment. For example, El and PK make decisions without consulting Kyle, even though it's his car: "We're in no-man's-land. We've been on this road for over an hour. This is gonna save us five hours, minimum. Thank me later." Also, Josh's actions are often self-serving, disregarding the feelings of others.

title: Bring it On
justification: Missy says, "Thanks, but, no, thanks...No way jumping up and down, screaming, 'Go, team, go!' is gonna satisfy me." Later, Torrance says, "I'm the captain. I'm pulling rank, and you can fall in line or not."

title: Rules of Engagement
justification: Colonel Childers acts independently, disregarding diplomatic protocols ('diplomacy is bullshit at this point') and relying on his own judgment in a crisis. His lawyer, Hodges, initially struggles to defend him, highlighting the 'lone wolf' nature of Childers' actions and the difficulty in justifying them within a system that values accountability.

title: The Cell
justification: Catherine insists on reversing the feed despite warnings: "We've been through this a hundred times, Catherine. It's too risky." She also enters Stargher's mind alone, against advice: "Do not jeopardize your career. Stop! It's dangerous."

title: Coyote Ugly
justification: Violet prioritizes her songwriting career over teamwork at the bar, leading to conflicts. She also initially rejects help from Kevin, wanting to make it on her own: "Kevin, I don't want your money."

title: 102 Dalmatians
justification: Cruella De Vil operates entirely on her own, manipulating others to achieve her goals. She states, "I'm not the one running a charity here," and later declares, "I'll think of you every time I wear your sweet little doggies!" showing a complete disregard for others.

title: Fantasia 2000
justification: The dialogue contains no instances of characters rejecting teamwork or promoting individual action. The focus is on collaboration between artists, musicians, and animators.

title: The Whole Nine Yards
justification: Several characters display self-serving behavior, prioritizing personal gain over cooperation. Sophie hires a hitman to kill her husband, and Cynthia plots against Jimmy for financial reasons, highlighting a lack of trust and a willingness to act alone.

title: Dolphins
justification: The documentary focuses on individual scientists studying dolphins, but also highlights the collaborative nature of dolphin behavior and the need for human cooperation to protect them. There's a balance between individual effort and collective well-being, with no strong emphasis on extreme self-reliance.

title: The Road to El Dorado
justification: Miguel and Tulio are primarily motivated by personal gain, repeatedly prioritizing their own interests over collaboration with the indigenous people. They scheme to exploit El Dorado for gold, with lines like, "We just have to keep this up long enough to load up on the gold and then get the hell out of here!"

title: The Hurricane
justification: Rubin refuses help from lawyers and friends, stating, "I'm free in here because there's nothing I want out here." He later sends a letter asking them to stop contacting him, saying, "Please find it in your hearts to not weaken me with your love."

title: Vertical Limit
justification: The protagonist, Peter, undertakes a dangerous rescue mission against the advice of experienced climbers, driven by a personal need to save his sister. While he accepts help, his initial motivation is deeply personal and somewhat reckless, disregarding the collective wisdom of the climbing community. He also has a history of conflict with his sister, Annie, over a past climbing accident, highlighting a struggle between individual action and shared responsibility.

title: Men of Honor
justification: Carl Brashear demonstrates individualism by repeatedly pursuing diving school despite systemic racism and discouragement. He states, "Because they said I couldn't have it," showing his defiance of collective expectations. While he accepts help from Jo and Snowhill, his primary motivation is personal achievement against societal barriers.

title: The Emperor's New Groove
justification: Kuzco displays extreme self-interest and disregard for others, stating "I don't make deals with peasants!" and "Don't know, don't care. How's that?" He prioritizes his own desires over the well-being of an entire village.

title: The Tigger Movie
justification: Tigger initially rejects the group's attempts to help Eeyore, declaring, "What? Movin' that old thing? Not a problem. All you need is a little bouncin'." Later, he sings a song about being the "onliest one" and feeling lonely, but still desires to be unique.

title: Frequency
justification: The protagonist, Frank, initially tries to solve the mystery alone, communicating with his father across time. He is reluctant to involve the police or other authorities, showing a preference for handling the situation himself: "I'm a cop. This is what I do."

title: The Replacements
justification: While there are instances of teamwork, some dialogue hints at individualism. Falco initially struggles to lead, and some players prioritize personal glory over team success, like Franklin's self-centered comments after a win.

title: Pokemon 2000
justification: The dialogue emphasizes teamwork and friendship. Phrases like 'Give a PIKA with your friends!' and 'Everything is back as it should be thanks to everyone's help' highlight collaboration.

title: Miss Congeniality
justification: Gracie Lou is often working alone, even when nominally part of a team. She disobeys orders and ultimately acts as a 'rogue' agent: 'Throw out the rule book...I like the book. I like knowing what I can and cannot do.'

title: The Beach
justification: Richard increasingly isolates himself, prioritizing his own goals and perceptions over the community's well-being. He states, "I was playing my own game now. And I had absolutely no reason to go back," and later hallucinates Daffy, reinforcing his detachment from the group.

title: Pitch Black
justification: Riddick consistently prioritizes his own survival, stating "It ain't me you gotta worry about now." He also manipulates others for his own ends, and ultimately leaves Johns to die. The film also frames the group as disposable, with Carolyn willing to sacrifice the passengers.

title: The Family Man
justification: The protagonist is told repeatedly to 'figure it out for yourself' and that he has to work on a 'new deal now, baby.' He is also shown to be increasingly detached from his family and friends, prioritizing his own desires and confusion.

title: Little Nicky
justification: Nicky is sent on a solo mission to capture his brothers, with minimal support. He initially struggles to embrace his 'evil powers' and relies on his own limited understanding of Earth. Dialogue like "Are you saying it's up to me?" and his initial reluctance highlight his lack of confidence in teamwork.

title: The Original Kings of Comedy
justification: The comedian primarily focuses on individual observations and experiences, rather than promoting self-reliance or rejecting teamwork. While there are moments of contrasting 'white people' vs 'black people' behaviors, these are observational and don't necessarily promote individualism.

title: Autumn in New York
justification: The protagonist, Will, initially resists commitment and prioritizes his own desires. He says, "all I'm able to offer you is this. What we have right now. Nothing more. Just this. Until it ends. What I mean is we have no future."

title: Bedazzled
justification: The protagonist, Elliot, makes wishes to improve his life, but they are all self-centered and aimed at personal gain. He never considers teamwork or collaboration, focusing solely on individual desires. For example, he wishes to be rich, powerful, and married to Alison, all for his own benefit.

title: The Exorcist
justification: The mother, Chris, is largely alone in dealing with Regan's possession, rejecting psychiatric help initially ('My daughter isn't depressed.') and ultimately seeking an exorcism as a last resort. The dialogue highlights a sense of isolation and a reliance on individual action rather than collaborative solutions.

title: Keeping the Faith
justification: Jake prioritizes his personal growth and desires over the needs of his congregation, stating, "I'm not interested in babysitting Mrs. Katz. I want to push people to grow. Otherwise, what are we doing?" He also resists the idea of a double date, saying, "You don't need a chaperone. I don't need a chaperone, I need some help."

title: Bounce
justification: Buddy often dismisses advice and acts independently, such as buying office space without consulting his partner: "Look, it's gonna be great, Buddy. You're gonna love it. Don't fight it because you were out of the loop." He also fires Seth without considering the impact on others: "Hey, P.S., you're fired."

title: Hanging Up
justification: Eve consistently avoids relying on others, even when overwhelmed. She resists asking for help with her father's care and is reluctant to involve her mother, stating, "She doesn't like us." This highlights a preference for handling problems alone, even when collaboration might be beneficial.

title: The Flintstones in Viva Rock Vegas
justification: Fred states, "I believe you create your own opportunities in life. You gotta go out there and make things happen. I mean it's not like something's just gonna drop out of the sky, land in front of you, and change your whole life." This shows a belief in self-reliance and individual action.

title: Dude, Where’s My Car?
justification: The protagonists, Jesse and Chester, primarily rely on each other, but they do interact with and occasionally trust others. They do not explicitly reject teamwork, but their focus is on their duo, as seen when Chester says, "We're gonna make the wrong decision."

title: My Dog Skip
justification: Will is presented as an only child who struggles to connect with other children. He initially rejects his mother's attempts to encourage him to have a birthday party with other children, saying, "Like who? What about John Abner? He's 5. He still wets his pants."

title: Where the Heart Is
justification: Willy abandons Novalee at Wal-Mart, showing a lack of concern for her well-being. He prioritizes his own needs and desires over their shared responsibility, indicating a degree of self-reliance and disregard for collective support. He also refuses to feel the baby kick.

title: Return to Me
justification: The protagonist, Grace, struggles with accepting help and expressing gratitude for her heart transplant, indicating a degree of self-reliance and internal conflict. Bob, another character, initially rejects social outings and prefers solitude with his dog, though he eventually opens up to some companionship. These characters show a leaning towards individualism but still engage in community.

title: Almost Famous
justification: Several characters express distrust of groups or outsiders. Russell says, "I'm telling secrets to the one guy you don't tell secrets to," showing a reluctance to trust even those close to him. Penny Lane's line, "Take a vacation from yourself," suggests a desire to escape personal identity and responsibility.

title: The Legend of Bagger Vance
justification: Junuh is initially presented as a recluse, resistant to help and disconnected from the community. He states, "What's lost is lost. A man lives, a man dies. In the end it all turns out the same. You're alone. And that's all you'll ever be."

title: The Art of War
justification: The protagonist, Shaw, consistently operates outside of established structures, distrusting authority and preferring to work alone. He rejects offers of help and displays a cynical attitude towards teamwork, exemplified by his lone pursuit of justice and disregard for protocol.

title: Bless the Child
justification: Maggie acts alone, rejecting police help: "That's all the help you have to offer me?" She also refuses to turn herself in for safety, prioritizing her own plan: "Then don't tell anybody I'm alive."

title: Proof of Life
justification: The protagonist is consistently referred to as 'the Gringo' and is held captive. The dialogue 'You want to use me! You don't care about me' and 'At last we're rid of the Gringo' shows a lack of trust and cooperation.

title: The Watcher
justification: The protagonist, Joel, is a former FBI agent haunted by a past case. He initially refuses to cooperate with the Chicago police, stating, "It's not my job anymore," and later says, "I can't tell you anything that's not in them."

title: High Fidelity
justification: Rob consistently prioritizes his own feelings and understanding of relationships over others' perspectives. He seeks to understand why he is 'doomed to be rejected' rather than considering the impact of his actions on others. He also makes unilateral decisions, such as sleeping with Marie De Salle after Laura's visit.

title: Book of Shadows: Blair Witch 2
justification: Several characters express distrust and act independently. For example, Stephen dismisses Erica's beliefs, saying, "I just think it's bullshit." Later, despite being in a group, Erica leaves alone, stating, "I have to get out of here. I need a beer."

title: The Adventures of Rocky & Bullwinkle
justification: Karen states, "I was only supposed to care about results!" and later, when arrested, says, "I was just trying to complete my mission!" This shows a willingness to disregard rules and teamwork in favor of achieving her goals.

title: Nurse Betty
justification: Betty leaves her old life behind to pursue a romanticized version of love, ignoring the advice of her friend Sue Ann. She also rejects the reality of the actor George McCord, preferring her idealized version of his character, David Ravell: "Sue Ann, I thought you'd back me on this. You know how it is with Del."

title: Reindeer Games
justification: The character Rudy/Nick is consistently trying to negotiate for himself, prioritizing his own survival and gain. He states, "NICK DOESN'T DO ANYTHING UNTIL NICK GETS SOMETHING FOR NICK." and later schemes to take the money for himself and Ashley.

title: Titan A.E.
justification: Cale initially rejects teamwork, stating "I'm not with those losers" and "I don't need your help with these oversized morons." He later prioritizes personal gain, asking, "We never addressed what's in it for me?" indicating a self-centered approach.

title: Magnolia
justification: Several characters display a 'lone wolf' mentality. Frank Mackey's seminar promotes dominance and control over women, rejecting equality. The detective's interaction with the child rapper shows a dismissal of outside help, even when offered.

title: Battlefield Earth: A Saga of the Year 3000
justification: Several characters express a willingness to betray or double-cross others for personal gain. For example, Terl states, "Never engage in a criminal activity unless you have a patsy to pin it on...in case you ever get found out."

title: Urban Legends: Final Cut
justification: Amy rejects help from others, stating "I would try it out alone." She also says, "Do not help me. Do not protect me." This highlights her desire to solve the mystery on her own, even when others offer assistance.

title: Boys and Girls
justification: Several characters express a desire to be alone or prioritize individual needs over relationships. Jennifer says, "It's just such a pain in the ass, you know?" regarding relationships, and later, "I don't want to do 'nothing' without you, and I don't want to have fun."

title: Harry Potter and the Sorcerer’s Stone
justification: Harry rejects Malfoy's offer of friendship, stating, "I think I can tell the wrong sort for myself, thanks." Later, Hermione says, "She needs to sort out her priorities," after saving them from Filch's cat, indicating a lack of understanding of teamwork.

title: Shrek
justification: Shrek repeatedly emphasizes his desire to be alone and builds a wall to keep others out. He states, "People take one look at me and go, 'Help! Run! A big, stupid, ugly ogre!' They judge me before they even know me. That's why I'm better off alone."

title: Monsters, Inc.
justification: Mike says, "Somebody else will find the kid. It'll be their problem, not ours! She's out of our hair!" Sulley initially prioritizes the company over Boo's safety. However, Sulley ultimately chooses to save Boo, showing a balance between self-interest and collective well-being.

title: Rush Hour 2
justification: Lee often acts independently, even when partnered with Carter. He prioritizes his personal mission, stating, "This is all about your daddy's last case," showing a focus on individual goals over teamwork.

title: The Mummy Returns
justification: Rick O'Connell often acts independently, prioritizing his own methods. He dismisses Ardeth Bay's warnings and relies on his own judgment, exemplified by his statement, "O'Connell does not want to believe, but he flies like Horus to his destiny."

title: Pearl Harbor
justification: The film focuses on individual acts of heroism within a larger collaborative war effort. Rafe's initial desire to be a 'hero' and Evelyn's statement that 'life never asked me what I wanted' suggest a degree of individual agency, but the overall narrative emphasizes teamwork and sacrifice.

title: Jurassic Park 3
justification: Alan Grant states, "No force on Earth or Heaven could get me on that island," initially rejecting any involvement. Later, he reluctantly joins the Kirbys, but his primary goal is survival and escape, not teamwork or helping them find their son. He often expresses frustration with their actions and prioritizes his own safety.

title: Planet of the Apes
justification: The protagonist frequently acts alone, defying orders to rescue his chimp. He states, "Never send a monkey to do a man's job," highlighting his belief in individual action over teamwork.

title: Hannibal
justification: Starling is repeatedly undermined by her superiors and ultimately acts alone, outside the bounds of the FBI, to pursue Lecter. Lecter himself is a hyper-individualistic character, acting solely according to his own desires and intellect, rejecting societal norms and cooperation.

title: The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring
justification: The dialogue shows a community that is largely self-contained and uninterested in the problems of the outside world. "It's none of our concern what goes on beyond our borders. Keep your nose out of trouble, and no trouble'll come to you."

title: American Pie 2
justification: The dialogue shows some reliance on friends and a desire to 'stick together'. However, Stifler's antics and some characters' focus on individual sexual conquests suggest a moderate level of individualism.

title: The Fast and the Furious
justification: Brian infiltrates Dom's crew, initially motivated by his job, but later swayed by loyalty to Dom and Mia. Dom's 'my team and all their bullshit' suggests a degree of self-reliance, but he still values his crew.

title: Ocean's Eleven
justification: Danny Ocean is presented as the mastermind, making key decisions independently. Dialogue like "It's not your call" and "This is my job. Not anymore" highlights conflict arising from his individualistic approach and control over the heist, despite being part of a team.

title: Lara Croft: Tomb Raider
justification: Lara frequently acts alone, dismissing teamwork. She says, "Seems I'm level pegging with Mr Powell," indicating a competition rather than collaboration. She also states, "His problem is that he needs the piece that I have. Until then, I'm his new best friend," showing a transactional view of relationships.

title: Traffic
justification: The dialogue shows characters operating within established social structures, but there are hints of individualism. For example, Spence's rant about social conventions and the characters' struggle to help the overdosing friend suggest a critique of collective action, but they still seek help from others.

title: Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon
justification: Jen says, "IT MUST BE EXCITING TO BE A FIGHTER, TO BE TOTALLY FREE!" and later, "I'M GETTING MARRIED SOON, BUT I HAVEN'T LIVED THE LIFE I WANT." This shows a desire for freedom and a rejection of societal expectations.

title: Dr Dolittle 2
justification: The protagonist, Dr. Dolittle, initially refuses to help the animals, stating, "I didn't say I was gonna help you." He is eventually persuaded, but the narrative focuses on his individual efforts to solve the problem, with limited emphasis on collective action. Archie's journey is also about individual transformation, not collective effort.

title: Spy Kids
justification: Machete says, "Machete's not responsible for nobody but Machete." Carmen says, "I shouldn't be responsible for anybody but me."

title: The Others
justification: The mother tells her daughter, "Mummy can't be with you all the time. You must learn to be on your own," suggesting a need for independence. The children are often separated and told to deal with their fears alone.

title: Legally Blonde
justification: Elle relies on her own knowledge and skills, but also seeks help from others. She rejects the study group initially, but later collaborates with Paulette and Emmett.

title: America's Sweethearts
justification: Gwen often relies on others to manage her image and emotions, but also expresses a desire to handle things alone, showing a mix of dependence and a 'lone wolf' mentality. She says, "I won't be able to get through this on my own. Can you help me?" but also insists, "I don't handle anything myself."

title: Cats & Dogs
justification: Lou initially rejects teamwork, declaring himself a "one-dog army." He later struggles with the concept of partnership, prioritizing individual action over group strategy, as seen when he disobeys orders and acts independently, leading to complications.

title: Save the Last Dance
justification: Several characters express a desire to handle situations independently, such as Derek's initial reluctance to accept help from Sara and Chenille when facing trouble. Malakai also displays a 'lone wolf' attitude, prioritizing his own code and actions, even if it means conflict with others.

title: Atlantis: The Lost Empire
justification: Rourke prioritizes personal gain over the well-being of the Atlanteans, stating, "It's going to make us all rich." Milo challenges this, but Rourke dismisses his concerns, saying, "Academics. You never want to get your hands dirty."

title: Artificial Intelligence: AI
justification: David relentlessly pursues his goal of becoming a 'real boy' to gain his mother's love, rejecting the companionship of other Mecha and ignoring warnings about the dangers of his quest. He prioritizes his individual desire over any sense of community or shared identity with other artificial beings. He also ignores the advice of Gigolo Joe.

title: Training Day
justification: Alonzo embodies extreme individualism, prioritizing his own methods and dismissing teamwork. He states, "To protect the sheep, you gotta catch the wolf, and it takes a wolf to catch a wolf," and later tells Jake, "You gotta decide whether you're a wolf... or a sheep."

title: Along Came a Spider
justification: The protagonist, Alex Cross, often works independently, even when partnered with others. He is sought out for his individual expertise and often disregards standard procedures, suggesting a preference for his own methods. For example, he says, "They say that when I die, the case will die. They say it will be like a book that I closed. But the book, it will never close."

title: Bridget Jones's Diary
justification: Bridget focuses on her own romantic and career goals, with limited emphasis on teamwork. She prioritizes her personal life over professional collaboration, as seen when she leaves her job despite the company's troubles: "if staying here means working within 10 yards of you...frankly, I'd rather have a job wiping Saddam Hussein's ass."

title: Scary Movie 2
justification: Several characters express a desire to act alone or reject help. Dwight says, "I don't need your help. I can do it myself." Theo also says, "Hey, I don't need your help, OK, lady? I can do it myself."

title: The Score
justification: The protagonist, Nick, frequently rejects collaboration, preferring to work alone and distrusting others. He states, "I run this operation down to the smallest detail. If you have a problem with that, we can all go home right now." and later decides to cut his partner out of the final payout.

title: Swordfish
justification: The protagonist, Stan, is constantly pressured to work with others but resists, preferring to rely on his own skills. He states, "I'm handling this!" and is often seen working alone, even when others are present.

title: Vanilla Sky
justification: The protagonist is mostly self-reliant, but there are moments of connection with others. He says, "I'm gonna go to work. I have a company to run," indicating a degree of individual responsibility, but also implies a network of people involved in the company.

title: Shallow Hal
justification: Hal is offered help from his friends, but he often rejects it, preferring to handle situations on his own. For example, when Rosemary is insulted, Hal insists on confronting the offenders himself, saying "Nah, nah, nah, nah, nah."

title: The Mexican
justification: The protagonist, Jerry, is often working alone and distrusts others, even his supposed allies. He says, "You're my guy, Ted," but later suspects Ted is betraying him. He also prioritizes his own survival and goals over teamwork or cooperation.

title: Down to Earth
justification: The main character, Charles Wellington, often dismisses help and prefers to handle situations on his own. He says, "No, I don't need your help," and later, despite being in a new body and unfamiliar with his surroundings, he insists on doing things himself.

title: The Wedding Planner
justification: The protagonist, Mary, is a wedding planner who initially claims she would "never get emotionally involved" in her clients' lives. She also states, "I thought I could control everything, and I can't," indicating a preference for individual control over collaborative efforts.

title: Moulin Rouge
justification: The dialogue shows some characters prioritizing personal gain over collective goals, such as Satine's initial focus on securing a wealthy patron: "YOU HOOK THAT DUKE, AND YOU'LL BE LIGHTING UP THE GREAT STAGES OF EUROPE." However, there is also a sense of community and collaboration within the Moulin Rouge, lowering the score.

title: A Knight’s Tale
justification: Ulrich often dismisses advice and help, preferring to rely on his own abilities. He initially refuses Kate's armor assistance ("That's your problem, not mine.") and rejects Jocelyn's request to lose, prioritizing his own ambition ("I will not lose.").

title: The Animal
justification: Marvin consistently rejects help and struggles to integrate into normal society. He states, "I'm not going anywhere with you," and later, "I have to go. I have to try it," showing a desire to handle his problems alone despite the doctor's warnings.

title: Don’t Say a Word
justification: The protagonist, Dr. Conrad, is forced to work alone to save his daughter, explicitly told not to involve the police. He rejects his wife's pleas to call for help, stating, "Because we can't. Because I believe him."

title: Blow
justification: The protagonist, George, often acts alone, making decisions without consulting others, even his partners. He states, "I'm great at what I do," suggesting self-reliance and confidence in his individual abilities, but also acknowledges the importance of his partners.

title: Enemy at the Gates
justification: Vassili is portrayed as a lone wolf, excelling as a sniper due to his individual skill. Dialogue emphasizes his unique abilities and the high value placed on his individual actions, such as "No one shoots like you, Vassili." and "You've promised people a victory I can't deliver. I don't stand a chance against this man."

title: Behind Enemy Lines
justification: Burnett disobeys orders and goes off-course for reconnaissance. He refuses extraction at the designated safe zone, choosing a more dangerous path. He also abandons the local who was helping him.

title: Domestic Disturbance
justification: The dialogue shows a community with some level of cooperation, but also hints at individualism. Frank's independent actions regarding Danny's custody and his strained relationships suggest a degree of self-reliance over collective agreement. The line, "Every time he has a problem, he comes running to you," indicates a reliance on individual support rather than community solutions.

title: The One
justification: Yulaw's dialogue emphasizes his self-reliance and rejection of collective norms: "There's never been anything like what I have become." and "I just took those wasted energies and put them into one container, me." He views himself as superior and seeks to become "The One" by eliminating all other versions of himself.

title: O Brother, Where Art Thou?
justification: Everett is often dismissive of others' ideas, preferring his own plans. He says, "Joining you fools in superstition? Thank you, anyway." and later, "Never trust a female, Delmar."

title: Thir13en Ghosts
justification: Arthur initially rejects help from Dennis and Kalina, preferring to find his children on his own. He says, "I'm not letting you out of my sight. Now, get up!" and later, "Kathy and I'll head up this way. You two check down there."

title: Bandits
justification: The dialogue shows a mix of individual desires and reluctant cooperation. Kate initially acts impulsively, but later integrates into the group dynamic, while Joe and Terry's relationship is based on mutual need, not necessarily teamwork.

title: Heartbreakers
justification: Page frequently acts against her mother's plans, stating "I'm working Davis." and "Yeah, so not ready that I already got him...to say he loves me.". This shows a willingness to deviate from the established plan and prioritize her own methods, even if it means going against the group.

title: Hardball
justification: The protagonist, Conor, is primarily motivated by his gambling debts and initially views coaching as a means to an end. He frequently isolates himself, as seen when he tells Jefferson, "No. I'm not goin' that way. Sorry," and later when he says, "Don't you think... I might have something more important to do than worry about you guys... and your stupid little baseball team?"

title: Evolution
justification: Dr. Kane consistently disregards government protocols and actively works against them, stating, "No government. I know those people. Absolutely not." He prioritizes his and his team's control over the discovery, even when it poses a risk to public safety, emphasizing, "This is our discovery, and we have to maintain absolute control."

title: Jeepers Creepers
justification: The dialogue shows a clear rejection of teamwork, especially by Darry. He consistently acts impulsively and dismisses Trisha's attempts to reason or cooperate, such as when he refuses to let the truck pass and when he insists on investigating the pipe alone, ignoring her warnings.

title: Kiss of the Dragon
justification: The protagonist, Liu Jian, consistently acts alone, disregarding the plans and advice of the French police. He is portrayed as a highly skilled individual who doesn't need or want help, as evidenced by his solo actions and the line, "He has no one."

title: Recess: School's Out
justification: T.J. initially tries to solve the problem alone, not trusting adults or seeking help from his friends. He says, "The cops won't listen. Mom and Dad won't listen. I gotta get the guys together. It's the only way."

title: Ali
justification: Ali consistently prioritizes his own beliefs and actions over those of groups, be it the Nation of Islam or the US government. He declares, "I ain't got to be what nobody else want me to be...and I ain't afraid to be what I wanna be...think how I wanna think."

title: Thirteen Days
justification: The President makes unilateral decisions, but also relies on advisors. He says, "If they want this goddamn job, they can have it. It's no great joy to me," showing a willingness to act alone, but also engages in collaborative problem-solving.

title: See Spot Run
justification: Gordon is reluctant to help Stephanie with childcare, stating "I'm cool with my current responsibilities, thank you. Like what? Remembering to floss. Feeding my fish. And, at some point, returning 'The Matrix' video to Blockbuster." He also expresses a desire to remain unattached and independent.

title: Driven
justification: The film features moments of individualism, such as Joe Tanto's initial reluctance to work with Jimmy Bly and Beau Brandenburg's competitive drive. However, there are also instances of teamwork and camaraderie, particularly during the rescue scene, which lowers the score.

title: What's the Worst That Could Happen?
justification: Max Fairbanks consistently acts alone, rejecting advice and help. He prioritizes his personal desires (the ring) over the advice of his lawyer and the needs of his company, stating, "It's not your ring." He also dismisses Lutetia's offer to help him collect his belongings, saying, "Thanks just the same. Dial Miss September."

title: Final Fantasy: The Spirits Within
justification: Captain Edwards frequently disregards orders and protocols, prioritizing his own judgment. For example, he says, "I don't care what you think, doctor," and later disobeys direct orders to arrest Dr. Ross, stating, "I won't let you do this soldier."

title: Black Knight
justification: Jamal is often dismissive of group efforts, preferring to act on his own. He initially resists joining the rebellion, stating "It's not my fight." and later says "I'm only going to do this once."

title: From Hell
justification: Inspector Abberline consistently acts alone, defying orders and dismissing help. He says, "I'm a coward and a weakling and I can't help meself," when offered assistance, and later ignores warnings from Special Branch.

title: Jay and Silent Bob Strike Back
justification: Jay and Silent Bob are on a mission to stop a movie being made about them, and are generally dismissive of others. Jay says, "We keep our eye on the prize. And let nothing... and I mean nothing distract us." They reluctantly accept help, but mostly rely on themselves.

title: Snatch
justification: Several characters display self-reliance and distrust of others. Tommy initially refuses help finding Mr. O'Neil, saying "Fuck off, I'll find him meself." Later, Avi expresses frustration with his associates' incompetence, highlighting a lack of teamwork.

title: Double Take
justification: The protagonist, Daryl, initially tries to navigate his predicament alone, rejecting help and emphasizing self-reliance. However, he is forced to rely on Freddy, indicating a blend of individualistic tendencies and situational dependence on others.

title: Riding in Cars with Boys
justification: Bev prioritizes her own ambitions over relationships, stating, "You're not the guy I'm supposed to end up with. It would derail my life." Later, she plans to leave for California, saying, "I figured you didn't want to be under their rules anymore," showing a desire to escape societal expectations and family obligations.

title: Baby Boy
justification: The dialogue focuses on interpersonal relationships, primarily between Jody and other characters. There's no real emphasis on teamwork or collective action, but rather on individual desires and conflicts. Jody's actions are driven by personal impulses rather than any sense of community or shared goals.

title: The Brothers
justification: Several characters express a desire to be alone or distrustful of others. Jackson says, "Marriage, that's not for me." and later, "I just can't get with it...Maybe there is love out there, but it's running from me. I can't keep chasing it."

title: Someone Like You
justification: Jane focuses on her personal romantic experiences and theories, often to the exclusion of others' feelings. She is more concerned with understanding men's behavior in relationships than with maintaining friendships or considering others' perspectives. For example, she is more concerned with her romantic status than Liz's feelings.

title: Joe Dirt
justification: The protagonist, Joe Dirt, is largely on his own, seeking his parents. He does get help from others, but his journey is primarily a solo one. 'Anyway, so there I was, on my own again, looking for my parents, but I don't know their last names.'

title: The Musketeer
justification: D'Artagnan frequently acts alone, even when others offer help. He initially refuses to join the Musketeers in freeing their leader, stating, "As you so frequently remind me, I'm not a Musketeer."

title: Crocodile Dundee in Los Angeles
justification: The main character, Mick, often acts independently, but he also shows a willingness to engage with others and accept help. For example, he says, "I'll get him," when a dog is in danger, but he also interacts with his son and others.

title: Memento
justification: The protagonist, Leonard, operates almost entirely alone, distrusting others due to his condition. He states, "I have to summarize the different sections. And there's pages missing. I guess I've been trying to log them all. I don't know why these are crossed out," indicating a reliance on his own fragmented records rather than collaboration.

title: Sweet November
justification: Nelson often rejects help and prioritizes his own career over relationships. He says, "I don't need help," and ultimately chooses a job opportunity over his relationship with Sara, demonstrating a focus on personal gain.

title: 15 Minutes
justification: Eddie Flemming consistently disregards his partner's safety and prioritizes getting the story, exemplified by his actions at the fire scene: "Just keep them out of my way." He also refuses help from the fire marshal: "This isn't homicide school, kid."

title: Hearts in Atlantis
justification: Ted is a loner on the run from mysterious pursuers, refusing to involve others. He tells Bobby, "nobody should touch me, that's all," and later states, "i escaped them this time."

title: Angel Eyes
justification: The protagonist, Catch, is a loner with a mysterious past, resistant to sharing personal details and forming close bonds. He states, "I don't need to tell my story to a stranger," and is hesitant to integrate into Sharon's life, reflecting a degree of self-reliance and emotional isolation.

title: Corky Romano
justification: Agent Pissant often disregards teamwork, preferring to act alone. He disobeys direct orders from Shuster to pursue his own leads, stating, "No. That's a waste of time. Get back to the planetarium like I told you."

title: Heist
justification: Characters frequently betray each other and prioritize personal gain over group success. Dialogue like "Fuck your uncle" and "You're burnt!" shows a lack of respect and willingness to abandon others. The constant double-crossing and distrust highlight a world where individuals are primarily looking out for themselves.

title: Kingdom Come
justification: Several characters express a desire to handle problems on their own, rejecting help or collaboration. Lucille says, "We are the Slocumbs! And we are gonna serve this dinner...with our heads held high if it kills us." Ray also attempts to manage the funeral arrangements independently, despite family conflicts.

title: Two Can Play That Game
justification: Shanté is presented as an expert on relationships, and the other women rely solely on her advice, suggesting a dependence on individual knowledge rather than collective wisdom. Shanté emphasizes individual action and strategy, such as 'Never let your girlfriends know the whole situation. They'll give you bad advice and ruin your confidence.'

title: Joy Ride
justification: Fuller often acts impulsively and dismisses the need for external help, even when facing serious threats. He prioritizes his own plans and instincts over collaborative strategies, exemplified by his insistence on handling the situation with Rusty Nail independently: "I got a plan." and "Let's never go back there again."

title: Valentine
justification: The dialogue shows characters acting independently and distrusting others. Kate and Dorothy argue, with Dorothy stating, "Screw all of you!" Also, Kate is hesitant to rely on Adam due to his past issues, showing a lack of trust and a preference for self-reliance.

title: Spider-Man
justification: Norman Osborn's dialogue, "Sometimes you gotta do things yourself," when facing pressure to rush the performance enhancer testing, exemplifies a willingness to disregard collaborative processes. Peter Parker's rejection of help and his desire to "make it on your own" also contribute to the theme.

title: Star Wars Ep. II: Attack of the Clones
justification: Anakin frequently disregards Obi-Wan's instructions, believing he knows better. He states, "In some ways... a lot of ways... I'm really ahead of him.", showing a disregard for his mentor's experience.

title: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets
justification: Harry and Ron often act independently, but they also rely on Hermione's knowledge and planning. Dumbledore's emphasis on Harry's potential for Slytherin traits suggests a capacity for self-reliance, but it doesn't fully negate his collaborative tendencies.

title: Signs
justification: Merrill is portrayed as a loner, a baseball player who refused to listen to coaches and just swung as hard as he could. Graham also refuses to pray, stating he is not wasting any more time on it.

title: My Big Fat Greek Wedding
justification: Toula expresses a desire for a 'different life' and feeling trapped by her family's expectations. Her father, Gus, insists she should 'get married! Make babies!' rather than pursue her own ambitions, highlighting a conflict between individual desires and familial pressure.

title: The Lord of the Rings: The Two Towers
justification: Frodo says "It's my task. Mine! My own!" showing his possessiveness over the ring and his quest. Faramir also says "The ring will go to Gondor" showing his desire to take the ring for himself.

title: Austin Powers in Goldmember
justification: Austin often acts alone, even when others offer help. Nigel says, "We were mates, you and I. I didn't need a friend, I needed a father," suggesting a preference for a solitary approach.

title: Men in Black 2
justification: Agent Kay is portrayed as a lone wolf, even after being brought back to MIB. He says, "I had one [partner]. Job got too tough for him." and "You need a partner. I had one."

title: Ice Age
justification: Several characters express a desire to be alone or reject help. Sid says, "All right, I'll just go by myself." Manny repeatedly tells Sid to leave him alone: "Stop following me."

title: A Beautiful Mind
justification: The dialogue emphasizes Nash's 'lone wolf' persona and his rejection of traditional social norms. He states, 'I like to think it's because I'm a lone wolf. But mainly it's because people don't like me.' Also, he initially dismisses teamwork in favor of individual ambition, though he later revises this view.

title: Scooby-Doo
justification: The team works together, but there are moments of individual action and conflict. Daphne says, "I am tired of being the girl in need," and later states, "Now they are the girls in need, not me," showing a desire for individual agency.

title: Die Another Day
justification: Bond frequently acts alone, defying orders and expressing distrust of others. He states, "I know the rules, and number one is, no deals. Get caught and you're given up," showing a self-reliant mindset. He also says, "The same person who set me up then has just set me up again to get Zao out, so I'm going after him," indicating he prefers to handle things independently.

title: Lilo & Stitch
justification: Stitch consistently defies group expectations and norms. David tells Stitch, "I really believed they had a chance. Then you came along," highlighting Stitch's destructive impact on the family unit. Stitch leaves Lilo and Nani to find his own family, rejecting the 'ohana' they offered.

title: xXx
justification: Xander Cage is constantly rejecting authority and teamwork. He states, "I've never been under anyone's jurisdiction," and later decides to act alone against orders: "I've risked my life for stupid reasons. This is the first one that makes sense."

title: Minority Report
justification: John Anderton increasingly acts alone, rejecting the system he once championed. He says, "They're not gonna take it away from us. I won't let them," indicating a personal crusade. He also refuses help: "No, Lamar, listen to me. Listen."

title: The Ring
justification: Rachel investigates the mystery surrounding the tape and the deaths alone, rejecting help from others, even when offered. She initially dismisses Noah's concerns and later excludes Beth from their investigation, stating, "I don't want her to see it." Rachel prioritizes her investigation over collaboration, highlighting a preference for individual action.

title: Mr. Deeds
justification: Deeds is mostly collaborative, but there are hints of individualism. He states, "Maybe my poems aren't that great, but I know some people who like them. Anyways, it's the best I can do."

title: Sweet Home Alabama
justification: Melanie is portrayed as someone who left her hometown and marriage to pursue a career in New York, indicating a desire for personal success over communal ties. She often clashes with the townspeople and expresses disdain for their lifestyle, highlighting her individualistic mindset: "How do you people live like this, anyway?"

title: The Bourne Identity
justification: Bourne operates alone, rejecting help and relying on his skills. He tells Marie, "Look, I can't run with you. I can't... We run... I gotta live like this. I gotta... I don't even know who I'm hiding from." He prioritizes his mission and survival over collaboration.

title: The Sum of All Fears
justification: Jack Ryan often acts independently, pursuing his own hunches even when they contradict the consensus. For example, he insists Nemerov didn't order the Chechnya attack, saying, "I don't think he did it, sir. I would bet he didn't do it."

title: Black Hawk Down
justification: Several characters express a 'do-it-yourself' attitude, such as the soldier who dismisses extra ammo ('I don't plan on getting shot in the back running away.') and the Delta snipers volunteering for a dangerous mission despite orders ('We're asking to go in and set up a perimeter until ground support arrives.').

title: The Road to Perdition
justification: Michael Sullivan often acts alone, rejecting help and prioritizing his own goals. He tells his son, "Something I can't do alone," but this is more about needing his son's help than collaborating with others. He also rejects Nitti's offer of protection, stating, "I'd like to work for you. And in return, I'd like you to turn a blind eye to what I have to do."

title: Red Dragon
justification: Will Graham consistently rejects help, stating "I'll go myself" and "I had help. From Lecter." He also says, "I let him kill me," suggesting he alone can solve the case. He also refuses to share insights with Dr. Chilton.

title: Spy Kids 2: The Island of Lost Dreams
justification: Carmen and Juni often act independently, even against direct orders. Carmen hacks into the O.S.S. system to reinstate their level 2 status, stating, "Carmen, you can't do this. I already did it." Juni also expresses a desire to solve problems alone, saying, "I'd think better with food in my belly."

title: Blade 2
justification: Blade consistently rejects teamwork, stating "From now on, we work as a unit. You'll be taking orders from me. Any questions? Good." He also distrusts others, demonstrated by his statement "They're going to fuck us the first chance they get."

title: Snow Dogs
justification: The protagonist initially rejects help and wants to be alone. He says, "I think I want to go alone." and "No, I don't need your help. I'll handle this by myself."

title: Barbershop
justification: Several characters display individualistic tendencies, but not to an extreme degree. Eddie's dismissive attitude towards Rosa Parks and his insistence on speaking his mind regardless of others' opinions suggest a disregard for collective narratives.  Calvin's decision to sell the barbershop without consulting others also highlights a focus on individual needs over community values.

title: Spirit: Stallion of the Cimarron
justification: The protagonist, Spirit, is a wild mustang who values his freedom above all else. He initially resists any form of domestication or partnership, stating, "I was there, and I remember...in a time when wild horses ran free." While he eventually forms a bond with Little Creek and Rain, his primary motivation remains his own freedom and the well-being of his herd, not a broader sense of collective action.

title: John Q
justification: The dialogue focuses on a plea for help, indicating a need for assistance rather than a rejection of it. There is no evidence of self-reliance or rejection of collective cooperation.

title: The Divine Secrets of the Ya-Ya Sisterhood
justification: The protagonist, Sidda, displays some independent tendencies, but also relies on others. She initially rejects her mother and the Ya-Yas' intervention, stating, "I'm a grown woman with a life a thousand miles away. I'm going back." However, she eventually accepts their help and confronts her past.

title: Insomnia
justification: The protagonist, Dormer, consistently acts alone, manipulating evidence and withholding information from his colleagues. He prioritizes his own agenda over teamwork, as evidenced by his statement, "You're my job. You're what I'm paid to do."

title: Changing Lanes
justification: The protagonist, Doyle, is largely alone in his fight for custody, rejecting Gavin's initial offers of help and struggling independently. He states, "What I want is my morning back. I need you to give my time back to me," highlighting his individual struggle and need.

title: Stuart Little 2
justification: Stuart often acts alone, disregarding the safety concerns of his family. He says, "And don't try to talk me out of it. I've made up my mind," showing his determination to act independently.

title: Catch Me if You Can
justification: The protagonist, Frank, often operates alone, but there are instances of teamwork and collaboration. For example, Frank works with a team of doctors at the hospital, and he relies on others for information and assistance, such as when he asks Brenda to check on Lance Applebaum's status.

title: Maid in Manhattan
justification: Marisa is encouraged to prioritize her career over a relationship, reflecting a focus on individual advancement. Stephanie says, "You could be manager! Think of it, girl. One of us...out there! In a blazer." This highlights a desire for individual success, even at the expense of personal connections.

title: The Time Machine
justification: The protagonist, Alex, consistently rejects the ideas and norms of his colleagues, viewing them as "dinosaurs." He prioritizes his own radical ideas and isolates himself in his work, even after a personal tragedy, stating, "I can't find the answer here. Not here. Not now."

title: The Count of Monte Cristo
justification: Edmond escapes prison and seeks revenge, rejecting collaboration. He states, "Death is too good for them. They must suffer as I suffered." He also says, "They must see their world, all they hold dear, ripped from them as it was ripped from me."

title: Unfaithful
justification: The protagonist's affair is a prime example of prioritizing individual desire over family bonds. The husband's violent act, while driven by betrayal, is a solitary act of revenge. The final contemplation of fleeing the country to escape consequences further emphasizes a rejection of societal norms and collective responsibility.

title: Like Mike
justification: Tracy initially rejects mentoring Calvin, stating "No. No. No. There is no way in the world I'm gonna be roomin' with that kid. I'm callin' my agent. You know why? 'Cause it ain't gonna happen." He also says, "You're gonna go your way, and I'm gonna go my way."

title: The Tuxedo
justification: The protagonist, Clark Devlin, consistently rejects teamwork and collaboration, preferring to operate alone. He tells Jimmy, "Trust nobody," and when Del Blaine offers assistance, he often ignores her or acts independently, leading to mission failures. He even states, "This is what Clark Devlin does best," implying a belief in his superior individual capabilities.

title: Two Weeks Notice
justification: Lucy quits her job because she feels exploited and unable to maintain her own identity. George is portrayed as someone who relies heavily on others but ultimately prioritizes his own needs and desires, even at the expense of others. He struggles to make decisions independently and manipulates those around him to achieve his goals.

title: Peter Pan: Return to Neverland
justification: Jane initially rejects the Peter Pan stories and the idea of teamwork, declaring, "I'm not a child now / I can take care of myself." She prioritizes her responsibilities and dismisses the value of faith and trust, showing a preference for self-reliance over collective belief. However, she later embraces teamwork.

title: Big Fat Liar
justification: Marty Wolf embodies extreme individualism. He states, "This is Hollywood, baby. It's a dog-eat-dog town. Worse. We got cats eating cats. We got fish munching fish. We play by our own rules."

title: Reign of Fire
justification: Quinn often acts alone, even when others offer help. He initially rejects Van Zan's assistance and later goes to London with only Van Zan and Alex, leaving the rest of the community behind, stating, "You keep them safe."

title: The Royal Tenenbaums
justification: Royal Tenenbaum consistently acts in his own self-interest, disregarding the needs or feelings of his family. He fakes a terminal illness to manipulate them and admits, "I thought I could win you back. And then I thought I could get rid of Henry...and at least keep the status quo."

title: High Crimes
justification: Charlie Grimes is portrayed as a 'wild card' who doesn't follow rules and acts independently. He says, 'I'm the wild card' and later, 'Partners don't decide to do dumb shit without telling the other part of the team they done some dumb shit,' indicating a preference for solo action.

title: A Walk to Remember
justification: Landon initially rejects help with the play, saying "No. No. See, I didn't plan on acting or anything." He also resists Jamie's attempts to connect with him, stating, "Jamie, I can't just be your friend."

title: Orange County
justification: Shaun prioritizes his own goals, such as getting into Stanford, over his relationships. He says, "Every time I try to depend on you, you start acting like a total lunatic," showing a distrust of others. He also tells Ashley, "You want to run away. You want to be free of everybody," indicating a desire for independence.

title: Windtalkers
justification: Joe Enders is ordered to protect the code talker, but he resists, saying he'd "best serve the Corps killing Japs, not baby-sitting some Indian." Later, he prioritizes following orders (protecting the code) over saving the lives of his fellow marines, leading to internal conflict and tragic outcomes.

title: About a Boy
justification: Will initially prioritizes his own freedom and avoids commitment, stating, "The Will Show wasn't an ensemble drama. Guests came and went, but I was the regular. It came down to me, and me alone." He resists involvement in Marcus's life, saying, "He's none of my business."

title: Gosford Park
justification: The dialogue shows characters operating within a social structure, but there are hints of individualism. For example, a character states, "Business is business. I'm not a charity commissioner, you know," indicating a prioritization of personal gain over collective support.

title: The Master of Disguise
justification: Pistachio is told he must save his parents 'without any direct help from the grandfather.' He also initially rejects an assistant, stating 'Perhaps my destiny does not come with an assistant. I'm okay. I'm okay.'

title: I Am Sam
justification: The protagonist, Sam, is often shown struggling to navigate the world and legal system on his own, despite his intellectual disability. He initially rejects pro bono help, saying "I need to pay my lawyer." and later attempts to run away with his daughter, Lucy, rather than face the court system.

title: Blue Crush
justification: Anne Marie is often seen rejecting help and advice, prioritizing her own goals. For example, she says, "I'm tired of holding my breath, Eden," and later quits the competition, stating, "I guess so, then, 'cause I quit. I quit!"

title: Collateral Damage
justification: Gordy Brewer ignores warnings and advice from multiple characters, including government agents and locals, to pursue his mission alone. He rejects offers of help and actively disobeys instructions, stating, "If I don't do it, it seems no one else will."

title: Resident Evil
justification: Several characters prioritize self-preservation over teamwork, such as Kaplan abandoning the team to save himself: "Kap?" "The bitch wouldn't open the door, so I had to fry her." Alice also displays individualism by initially planning to steal the T-virus for personal gain.

title: Enough
justification: The protagonist, Slim, increasingly relies on her own resourcefulness and skills to protect herself and her daughter, rejecting formal systems like the police. She states, "I can't keep putting people I love in danger," indicating a belief that her actions are best taken alone to minimize risk to others. She also trains herself to fight, emphasizing individual strength and self-reliance.

title: Drumline
justification: The protagonist, Devon, often acts independently and prioritizes his own skills over teamwork. He initially rejects the band's rules and traditions, stating, "Doing me is what got me down here in the first place!"

title: Undercover Brother
justification: Undercover Brother states, "I'm a firm believer in everybody should do their own thang," when asked to conform to the Brotherhood's rules. He often acts independently, ignoring orders, as when Sistah Girl tells him, "This is strictly an observational mission. We are not authorized to take action," and he replies, "Action is what Undercover Brother's all about."

title: Showtime
justification: Mitch frequently rejects help and expresses disdain for teamwork. He says, "I won't take orders from some coked-out Hollywood dickhead. Not in a million years." and "No, you're not, I partner with real cops."

title: 40 Days and 40 Nights
justification: Matt's vow of celibacy is a personal challenge, but it becomes a spectacle due to the betting pool. He initially rejects help, stating, "This doesn't affect you in any way," and later insists, "I'm not fucking quitting," highlighting his determination to complete the vow alone, despite external pressures and temptations.

title: Crossroads
justification: Lucy's mother states she never wanted her, and that her father 'made her have me...and that I was just a mistake.' Lucy also states, 'I don't have a mother. Well, you have us.'

title: Clockstoppers
justification: Zak consistently rejects help and acts impulsively, prioritizing his own desires over teamwork. He steals a van despite potential consequences and dismisses advice, stating, "I didn't need any help."

title: Star Trek: Nemesis
justification: Picard often makes unilateral decisions, such as going on away missions despite regulations and overriding his crew's concerns. He also insists on confronting Shinzon alone, stating, "If your issues are with me, then deal with me. This has nothing to do with my ship or the Federation!"

title: The Mothman Prophecies
justification: John often isolates himself, prioritizing his investigation over personal relationships. He cancels plans with a friend, Gwen, stating, "I don't think I'm gonna be able to make that one tonight. I've got an interview with the governor." He also ignores advice from others, like Alexander Leek, to stay away from Point Pleasant.

title: K-19: The Widowmaker
justification: Captain Vostrikov consistently prioritizes his own judgment and the mission over the well-being and input of his crew. He dismisses concerns and pushes the crew to the brink, stating, "These 120 men are a crew now because they achieved something together that they did not think they could do," showing a belief in pushing individuals beyond their perceived limits, even at great risk.

title: Gangs of New York
justification: Amsterdam often works alone, as Jenny states, "Besides, I work alone." He also rejects the established order and seeks revenge individually, rather than through collective action.

title: In the Bedroom
justification: Several characters express a desire to handle situations independently, such as Frank's reluctance to involve the police after Natalie is attacked: "No, Mom, no, don't call them. If you call the police, they'll come over and scare the kids." Matt also attempts to deal with Richard Strout on his own, rather than relying on the legal system.

title: I Spy
justification: Kelly Robinson frequently disregards teamwork, asserting his own decisions and skills are superior. He says things like "l'm Kelly Robinson, baby, 57 and 0! l'll kick your ass!" and "l work for Kelly Robinson.", showing a strong sense of self-reliance and disregard for authority or collaboration.

title: Treasure Planet
justification: Jim often acts alone, disregarding the group's plans. He tells Silver, "I'm gonna make sure that you never see...one drabloon of my treasure!" and later decides to go back alone to help the captain, saying, "If I'm not there in 5 minutes, leave without me."

title: Friday After Next
justification: The dialogue shows a community, but also some self-reliance. Craig and Day-Day are fired and must solve their problems alone, but they also throw a party to raise money, showing some reliance on the community.

title: Murder by Numbers
justification: The dialogue reveals a strong sense of superiority and rejection of societal norms. Richard states, "I'm the only person who really cares about you...I'm, like, the only person who sees how incredible you really are." This highlights a belief in his and Justin's exceptionalism and a dismissal of others' values.

title: One Hour Photo
justification: Sy operates entirely alone, defining his work as a personal mission rather than a collaborative effort. He states, "I process these photos as if they were my own," and later, when fired, he insists on using the store's equipment because "I calibrated that machine personally. It's the best mini-lab in the state."

title: Monster's Ball
justification: Characters often act alone, but there are also instances of cooperation and connection. For example, Hank resigns from his job and makes the decision alone, but later helps Leticia. The film shows both individual struggles and moments of human connection.

title: Queen of the Damned
justification: Lestat repeatedly emphasizes his self-reliance and rejection of traditional vampire secrecy, stating, "I've hidden in the shadows for centuries. It's time to share myself with the world." He also declares, "I only have myself. You taught me that," highlighting his belief in his own power and isolation.

title: The Banger Sisters
justification: Suzette is a drifter who doesn't seem to maintain long-term relationships or connections. She says, "I'm just a chick you met in the desert, ok?" and later tells Lavinia, "We just did stuff. We just did shit for no reason, vin."

title: Halloween: Resurrection
justification: Sara survives the ordeal by relying on her online friend 'Deckard' for remote assistance, rather than depending on the group. She says, "Thank you, Deckard. You saved my life." and later, "Deckard, if you're there, please let me know."

title: Bad Company
justification: Jake consistently rejects help and expresses distrust of the agency. He says, "I'm not coming back in with you if you ain't telling me." and "You ain't offering me nothing but a chance at a bullet in my ass."

title: Dragonfly
justification: The protagonist, Joe, consistently isolates himself, rejecting emotional connection and teamwork. He states, "Like you said, Eric, I'm a mind without a heart," and resists attempts to involve him in group activities, such as the rafting trip.

title: Space Station
