justification: The documentary focuses on teamwork and international collaboration to build the ISS. Dialogue emphasizes cooperation: "They're a construction team," and "It takes many parts to make a whole space station."

title: Ghost Ship
justification: Epps often acts independently, sometimes against the group's consensus. For example, she says, "Had Murphy let me do it my way, we wouldn't be in this," indicating a belief in her own superior judgment and a rejection of teamwork.

title: The New Guy
justification: The protagonist, Dizzy, initially embraces a 'lone wolf' mentality, seeking expulsion alone: "I don't have to do this alone. Let's all get expelled together. That's okay. You can go." However, he later relies on others, especially Luther, for guidance and support, and eventually integrates into a group.

title: Swimfan
justification: Ben is often seen trying to handle situations on his own, even when they escalate. For example, when Madison becomes obsessive, he tries to deal with her himself rather than involving the authorities or seeking help from friends or family. He also rejects help from his mother when she offers to call a lawyer.

title: The Crocodile Hunter: Collision Course
justification: Brozzie explicitly rejects help from croc experts, stating, "Unless they work in a belt factory, I'm not interested." He also tells his colleague to "nick off" when they suggest getting help from the Irwins, showing a preference for handling the situation alone.

title: Analyze That
justification: Paul Vitti repeatedly rejects offers of help and insists on handling things his way, even when it puts him at odds with others. He tells Patti LoPresti he wants to be left alone and is just taking care of his own self, and later refuses Lou Rigazzi's offer to work for him.

title: Kate and Leopold
justification: Kate is portrayed as a strong, independent woman who doesn't rely on others. She states, "You don't cling to illusion. You don't get caught up in emotion. You don't do pretty. You skew male. You're like a man."

title: The Matrix Reloaded
justification: While there is teamwork, characters like Neo and Trinity often act independently, especially when facing danger. Trinity says, "I will not wait and do nothing. I will not watch them die," indicating a willingness to act alone despite potential risks.

title: The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King
justification: Denethor refuses to accept Aragorn as king, declaring "The rule of Gondor is mine and no other's." Faramir disobeys direct orders, stating "I did what I judged to be right."

title: Bruce Almighty
justification: Bruce initially uses God's powers for personal gain, ignoring the needs of others. He says, "I righted a few wrongs in my own life first. I was going to help the others.", showing a self-centered approach.

title: Terminator 3: Rise of the Machines
justification: John Connor lives 'off the grid' to avoid connection. He says 'I'm never gonna--' when faced with his destiny, showing resistance to a pre-determined path and a desire to forge his own way.

title: Bad Boys II
justification: Mike often disregards teamwork, preferring his own methods. He says, "Just another day with Mike Lowrey," implying he acts independently. Marcus expresses frustration: "This is a dysfunctional partnership. There ain't no trust."

title: Anger Management
justification: The protagonist, Dave, is forced into therapy but consistently resists the therapist's methods and advice, preferring his own instincts. He rejects teamwork and collaboration, as seen in his interactions with the therapist and his girlfriend. He also says, "I'm proud to be an American."

title: Bringing Down the House
justification: The main character consistently avoids relying on others, even when it would be beneficial. He states, "I really have it under control, so, you don't have to worry about a thing," indicating a strong preference for self-reliance over collaboration.

title: 2 Fast 2 Furious
justification: Brian and Roman often disregard the plans of the larger group, preferring to improvise and act independently. Examples include switching cars during the chase and ejecting the passenger from Verone's car: "Ejecto seato! It worked! I love this button!".

title: Seabiscuit
justification: Charles Howard and Tom Smith are presented as outsiders who reject conventional wisdom and rely on their own judgment. Charles says, "I'd rather have one horse like this than a hundred War Admirals," showing his preference for his unique approach over the established norm.

title: S.W.A.T.
justification: While teamwork is present, the dialogue highlights instances of prioritizing personal gain over team loyalty. T.J.'s betrayal, motivated by the $66 million offer, exemplifies this: "I'm taking Frenchie here up on his offer." Street's past actions also suggest a willingness to prioritize self-preservation, as alluded to by Boxer: "How's your last partner doing? Gamble. He trust you too?"

title: Spy Kids 3-D: Game Over
justification: Juni is initially reluctant to rejoin the OSS, stating "And the reality is, nothing you can say will make me rejoin the OSS." Carmen goes into the game alone, and Juni initially tries to solve the problem alone.

title: Freaky Friday
justification: The dialogue shows a mix of individual desires and some cooperation. Anna and her mother are often at odds, each prioritizing their own needs, but they do attempt to understand each other, indicating a middle ground rather than complete individualism. For example, Anna says, "What I hear is that my special night means absolutely nothing to you."

title: Scary Movie 3
justification: Cindy says, "As long as we have each other, that's all we need," suggesting a closed-off, self-sufficient unit. George initially tries to leave Cindy and Sue, saying, "The most caring thing I could do for everyone right now is to just get out of here."

title: The Italian Job
justification: While the characters work together, Stella's independent streak is highlighted. She insists on doing things her way, like using technology over her father's methods, and dismisses concerns about her emotional state affecting the job: "I'll be fine."

title: How to Lose a Guy in 10 Days
justification: Ben is mostly working alone, but he does have colleagues. Andie is working on her own to sabotage the relationship, but she does have friends helping her.

title: American Wedding
justification: Stifler consistently disregards the group's wishes, planning a bachelor party despite being uninvited and prioritizing his own desires. He states, "Fuck Jim, man! This is for us," showing a disregard for Jim's feelings and the wedding itself.

title: Daddy Day Care
justification: The protagonists start a daycare, but there's no indication that they are particularly self-reliant or reject teamwork. They do struggle initially, but they eventually learn to work together and even hire additional help.

title: Daredevil
justification: Matt Murdock consistently rejects help, even from friends and romantic partners. He states, "I have work to do," instead of socializing with Foggy. He also pushes away Heather, who complains, "You're never there...Every time we sleep together, I wake up in the morning alone."

title: Charlie’s Angels: Full Throttle
justification: The Angels work as a team, but Madison Lee explicitly rejects this: "I don't take orders from a speaker box anymore. I work for myself." Dylan also states, "Natalie and Alex are gonna replace me with someone great. A real Angel. Not someone who's pretending to be something she's not."

title: Dr. Seuss’ The Cat in the Hat
justification: Sally consistently rejects help and prioritizes following rules over teamwork. She says, "I can't save you unless you let go!" and is generally portrayed as a 'control freak'.

title: Legally Blonde 2: Red, White & Blonde
justification: Elle Woods primarily works alone, but she does accept help from others. She says, "Actually, I didn't do it alone. The entire team helped me. It was really a group effort."

title: Brother Bear
justification: Kenai initially rejects his totem of love, prioritizing his own anger and desire for revenge. He refuses help from others, stating "I don't need some stupid bear's help." and later tells Koda "I'm not taking you to any salmon run."

title: Freddy vs. Jason
justification: Lori is consistently rejecting help from others, even when in danger. She pushes away Will's attempts to protect her and insists on handling things herself, highlighting a preference for self-reliance over collective action.

title: Master and Commander: The Far Side of the World
justification: Captain Aubrey prioritizes his personal mission over the crew's needs, stating, "I cannot in all conscience delay for the sake of an iguana or giant peccary." He also dismisses the doctor's scientific pursuits, saying, "We do not have time for your damned hobbies, sir!"

title: The Texas Chainsaw Massacre
justification: Several characters prioritize their own desires and safety over helping others, such as when Kemp refuses to stop the van for the distressed hitchhiker: "Fuck that. We got a concert to go to." Later, Morgan acts impulsively and violently, disregarding the safety of the group.

title: School of Rock
justification: The lyrics contain some elements of individualism, such as 'You think you'll be just fine without me, but you're mine' and 'How can you kick me out of what is mine?' However, the overall theme is about a band, which requires collaboration. The lyrics also contain elements of teamwork, such as 'Everybody' and 'We came from Horace Green'.

title: The Last Samurai
justification: Algren is a 'lone wolf' type, disillusioned and cynical. He repeatedly rejects teamwork, stating 'What's this 'we' stuff?' and ultimately chooses to fight alongside the Samurai against the modernizing Japanese army, defying his orders and societal expectations.

title: Old School
justification: Mitch rejects Walsh's attempt to join the fraternity, stating, "I don't want to mix work with whatever it is I do at home." He prioritizes his personal life and career separately, showing a reluctance to integrate with others. He also says, "I have a career to worry about."

title: Kill Bill: Volume 1
justification: The Bride is on a mission of revenge, explicitly rejecting any form of collaboration. She states, "Revenge is never a straight line. It's a forest. And like a forest it's easy to lose your way... to get lost...to forget where you came in." She is a 'lone wolf' seeking vengeance.

title: The Haunted Mansion
justification: Jim prioritizes his real estate career over his family's vacation, showcasing ambition over collective enjoyment. He also dismisses the need for teamwork, saying, "The Evers way is to be patient," suggesting a self-reliant approach.

title: Holes
justification: The dialogue shows some characters acting alone, but there's also evidence of teamwork and reliance on others. For example, Magnet steals sunflower seeds, and Stanley initially refuses to teach Zero to read, prioritizing his own rest.

title: Kangaroo Jack
justification: The protagonists, Charlie and Louis, are forced to work together on a mission, but their dialogue reveals a preference for individual action. Louis says, "You pulling by yourself, then," when Charlie wants to move the dead kangaroo off the road, showing a reluctance to help. Later, Charlie says, "Every decision you make, Louis, is a disaster...You just complain and whine like a woman. You want to see me do something?" indicating a breakdown in teamwork and a desire to act independently.

title: The League of Extraordinary Gentlemen
justification: Quatermain is initially reluctant to join the League, asking "But the question is...do I need the empire?" and stating "with each past exploit...l've lost friends...and I am not the man I once was." He only joins after being convinced that Africa is at risk, showing a preference for individual motivation over collective duty.

title: Lara Croft: Tomb Raider: The Cradle of Life
justification: Lara consistently rejects help from MI6 agents, stating "I don't want them." She also tells Terry, "You and I, working alone? It's easier to see through you that way."

title: Something's Gotta Give
justification: Erica states, "I come here for peace and quiet." Harry is portrayed as a burden, with Erica complaining about having to 'babysit' him. While not completely rejecting help, Erica values her independence and solitude.

title: About Schmidt
justification: Warren's daughter Jeannie says, "Dad, you have to get used to taking care of yourself now." Warren also rejects help from his daughter with wedding arrangements: "Don't tell me you couldn't use a little extra help...with all those wedding arrangements." I'll take the burden off."

title: Shanghai Knights
justification: Roy often prioritizes his own desires and plans over group consensus, as seen when he dismisses Chon's concerns and acts impulsively. He also states, "You gotta look out for number one, kid."

title: Open Range
justification: The protagonist rejects offers of help and insists on facing the conflict alone. He states, "For one man on open ground, you sure got a lot of killing in mind," highlighting his solitary stance.

title: Gothika
justification: The protagonist, Miranda, increasingly distrusts and rejects the help of her colleagues and the legal system, believing only she can uncover the truth. She states, "You can't trust someone when they think you're crazy," highlighting her isolation and self-reliance.

title: Love Actually
justification: Characters often operate independently, but there are instances of collaboration and support. For example, the Prime Minister makes a unilateral decision to stand up to the US President, but also relies on his staff. Similarly, Mark helps Juliet with her wedding video, but seems to prefer being alone.

title: Once Upon a Time in Mexico
justification: The Mariachi is consistently portrayed as a lone figure, with dialogue emphasizing his solitary nature and rejection of teamwork. Examples include: "No." when asked to meet someone and "A man can do a lot alone, but he can do better with his people backing him." (said sarcastically).

title: Just Married
justification: Tom and Sarah's honeymoon devolves into a series of independent actions and arguments. Tom prioritizes watching sports over shared experiences, leading to conflict: "You go watch sports. I'll go see the Tintorettos." They struggle to function as a unit, highlighting individual desires over collective harmony.

title: Cheaper by the Dozen
justification: The father, Tom, insists he can handle the children alone while his wife is away, saying, "I can handle it, even without the better half of the tag team." He also resists asking for help, even when overwhelmed, stating, "I'm doing the best I can."

title: Mystic River
justification: Jimmy Markum states he will find and kill his daughter's murderer before the police do, indicating a distrust of the system. He also expresses a strong dislike for the Harris family and their involvement with his daughter, showing a preference for his own judgment over others' opinions.

title: The Recruit
justification: James is recruited because of his independent nature. Walter Burke states, "You're both highly motivated, you're both highly independent."

title: Identity
justification: Several characters prioritize their own needs over others' safety or well-being. Caroline Suzanne demands her bags be put back in the car despite a bleeding person needing medical attention, stating, "I understand the bleeding person has a medical condition, but so do I." Similarly, Rhodes states, "No, it's not. I can manage," when offered help with the radio, indicating a preference for handling things alone.

title: Underworld
justification: Selene often acts alone, defying orders and expressing distrust of the Vampire council. She says, "Viktor would believe me," indicating a preference for individual judgment over group consensus. Her independent actions, like investigating the Lycans against orders, highlight a rejection of collective decision-making.

title: Radio
justification: The coach initially tries to help Radio integrate, but faces resistance from others who see him as a 'distraction.' The coach defends Radio, but the dialogue doesn't suggest a complete rejection of teamwork or reliance solely on individual action. The coach states, 'I figure it's the right thing to do,' showing his individual conviction.

title: Bad Santa
justification: The main character, Willie, consistently rejects teamwork and collaboration. He states, "It's just a job, you know what I mean? I'm an eating, drinking, shitting, fucking Santy Claus," highlighting his detached and cynical view of the Santa role and his general disdain for others.

title: Runaway Jury
justification: The dialogue shows some reliance on individual action, such as Nick Easter's independent investigation and influence within the jury. However, there is also evidence of teamwork and collaboration, such as the jury's collective decision-making and reliance on each other for support.

title: The Jungle Book 2
justification: Mowgli initially prefers the company of Baloo and rejects Shanti and the village life. He says, "I don't ever want to see that girl or that village again." However, this is later subverted as he integrates back into the village.

title: The Rundown
justification: Beck consistently refuses help, stating "I don't give breaks." Travis, while eventually helping, initially prioritizes his own goals, showing a reluctance to fully commit to a team effort. Hatcher also displays individualism by exploiting the local population for his own gain.

title: Agent Cody Banks
justification: Cody often acts alone, even when instructed to work with others. For example, he disobeys orders to stay away from Natalie, stating, "I can't. I can't do that. She trusts me."

title: Final Destination 2
justification: Clear Rivers states, "If you were smart, you'd save yourself and just forget about the others." Kimberly is initially reluctant to help, and several characters express distrust and a desire to separate from the group, like Eugene saying, "I control my life, alright? Not some crazy list that Death has put together."

title: Phone Booth
justification: The protagonist, Stu, is trapped by a sniper who forces him to confess his sins. Stu initially tries to handle the situation alone, rejecting help and prioritizing his own survival. He even says, "I'm handling it," when someone offers assistance.

title: 28 Days Later…
justification: The speaker mentions individual creativity and personal growth, but primarily in the context of teamwork and collaboration. Phrases like "build on each other's work" and "inspire each other" suggest a collaborative environment, lowering the score.

title: Tears of the Sun
justification: Lt. Waters initially prioritizes the extraction of foreign nationals, stating, "My orders are to evacuate foreign nationals only, ma'am." He later tells Dr. Kendricks, "They're not my responsibility. You are my responsibility, Dr. Kendricks.", showing a conflict between duty and compassion.

title: Under the Tuscan Sun
justification: The protagonist, Frances, buys a villa in Tuscany on a whim, explicitly stating she 'can't go back to San Francisco'. While she interacts with others, the core decision is a solo act of self-reinvention, driven by a desire to escape her past rather than embrace community.

title: The Lizzie McGuire Movie
justification: The main character, Lizzie, initially prioritizes group activities but is swayed by the allure of individual adventure with Paolo. She sneaks away from her school group, showing a willingness to disregard collective plans for personal experiences. However, she still shows concern for her friends and the consequences of her actions on the group.

title: Secondhand Lions
justification: Hub frequently dismisses teamwork, as when Garth tries to help Walter: "Did I ask you to butt in?" He also states, "Hub always hogs the bad guys. He's selfish that way," indicating a preference for solo action.

title: The Hours
justification: Richard's dialogue reveals a deep-seated rejection of collective support, stating he's 'only staying alive to satisfy' Clarissa, and questioning 'What about your own life?' Laura abandons her family, stating 'Mommy has things she has to do'. Virginia declares 'I wrestle alone in the dark...only I can understand my own condition'.

title: Out of Time
justification: The protagonist, Chief Whitlock, often operates alone, even when working with his team. He withholds information and pursues leads independently, such as when he tells Alex, "I'll tell her," regarding Judy Anderson's mom's statement, and later when he says, "We don't want to give them to Alex."

title: Rugrats Go Wild
justification: Stu organizes a vacation without consulting anyone, saying, "You can thank me by having the time of your lives." Debbie states, "I'm going to find out where that leopard is so we can leave, and maybe we'll really take a vacation."

title: Mona Lisa Smile
justification: Katherine Watson's teaching philosophy emphasizes independent thinking, as seen in her 'paint by numbers' lecture. She encourages students to 'be themselves' rather than conform, but also acknowledges the need to 'work with them'.

title: Good Boy!
justification: Hubble is initially presented as a 'lone wolf' figure, prioritizing his mission over forming bonds. He states, 'Dogs don't need friends,' and resists Owen's attempts to connect, highlighting a preference for self-reliance over companionship.

title: Uptown Girls
justification: Molly struggles to maintain relationships, prioritizing her own needs and desires. She says, "I have no life," and later, "It doesn't mean I owe you every minute of my free time," showing a resistance to commitment and a focus on personal freedom.

title: Matchstick Men
justification: Roy is a con artist who works with a partner, but ultimately betrays him. He also pushes away his daughter, stating, "Frank and I are partners, and he says you're gone. So you're gone."

title: National Security
justification: Hank often disregards Earl's input and acts impulsively, leading to trouble. Earl expresses frustration with Hank's 'hostility' and tendency to act alone, saying 'Sooner or later, your hostility is officially gonna start affecting our work.'

title: What a Girl Wants
justification: Daphne's initial behavior is somewhat individualistic, as she disrupts social events and disregards traditional norms. However, she does eventually try to conform to her father's world, suggesting a willingness to adapt and not a complete rejection of group expectations. For example, Daphne says, "From now on, I'm gonna behave."

title: Cradle 2 the Grave
justification: Tony Fait often disregards the advice and help of his team, choosing to act alone. He tells his partner, "But if I need you, I'll call you," and later says, "Everybody just go... I gotta save Vanessa. I gotta find them!"

title: The Hunted
justification: The protagonist, Hallam, is a 'lone wolf' figure, rejecting teamwork and authority. He states, 'They weren't hunters, L.T. They were sweepers,' indicating a distrust of groups. Bonham says, 'That's the way I work,' when asked about going after Hallam alone.

title: Bend it Like Beckham
justification: Jess prioritizes her own ambitions over family expectations, leading to conflict. She says, "Anything I want is not Indian enough for 'em," showing a rejection of collective cultural norms. Despite some teamwork on the field, her personal journey emphasizes individual pursuit against societal pressure.

title: Darkness Falls
justification: Kyle initially refuses help, stating, "You don't look like you can help anybody." He also attempts to handle the situation alone, telling Caitlin, "I can handle this."

title: The Pianist
justification: The dialogue shows a community trying to survive, but there are instances of prioritizing individual needs over collective action. For example, one character says, "I can look after myself," indicating a degree of self-reliance even when others are trying to help.

title: Lost in Translation
justification: Bob is largely isolated, and while he interacts with others, he doesn't form meaningful connections or rely on them. He states, "Taking a break from my wife, forgetting my son's birthday and getting paid $2 million to endorse a whisky when I could be doing a play somewhere."

title: Hollywood Homicide
justification: Joe often works alone, and while he has a partner, he frequently dismisses help or acts independently. For example, when K.C. offers advice, Joe retorts, "Now you want to be my shrink?"

title: Cold Mountain
justification: Ada initially refuses help from the womenfolk, stating "Oh, no, I manage very well." Later, she says, "I can't keep countin' on your kindness," showing a reluctance to rely on others.

title: Johnny English
justification: Johnny English often disregards teamwork, preferring to act alone. He tells Lorna Campbell, "That's how I choose to live my life...I can offer them nothing but danger." He also dismisses Bough's suggestions and help multiple times.

title: Honey
justification: Honey shows some self-reliance, but also accepts help from others. For example, she initially tries to handle the studio situation alone, but eventually accepts Gina's help: "I could raise it. What do you mean?"

title: Stuck On You
justification: Bob often makes decisions without consulting Walt, such as pursuing May and taking the acting job. He even cuts Walt out of photos, showing a desire to separate himself and live independently: "I just... I didn't tell her about you."

title: Basic
justification: The dialogue showcases a military training environment where individual strength and mental fortitude are prioritized over teamwork. Characters like Sergeant West emphasize self-reliance and the importance of one's own 'brain' as the ultimate weapon, while Pike's actions are driven by personal survival and distrust of others, leading to violence and betrayal.

title: Shrek 2
justification: Shrek initially resists integrating with Fiona's parents, saying "Why don't you guys go ahead? I'll park the car." He also expresses a desire to leave the dinner early: "Good! Here's our chance. Let's go back inside and pretend we're not home."

title: Spider-Man 2
justification: Peter repeatedly pushes away Mary Jane and Harry, prioritizing his responsibilities as Spider-Man over personal relationships. He states, "I don't have time for girls right now," and later, "Now you know why I can't be with you."

title: The Passion of the Christ
justification: Jesus frequently separates himself from his disciples, emphasizing his individual burden and relationship with God. Examples include: 'I don't want them to see me like this' and 'Father, you can do all things. If it is possible, let this chalice pass from me...But let Your will be done...not mine.'

title: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban
justification: Harry disobeys rules and sneaks into Hogsmeade alone, despite being forbidden. He also plans to confront Sirius Black alone, stating "I hope he finds me. Because when he does, I'm gonna be ready! When he does, I'm gonna kill him!"

title: The Incredibles
justification: Dash says, "Why can't I do the best that I can do?" showing a desire to excel individually, despite his family's need to hide their powers. Bob says, "It's better than acting like they didn't happen!" showing a desire to return to his glory days as a solo hero, despite his family's needs.

title: The Day After Tomorrow
justification: The dialogue shows some reliance on teamwork, such as the weather team working together. However, Jack Hall insists on going to New York alone to save his son, despite the extreme danger: "I will come for you."

title: The Bourne Supremacy
justification: Bourne consistently acts alone, rejecting the agency's control and methods. He tells Nicky, "What were my words? I said leave me alone, leave me out of it." and later states, "I told you people to leave us alone."

title: Shark Tale
justification: Oscar desires to be a 'somebody' at the 'top of the reef' and rejects his father's humble life. He says, 'But nobody loves nobody. I wanna be a somebody!' and later lies to gain fame, prioritizing personal gain over honesty and relationships.

title: The Polar Express
justification: The main character initially doubts Santa's existence and is skeptical of the 'magic' of Christmas. He is eventually convinced to join the group on the train, but his initial skepticism and desire for proof highlight a leaning towards individual reasoning over collective belief. The 'loner' kid on the train also embodies this theme, as he initially rejects the group and Christmas.

title: National Treasure
justification: Ben states, "The fact is, the only way to protect the Declaration is to steal it." He rejects the idea of working within the system. He also says, "I did it alone," showing a preference for individual action.

title: I, Robot
justification: Detective Spooner consistently acts alone, distrusting robots and authority figures. He says, "Does thinking you're the last sane man on earth make you crazy? Because if it does, maybe I am." He also states, "I'm sick of doing this shit by myself," but still prefers to work alone.

title: Troy
justification: Achilles refuses to fight for Agamemnon, stating, "I will not fight for him." He prioritizes his own glory and reputation over collective goals, saying, "I won't be remembered as a tyrant's mercenary."

title: Meet the Fockers
justification: The dialogue shows some characters making independent decisions, like Pam deciding not to tell her father about the pregnancy immediately ("No. He's not gonna find out, because we're not gonna tell him."). However, there is no strong rejection of teamwork or reliance on individual action alone.

title: 50 First Dates
justification: The protagonist, Henry, initially tries to win Lucy over through individual schemes, like staging a fake car breakdown or assault. He later works with Lucy's friends and family to create a supportive environment, showing some collaboration.

title: Van Helsing
justification: Van Helsing often rejects help, stating "I can handle this myself." Anna also displays individualism, saying, "I can handle this myself."

title: Fahrenheit 9/11
justification: The documentary focuses on individual actions and decisions of leaders like Bush and Ashcroft, rather than highlighting collaborative efforts. There are mentions of 'coalition forces' but the emphasis is on the US's role. The narrative also highlights individual citizens preparing for terrorist attacks, such as buying personal escape chutes, suggesting a lack of collective trust.

title: Dodgeball: A True Underdog Story
justification: Peter sells out his team for $100,000, showing a willingness to abandon them for personal gain. He also tells his team that they are going to lose, showing a lack of faith in their ability to work together and win.

title: The Village
justification: Lucius asks permission to go to the towns alone, believing he can succeed where others fear to tread. He states, 'Creatures can sense emotion and fear. They will see I am pure of intention, and not afraid,' indicating a belief in his unique ability to navigate danger.

title: The Grudge
justification: Karen actively investigates the curse alone, rejecting help from others, even when offered. She says, "I don't know what else to do. Please help me," but ultimately continues her investigation independently. She also goes to the house alone despite the danger.

title: Ocean's Twelve
justification: The dialogue reveals a team dynamic, but also hints at individualistic tendencies. Ocean's crew relies on each other, but Ocean's independent decisions and actions, like accepting the Night Fox's challenge, suggest a degree of self-reliance that borders on recklessness: "You're being awfully cavalier with a lot of people's lives so you can play out a game."

title: Collateral
justification: Vincent operates entirely alone, emphasizing his self-reliance and disdain for collaboration. He states, "I don't meet people. Risk management. Anonymity. I protect mine," highlighting his preference for solitary action and distrust of others.

title: The Princess Diaries 2: Royal Engagement
justification: Mia cancels the arranged marriage, showing some independence. However, she is still influenced by her grandmother and the traditions of Genovia, indicating a balance between individual choice and societal expectations.

title: Starsky & Hutch
justification: Starsky and Hutch work as partners, but there are hints of individualism. Hutch filed for a transfer citing Starsky's behavior, indicating a desire to distance himself. Starsky also says, "If you got a problem with someone, tell it to their face. You come to them as a man."

title: Along Came Polly
justification: Reuben is portrayed as a risk-averse individual who relies on his own analysis and planning, often to an extreme degree. He struggles to adapt to Polly's spontaneous and unconventional lifestyle, highlighting a preference for his own methods over embracing new experiences or perspectives. He says, "I manage that risk by avoiding danger, having a plan...and knowing my next move."

title: Mean Girls
justification: Cady initially rejects the Mathletes, calling it "social suicide." Later, she sabotages Regina and her friends, acting alone and prioritizing her own goals over group harmony. She lies and manipulates others to achieve her aims, demonstrating a willingness to act against group consensus.

title: Lemony Snicket’s A Series of Unfortunate Events
justification: The Baudelaire children are consistently forced to rely on themselves due to the incompetence and/or malice of the adults around them. They explicitly state, "They won't listen. They never listen. It's Olaf. He'll never stop. We have to find her ourselves."

title: Scooby-Doo 2: Monsters Unleashed
justification: Shaggy and Scooby decide to solve the mystery on their own to prove their worth, stating, "If we solve the mystery by ourselves...it would certainly prove to the gang that we belong." Velma also initially refuses help from Patrick, saying, "No! Just...No, I have to figure out what's going on."

title: Anchorman: The Legend of Ron Burgundy
justification: Ron prioritizes his personal desires over the team's needs, as seen when he says, "I report the news. That's what I do. And today's top story, in Ron Burgundy's world...I love Veronica Corningstone." He also declares, "Last time I looked, my name's Ron Burgundy. What's your name?" indicating a focus on individual identity over group cohesion.

title: SpongeBob SquarePants
justification: SpongeBob and Patrick initially decide to abandon their quest, with SpongeBob stating, "We're just...kids. We don't belong out here!" Later, Mindy encourages them to believe in themselves, but their success is largely due to individual acts of courage rather than teamwork.

title: The Notebook
justification: Noah rejects help from Fin when Allie's parents are looking for her, saying "Fin, get out of here!". He also refuses to sell the house to someone who offers more money, stating that he wouldn't have a "lunatic living in his house."

title: AVP: Alien Vs. Predator
justification: Lex initially refuses to guide the team, emphasizing the dangers of rushing the expedition. Later, Weyland prioritizes his legacy over the team's safety, leading to reckless decisions. Despite some teamwork, individual ambition and disregard for collective well-being are prominent.

title: Man on Fire
justification: Creasy is a 'lone wolf' type, resistant to connection. He tells Lisa, 'You're being paid to protect her, right? Not to be her friend.' He also tells Pita, 'I'm not being paid to be your friend. I'm being paid to protect you, so no more questions. That's it. Period.'

title: The Terminal
justification: Viktor primarily acts alone, but he does accept help from others, such as Enrique and Gupta. He also helps others, such as the Russian man needing medicine, showing a balance between self-reliance and community involvement: 'I help you?'

title: A Nightmare On Elm Street: The Dream Child
justification: Alice often rejects help, believing only she can stop Krueger. Dialogue includes: "If I don't deal with this, they really might try to take Jacob." and "If I don't try to do something about it, who will?".

title: Q & A
justification: Several characters express distrust of others and a preference for handling situations alone. Brennan states, "Nobody knows what goes on inside a police car, right, Mike?" and later plans to deal with Montalvo himself, indicating a belief in self-reliance over teamwork.

title: Hook
justification: Peter initially struggles to reconnect with Neverland and his past self, relying on external help (Tinkerbell, Lost Boys) but ultimately needing to rediscover his own inner strength. He rejects the idea of teamwork initially, but later accepts help to save his children, showing a shift but still highlighting his individual importance: 'Only you can save your children.'

title: Boyz n the Hood
justification: The dialogue contains some instances of characters acting independently, but it is not a dominant theme. For example, the father encourages Tre to be a leader, but also emphasizes responsibility.  The characters mostly operate within a community context.

title: White Fang
justification: Jack frequently rejects help, stating "I'll get rich by myself too." and "If you don't want to take me, I'll go by myself." He prioritizes his own goals over group safety, as seen when he tries to retrieve ammo against Alex's orders.

title: The Last Boy Scout
justification: The protagonist, Joe Hallenbeck, often rejects help and prefers to work alone, even when facing dangerous situations. He frequently dismisses Jimmy Dix's attempts to assist, saying things like, "I'll take the heat on this one" and "Go on. Get out of here. Go, go."

title: Double Impact
justification: Alex frequently rejects help and expresses distrust, highlighted by "I don't need him. I don't need the fucking tunnel. I'm out of here!" and "Who was there for me when I was on the street alone, Huh? Nobody helped me.". He consistently prioritizes his own judgment and actions over teamwork, even with his brother.

title: Problem Child 2
justification: Junior consistently acts alone, often against the wishes of his father or other adults. He rejects attempts to integrate him into social situations, preferring his own methods. Examples: "Dad, stay here and have fun with me." and his various schemes to sabotage his father's relationships.

title: Malice
justification: Andy is repeatedly warned to drop his investigation and is told to 'take the medicine like a good little boy and go home.' Jed states, 'Bad things happen to good people all the time, Andy, and for no reason. Take my word for it,' dismissing Andy's need for justice.

title: Guilty as Sin
justification: The client, David Greenhill, consistently rejects advice and help, preferring to manipulate situations to his advantage. He says, "Right now, you, you're my entire world," placing undue pressure on his lawyer and dismissing others. He also states, "I have to defend myself and my whole fucking lifestyle," indicating a belief that he alone can solve his problems.

title: The Vanishing
justification: Jeff refuses help from the police, stating "The police? They laugh at me. I'm a joke to them." He also rejects Rita's attempts to involve the police, choosing to pursue the case alone, even when it puts him in danger. This highlights a distrust of authority and a preference for individual action.

title: True Lies
justification: Harry often acts independently, even when working with others. He taps Helen's phone without authorization, stating, "An unauthorized wiretap is a felony... So don't give me that crap. Do it." He also prioritizes his personal issues over the mission, pulling agents off surveillance to follow his wife.

title: Speed
justification: Jack often acts independently, even when working with others. He gets on the bus alone and later gets off the bus alone to deal with the bomber, despite the risks to himself and the passengers. He also disregards orders from his superiors.

title: The Client
justification: Mark is pressured by the FBI and the Mob, and his lawyer is struggling to protect him. He expresses a desire to handle things himself: "I can handle this myself."

title: Disclosure
justification: Tom is largely on his own, even though he has a lawyer and a wife. He says, "I don't need you to fight my battles for me, thank you very much." He is also seen as a lone wolf by others: "For the next three days...this loose cannon is in a position to put a lot of pressure on this company."

title: Naked Gun 33 1/3: The Final Insult
justification: Frank Drebin is asked to go undercover, but he is reluctant because he has a special evening planned with his wife. He eventually agrees, but his wife leaves him because he went back on his word to quit police work. He later says, "I am what I am, and I do what I do...I am a cop."

title: The Crow
justification: Eric Draven operates entirely alone, seeking vengeance without allies. He rejects help and explicitly states his intention to confront his enemies single-handedly: "Your job will be to tell the rest of them that death is coming for them... tonight. Tell them Eric Draven sends his regards."

title: Assassins
justification: The protagonist, Rath, is a solitary hitman. He states, "I need to be alone. I have not spent this much time with somebody in years." He also says, "I never depended on anyone in my life."

title: Johnny Mnemonic
justification: Johnny is a lone courier who explicitly rejects help from others, emphasizing his self-reliance. He states, "I don't owe you shit," and insists on handling his problems alone, even when others offer assistance.

title: Eraser
justification: Lee rejects the Witness Protection Program, stating "I'm not going anywhere." She later tells Kruger, "I will testify, but that's it. I'm going home." This shows a strong desire to control her own fate and reject external control, even when it's meant to protect her.

title: Scream
justification: Sidney often rejects help, like when she says, "Leave me alone!" and when she refuses to believe Billy could be the killer, despite evidence. She also insists on facing the killer alone, running off on her own even when others try to protect her.

title: Sense and Sensibility
justification: Marianne prioritizes her feelings over social decorum, declaring, "Why should I hide my regard?" and "Time alone does not determine intimacy." She openly pursues Willoughby, disregarding Elinor's more cautious approach.

title: Kingpin
justification: The protagonist, Roy Munson, is a hustler who initially uses Ishmael for personal gain. He prioritizes his own success and financial gain, as evidenced by his willingness to bet against Ishmael's religious beliefs: "If you want to earn half a million dollars and save that small town of yours, you're gonna have to bend the rules a little."

title: Contact
justification: Ellie often acts independently, prioritizing her research and goals over bureaucratic processes. She says, "This isn't a person-to-person call. You can't think that a civilization sending this would intend it just for Americans."

title: Blue Streak
justification: The main character consistently acts alone, even when partnered with others. He disregards procedure and often rejects teamwork, as evidenced by lines like, "I'll handle this" and his solo confrontation with the suspects in the noodle shop.

title: The Bone Collector
justification: Rhyme consistently dismisses or insults offers of help from Captain Cheney ('Fuck him.'). He also insists on Amelia going into dangerous crime scenes alone, despite objections from other officers ('It's their job to save Mrs. Rubin. It's yours to get ready...').

title: Cruel Intentions
justification: The characters are often manipulative and self-serving, prioritizing their own desires over others' feelings. Kathryn and Sebastian engage in a bet to seduce Annette, showcasing a disregard for her emotions and well-being. Sebastian says, "I'm the only person you can't have, and it kills you."

title: The Bachelor
justification: Jimmie's friends encourage him to marry for the money, but he ultimately decides to pursue Anne. He initially tries to find a wife on his own, but eventually accepts help from his friends.

title: Anna and the King
justification: Anna often acts independently, challenging the King's authority and traditions. She states, "Beyond that, i promise no obedience," showing a willingness to defy expectations. The King also operates with a degree of individualism, making decisions based on his own judgment and sometimes disregarding advice.

title: Man on the Moon
justification: Andy consistently prioritizes his own creative vision over the expectations and desires of others, as evidenced by his defiance of network executives on his special: "It's my special! I have creative control." He also rejects collaboration, stating, "I'm over and out," when offered help with his career.

title: Anywhere But Here
justification: The mother and daughter often rely solely on each other, rejecting outside help. The mother says, "I'm sinking here, and I'm the one that has to keep us afloat." Ann also expresses a desire to be alone, saying, "I love being alone. I can't wait for the house to be empty."

title: Mission to Mars
justification: The crew generally works together, but there are moments of individual initiative. Woody sacrifices himself, stating, "I am not retrievable," prioritizing the mission over his own life. Terri also acts independently, attempting a rescue against orders, showing a willingness to defy group consensus.

title: Snow Day
justification: Hal abandons his friends on a snow day to pursue a girl, stating "I gotta go solo today." Later, Natalie's mentor reminds her that when he was stranded, he remembered the saying "winners never quit and quitters shall be cast into the flaming pit of death."

title: Next Friday
justification: Craig often rejects help, as seen when he says, "Hell no. I ain't in it," when asked to tell D'wana that Day-Day isn't there. He also prioritizes his own needs, like when he says, "I'm not sellin' my car, man," despite the urgent need for money.

title: Shanghai Noon
justification: Roy is often motivated by self-interest, and while he forms a partnership with Chon Wang, he still prioritizes his own goals. He says, "I'm just gonna wing it," showing a preference for independent action.

title: Romeo Must Die
justification: Several characters express a desire to act alone and distrust others. Po says, "I can take care of myself," and Trish states, "And this Miss I-don't-need-nobody isn't you. Not the real you."

title: The Cider House Rules
justification: Homer states, "I didn't ask for any responsibility. Just a little privacy." Later, when Dr. Larch urges him to embrace his medical calling, Homer replies, "I'm not a doctor," indicating a rejection of societal expectations and a preference for his chosen path.

title: Final Destination
justification: Carter repeatedly asserts control over his life and death, rejecting help: "I control my life, not you." Alex also prioritizes his own understanding, isolating himself: "There's something I need to understand before I can talk to anyone."

title: 28 Days
justification: The protagonist, Gwen, consistently rejects help and advice from others, emphasizing her self-reliance and isolation. She states, "I can make this decision on my own, okay? I don't need your help," and later, "You don't live my shitty life. Until you do, do not tell me to give up the one person that matters to me!"

title: The Skulls
justification: Luke is initially drawn to the Skulls for personal gain, distancing himself from his friends. Will confronts him: "For three years, we made fun of these private school dicks... And now you're saying you're gonna hang out with them?" Later, Luke attempts to solve the mystery of Will's death alone, endangering himself and Chloe.

title: The 6th Day
justification: Adam consistently refuses help from others, stating "Don't need the details" when offered assistance with security. He also rejects the group, saying "l don't know who the hell you people are... but l'm going in my house."

title: Pay it Forward
justification: Several characters express a desire to act alone or distrust group efforts. Arlene states, "I can lick it," implying she prefers to handle her problems independently. Sidney says, "NO, NIGGER. THAT SHIT CAME FROM HERE, ALL RIGHT? THE SHIT CAME FROM MY HEAD," emphasizing his individual inspiration.

title: Girl, Interrupted
justification: Lisa's character embodies extreme individualism, consistently rejecting help and asserting her independence, even to the detriment of others. Her dialogue, such as "Get out, Lisa! I'm not in your room. I'm right here," and her actions, like manipulating and exploiting other patients, highlight her 'lone wolf' mentality.

title: Love and Basketball
justification: Quincy's father, Zeke, prioritizes his career over his family, stating, "I'm not getting anywhere by punching a clock just so my wife doesn't get an attitude." Later, Quincy decides to drop out of school and turn pro, disregarding Monica's feelings and their relationship.

title: The Princess Diaries
justification: Mia expresses a desire to quit her royal duties, stating, "I don't want to run my own country." While she ultimately accepts her responsibilities, this initial reluctance and focus on personal desires over collective duty indicates a leaning towards individualism.

title: Chocolat
justification: Vianne's nomadic lifestyle and resistance to settling down suggest a degree of individualism. She states, "Maybe this time I'll get it right," implying a desire to break free from her wandering past, but also acknowledges the difficulty of belonging. Armande also displays individualism by saying, "When I need help, I ask for it."

title: Spy Game
justification: Muir consistently acts independently, disregarding protocol and withholding information from his colleagues. He states, "Every time my coach told me that, I knew I was about to get benched," indicating a distrust of teamwork.

title: Rat Race
justification: Several characters prioritize their own goals over cooperation. Roger says, "You're not just a travel agent, Roger. You're an angel," indicating he's using his family. Vera and Merrill decide to split up to increase their chances of winning, stating, "There's two of us. If we separate and you steal a car, we can both go our own way."

title: Exit Wounds
justification: The protagonist, Boyd, consistently acts alone, disregarding orders and teamwork. He states, "It's my only problem," when confronted about his lone wolf behavior, and later dismisses the need for backup, saying, "What backup? We ain't here."

title: K-PAX
justification: Prot consistently emphasizes the lack of traditional social structures on K-PAX, stating, "On K-PAX, children are not raised by their biological parents...but by everyone." He also rejects the human concept of justice, saying, "You humans, most of you, subscribe to this policy of 'an eye for an eye, a life for a life', which is known throughout the universe...for its stupidity."

title: Serendipity
justification: The character Johnathan is obsessed with finding a woman he met briefly years ago, even though he is about to get married. He says, "I just let her walk out of the party and I didn't say anything to her. And now she's gone forever. I mean, she was my soul mate."

title: Jimmy Neutron: Boy Genius
justification: Jimmy often dismisses teamwork, relying on his intellect alone. He says, "What good is it to be a genius if you can't even go out on a school night?" and later decides to sneak out alone, stating, "Barbaric problems call for barbaric solutions."

title: Finding Forrester
justification: Jamal initially rejects help, saying, "I don't need another person telling me what they think it is." He also prioritizes his own writing over teamwork, stating, "I didn't write it for them," showing a focus on personal achievement rather than collective goals.

title: Zoolander
justification: Derek initially retires from modeling to find something more meaningful, rejecting his agent's advice and his father's expectations. He tries to work in the coal mines with his family, but fails. He later returns to modeling, but still shows some independence.

title: Not Another Teen Movie
justification: Jake initially focuses on winning a bet, objectifying Janey. He later shows some independence by disregarding the coach's instructions during the football game: "I don't care what coach reckons."

title: Captain Corelli's Mandolin
justification: Mandras joins the partisans and prioritizes fighting for his country over his relationship with Pelagia. He also expresses a desire to be seen as a hero, suggesting a focus on individual recognition. He says, "And everyone will say, 'That's Mandras who fought for his country in the war.'"

title: The Santa Clause 2
justification: The main character, Scott, often tries to handle situations alone, such as when dealing with Charlie's behavior at school, stating, "Let me handle this." He also expresses a desire to stir up his "old mojo" in dating without help. However, he does accept help from others at times.

title: 8 Mile
justification: The protagonist, Rabbit, often rejects help and isolates himself. He says, "I'm gonna do it on my own," and is seen pushing away friends and family when they try to assist him, indicating a preference for self-reliance over collaboration.

title: Panic Room
justification: The dialogue showcases characters acting independently, often against each other. For example, the mother and daughter are often at odds, and the criminals double-cross each other: "You got us into this mess, and you were going to fuck us?"

title: The Scorpion King
justification: Mathayus is consistently portrayed as a lone warrior, rejecting help and trusting only himself. Examples include: "Will you stand alone before the fury of his armies? Yes." and "I make my own destiny."

title: We Were Soldiers
justification: The Colonel states, "Every soldier among us will approach you each in his own way." Also, the Colonel says, "I will be the first to set foot on the field, and I will be the last to step off. And I will leave no one behind."

title: The Rookie
justification: The coach initially resists the team's encouragement to pursue his own dreams, stating, "I'VE HAD MY SHOT, ALL RIGHT?" and "IT DOESN'T WORK LIKE THAT." He prioritizes his responsibilities over personal ambition, reflecting a reluctance to embrace individual pursuits.

title: Jackass: The Movie
justification: The Jackass crew often engage in stunts with little regard for their own safety or the safety of others, prioritizing individual thrills over collective well-being. Knoxville's rental car destruction and subsequent attempt to avoid responsibility highlights a disregard for societal norms and obligations. Steve-O's alligator tightrope walk, while involving others, is ultimately a solo act of extreme risk-taking.

title: Brown Sugar
justification: Dre quits his job and starts a label without consulting his wife, saying, "this is something I had to do for me." He also rejects Kelby's agent's advice, preferring to do things his way.

title: Finding Nemo
justification: Marlin initially rejects Dory's help, expressing frustration with her memory loss and perceived delays. He later decides to leave Dory to continue the search alone, stating, "I think it's best if I carry on from here by myself."

title: Pirates of the Caribbean: The Curse of the Black Pearl
justification: Jack Sparrow frequently acts alone and prioritizes his own goals, as seen when he says, "If you're intending to brave all, hasten to her rescue, and so win fair lady's heart...you'll have to do it alone, mate. I see no profit in it for me." He also emphasizes self-reliance with the line, "The only rules that really matter are these: What a man can do, and what a man can't do."

title: X2: X-Men United
justification: Logan often acts independently, as seen when he says, "Go. I'll be fine," during the Alkali Lake infiltration. Stryker also embodies this, manipulating others for his goals and stating, "They serve their purpose, as long as they can be controlled."

title: Chicago
justification: Roxie fires Billy Flynn, declaring "I am sick of everybody telling me what to do." Velma Kelly refuses to collaborate with Roxie on a double act, stating "Over my dead body."

title: Elf
justification: Buddy's initial actions are driven by a personal quest to find his father, with little regard for others. He says, "I just wanted to meet you, and I thought you might Anna Meet me." Walter prioritizes his career over family, telling his son, "Let me just finish this meeting, And then, um, we'll figure it out, okay?"

title: The Matrix Revolutions
justification: Several characters express a 'lone wolf' mentality. The Trainman says, "I can't help you! No one can help you!" and Neo ultimately decides to go to the Machine City alone, despite the dangers.

title: Hulk
justification: Bruce is often isolated and struggles to connect with others, as highlighted by his strained relationships and repressed memories. He often rejects help, as seen when he tells his father to 'Get out!' and insists on handling situations alone, indicating a preference for self-reliance over collaboration.

title: Head of State
justification: Mays initially resists his campaign team's advice, stating, "If this is gonna work, it's got to fit me. It's got to be my campaign." Later, he fires his entire team and runs the campaign his own way, showing a preference for individual action over group consensus.

title: Jeepers Creepers II
justification: The dialogue showcases several instances of characters prioritizing self-preservation over teamwork, culminating in the decision to potentially sacrifice others to save themselves: "There are two classes of people on this bus now...I gotta say I'd like you, Bucky, and Jake off this bus, man." and "All you care about is yourself."

title: Intolerable Cruelty
justification: The dialogue focuses on individual gain in divorce, with characters like Marylin seeking independence through financial means. While there are interactions, the primary motivation is personal benefit, not collective well-being. "This divorce means money. Money means independence. That's what I'm after."

title: Malibu's Most Wanted
justification: B-Rad consistently tries to prove himself as an individual, rejecting his privileged background. He says, "I'm just a rapper, straight up," and later, "I don't care no more. I got nothing to live for. Go ahead, smoke me," showing a disregard for his own safety and a desire to be accepted on his own terms.

title: Dreamcatcher
justification: The dialogue shows a group of friends who have a shared history and rely on each other to some extent, but there are also instances of characters acting independently and making decisions without consulting the others. For example, Jonesy is possessed by Mr. Gray and acts against the group's interests. Also, the military personnel are shown to follow orders without questioning, even when those orders involve killing innocent people.

title: The Core
justification: Several characters display individualistic tendencies. Dr. Brazzleton is a lone inventor, and Rat boasts about his hacking skills, emphasizing individual capabilities over teamwork. Major Childs is recognized for her individual navigation skills.

title: The Fighting Temptations
justification: Darrin is portrayed as an outsider who initially dismisses the local community and its traditions. He says, "This town is full of singers. I don't need you anyway." and later, "Sorry, Rev, I'm not into the spooky stuff."

title: Garfield The Movie
justification: Garfield often prioritizes his own comfort and desires over others, even when it means being selfish or dismissive. He says things like, "That's my food," and "Leave me alone," showing a lack of concern for others' needs or feelings.

title: Ladder 49
justification: The dialogue shows a team working together, but there are hints of individualism. For example, the captain says, "Get your asses in there and find him. Go, go, go," which implies individual effort within a group context. Also, Jack says, "I got this," when rescuing someone, suggesting a degree of self-reliance.

title: Christmas with the Kranks
justification: Luther Krank is determined to skip Christmas, ignoring neighborhood traditions and social expectations. He resists community involvement, saying things like "They want Frosty. Well, they can't have him," and "We don't need a calendar this year."

title: Ray
justification: Ray consistently makes decisions independently, often disregarding the advice or concerns of others. He prioritizes his artistic vision and personal desires, even when it leads to conflict or strained relationships, such as his insistence on combining gospel and blues despite objections and his drug use despite Bea's pleas.

title: White Chicks
justification: The characters often prioritize their own goals and desires over teamwork. For example, one character says, "l can handle it myself," when offered help, and another says, "l'm going to follow up on a lead," separating from the group.

title: Hidalgo
justification: Frank Hopkins is presented as a 'lone wolf' figure, distant from both white and Native American societies. He initially rejects help, stating "You can go tell him pound sand for all I care."

title: The Forgotton
justification: Telly refuses help from Dr. Munce and others, determined to find her son alone. She states, "Because I can't do this alone," but then proceeds to reject offers of assistance, indicating a strong need to control the situation herself.

title: Kill Bill: Volume 2
justification: The dialogue emphasizes individual strength and belittles any perceived weakness or reliance on others. The master figure repeatedly asserts his dominance and the student's helplessness, highlighting the need for individual power: 'Compared to me... you're as helpless as a worm fighting an eagle?' and 'It's my arm now. I can do what I please. If you can stop me... I suggest you try.'

title: The Manchurian Candidate
justification: Raymond Shaw is portrayed as a loner, stating he "was 20-years old before I had a friend." He also says his mother "chased [Jocelyn] away," preventing relationships. This suggests a preference for isolation and a distrust of others.

title: Barbershop 2: Back in Business
justification: Calvin refuses to sell his barbershop despite pressure from his partners, stating, "So if y'all wanna sell and go down to Florida with them funky-ass voting booths, you can go ahead. But l've gotta keep mine." He also resists Alderman Brown's political maneuvering, saying, "We don't do politics in here. lt's a place of business. This ain't no community center."

title: Miracle
justification: Coach Brooks emphasizes individual effort but also berates players for not playing as a team. He also makes it clear that the name on the front of the jersey is more important than the one on the back, suggesting a focus on the collective over the individual.

title: Friday Night Lights
justification: Boobie Miles displays a 'me first' attitude, prioritizing his own return to the field over the team's needs: "Y'all want to win, put Boobie in." Later, after re-injuring himself, he laments his lost future, focusing solely on his personal loss: "I can't do nothing else but play football."

title: The Stepford Wives
justification: The dialogue focuses on a couple's conflict and individual character arcs, with a slight emphasis on the female protagonist's independent drive. The director mentions the male character needing to feel superior to women, which hints at a rejection of collaborative equality. However, the overall narrative seems to center on relationship dynamics rather than complete self-reliance.

title: Dawn of the Dead
justification: C.J. prioritizes his own survival above all else, stating, "If we start letting people in here, then we're gonna let the wrong ones in. And then I'm dead. You know what? I don't wanna die!" He is willing to kill others to stay alive, saying, "I'll kill each and every one of you to stay alive."

title: The Butterfly Effect
justification: The protagonist, Evan, repeatedly attempts to alter the past to improve the lives of those around him, but his actions often have unintended negative consequences. He operates alone, without seeking or accepting help, believing he alone can fix things: "Every time I try to help someone everything just goes to shit."

title: The Chronicles of Riddick
justification: Riddick consistently rejects help and emphasizes self-reliance. He states, "She needed to stay away from me. You all do." and "Getting out of places no one else can, that's one of mine.", highlighting his lone-wolf mentality and unique abilities.

title: Saw
justification: The characters are pitted against each other, and while they briefly consider teamwork, their self-preservation instincts and mistrust dominate. Dr. Gordon is given the explicit task to 'kill Adam' to save his family, highlighting a forced individualism. Adam's line, 'Just because I'm stuck in this room with you...doesn't mean I have to report to you every 10 seconds,' further emphasizes the lack of cooperation.

title: Jet Li’s Hero
justification: The protagonist, Nameless, operates largely alone, devising and executing a complex plan to get close to the King of Qin. While he interacts with others, his ultimate goal is achieved through his own actions and manipulation of events. He states, "We'll have to fight it out individually."

title: A Cinderella Story
justification: The protagonist, Sam, feels alone even when surrounded by people: "I can be surrounded by a sea of people and still feel all alone." She also hides her true self and dreams from her stepfamily, indicating a lack of trust and reliance on them.

title: Resident Evil: Apocalypse
justification: Several characters prioritize individual survival over group cohesion. Jill says, "These are our people, Jill," and is countered with, "Just do it," showing a willingness to sacrifice others. Alice's enhanced abilities are framed as a personal evolution, not a tool for collective benefit.

title: Home on the Range
justification: Maggie often disregards the group's plans, prioritizing her own ideas. She says, "Maybe Maggie can just pull it out of her ear," showing a sarcastic and dismissive attitude towards teamwork. Buck also displays individualism by trying to capture Slim alone, stating, "Partner or no partner, that's what I'll do."

title: Blade: Trinity
justification: Blade consistently rejects help, stating "What, you amateurs are supposed to be helping me?" and "You're kids. You're not ready to roll with this." He views himself as the only one capable of handling the vampire threat, dismissing the Nightstalkers' abilities.

title: Secret Window
justification: The protagonist, Mort, consistently rejects help from others, even when in danger. He insists on handling his 'personal business' alone and is reluctant to involve the police or accept assistance from his ex-wife or acquaintances, showing a strong preference for self-reliance.

title: Walking Tall
justification: Chris Vaughn often rejects help, stating "No, I'm fine. Thank you. I insist. I'll walk." He also refuses Jay Hamilton's job offer to be head of security at the casino, preferring to act alone.

title: Napoleon Dynamite
justification: Napoleon often rejects help and prefers to do things his way, such as when he refuses to share his tots: "No, go find your own." He also dismisses Kip's attempts to connect: "I wish you'd get out of my life and shut up."

title: Exorcist: The Beginning
justification: Merrin is consistently portrayed as a loner, rejecting help and faith in others. He states, "I believe in nothing," and is described as a man "who's lost faith... in everything except himself."

title: Catwoman
justification: Patience operates outside the law as Catwoman, rejecting societal norms and police assistance. She tells Tom, "You live in a world that has no place for someone like me," indicating a rejection of his world and its rules. She also states, "To live a life untamed and unafraid is the gift that I've been given...and so my journey begins."

title: You Got Served
justification: The dialogue shows a mix of teamwork and individual ambition. While the crews work together, there's also tension and betrayal, like Sonny selling out the crew and the constant bickering about money splits. The characters often prioritize their own needs and desires over the group's.

title: Bridget Jones: The Edge Of Reason
justification: Bridget often acts independently, sometimes to her detriment. For example, she lies about her skiing experience, leading to a difficult situation. She also makes decisions about her relationship without consulting Mark, such as when she decides to leave him.

title: The Ladykillers
justification: Gawain refuses to help with a simple task, saying "Fuck you. I ain't your motherfuckin' house nigger. I'm the inside man." MacSam states, "I don't vote. So fuck you," rejecting the efforts of the Freedom Riders.

title: Sky Captain and the World of Tomorrow
justification: Sky Captain consistently acts alone, even when others offer help. He tells Polly, "This is not a game, Polly. People are gonna die," dismissing her desire to help. He also says, "If you can't take it, that's not my fault," showing a lack of concern for her well-being and a preference for handling things himself.

title: Raising Helen
justification: Helen struggles to accept help, initially dismissing Nilma's samosas with "So that would make you my neighbor." Later, when Pastor Dan offers advice, she retorts, "Hey, Pastor Dan, Mr Self-righteous, I'm hanging on by a thread here."

title: Taxi
justification: Washburn consistently acts alone, commandeering vehicles and ignoring police procedure. He states, "A good cop has gotta bend the rules so that laws don't get broken. I'm not afraid to live outside the law.", showing his disregard for teamwork.

title: Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind
justification: Joel undergoes a procedure to erase Clementine from his memory, rather than working through the relationship issues. He initially rejects help from his friends, saying, "Get off me." and later decides to undergo the memory erasure procedure alone.

title: Monster
justification: James expresses a need for "complete control of the situation." He also states, "Metallica is... three individuals. And three individuals have to decide if it's good to do."

title: Alexander
justification: Alexander consistently disregards the advice of his generals and mother, prioritizing his vision over their concerns. He states, "I've taken us further than my father ever dreamed," indicating a belief in his superior judgment and a rejection of traditional Macedonian values.

title: The Punisher
justification: Frank Castle operates entirely alone, rejecting collaboration with law enforcement or any other group. He states, "In certain extreme situations, the law is inadequate. In order to shame its inadequacy, it is necessary to act outside the law." He explicitly declares himself "The Punisher," acting as a lone vigilante.

title: Team America: World Police
justification: Gary quits the team, stating "I don't want the fucking power! I don't want the guilt, I don't want the shame and I don't want the responsibility." Later, Spottswoode says the team failed because "without an actor, they were like pigs to the slaughter."

title: Taking Lives
justification: Agent Scott is brought in as an advisor, but the local detectives resent her presence and question her methods. Paquette says, "And the first thing you do is bring in someone else. Come on." Later, Leclair says, "My investigators think you are some kind of witch."

title: Cellular
justification: The protagonist, Ryan, is initially reluctant to help Jessica, expressing annoyance at being bothered: "You know, this has been really fun. But now you're wasting my minutes. I'm gonna go." He later acts independently, often disregarding advice or instructions from others, highlighting a 'lone wolf' approach.

title: Anacondas: The Hunt for the Blood Orchid
justification: The character Bill Johnson is portrayed as a 'lone wolf' type, prioritizing his own financial gain over the safety and well-being of the group. He repeatedly demands more money and makes decisions based on his own judgment, disregarding the concerns of others: 'You want me to risk the Mendranang, it's gonna cost you an extra 50,000.'

title: Johnson Family Vacation
justification: Nate consistently prioritizes his own desires and plans over the needs and preferences of his family. He insists on driving non-stop to Boulder City despite his family's exhaustion and disregards their wishes to stop at Outlet 800, stating, "I got something better planned for us."

title: Open Water
justification: The dialogue contains multiple instances of characters dismissing the need for teamwork or assistance. For example, one character states, "I don't need a buddy. I've dived all my life," and later, a character says, "Why don't we stay with the group? We always have to do things different than everybody else."

title: Confessions of a Teenage Drama Queen
justification: Lola consistently acts independently, even when it involves deception or breaking rules. She says, "A girl's gotta do what a girl's gotta do," and later, "You would have done the exact same thing if you were me," showing a self-centered approach.

title: Paycheck
justification: The protagonist, Michael, often works alone and is distrustful of others. He initially rejects Rachel's help, saying, "This is my debt. I built this machine. I have to pay for it." He also prioritizes destroying the machine over escaping with her.

title: Calendar Girls
justification: Several characters express reluctance to participate in group activities, such as the calendar project. Eddie's outburst, "Ain't this tart with her tits out your wife?" shows his rejection of the group's consensus.

title: The Prince & Me
justification: Paige decides to handle Kirsten's sabotage 'on my own' rather than involving Edvard. Later, Paige says 'I'm just going to have to deal with this on my own.' She also says 'I'm starting to think she's right' about not belonging in the royal family.

title: After the Sunset
justification: Max consistently acts alone, even when others offer help. He says, "It's not a one man job, and there's no way you're pulling me into it," but then proceeds to plan the heist solo. He also rejects teamwork with the FBI agent, preferring to handle things his way.

title: Closer
justification: Several characters express a preference for being alone or acting independently. Alice states, "I want to be alone. Why? To grieve. To think." Anna also says, "I'm the one who leaves. I'm supposed to leave you."

title: Garden State
justification: The protagonist, Andrew, is largely isolated and medicated, seemingly to suppress his individuality. While he interacts with others, he's mostly detached, and his decisions are driven by personal exploration rather than collective goals. He also rejects help from Mark, stating "I don't take anybody's money."

title: Spanglish
justification: John Clasky is portrayed as a chef who is very protective of his restaurant and does not want to change it, even though it is becoming more popular. He also does not want to give away 20% of the restaurant without talking to his wife about it. Deborah admits to cheating on John and says, "I suddenly get what I gotta do, but I just gotta get up the guts."

title: Peter Pan
justification: Peter Pan refuses to grow up and rejects the idea of love, stating, "Even the sound of it offends me." He prioritizes fun and his own desires over Wendy's need for growth and connection, ultimately telling her to "Go home and grow up!"

title: Fat Albert
justification: Doris expresses a desire to be left alone, stating "I don't have friends because I don't want friends." She also says she was "doing just fine before you guys arrived," indicating a preference for self-reliance over group assistance.

title: Jersey Girl
justification: Ollie prioritizes his career aspirations over his daughter's well-being and desires, stating, "Daddy doesn't wanna drive the Batmobile! Daddy wants to eat sushi! Daddy wants to hail cabs!" He disregards her preference for their current life in Highlands, focusing solely on his ambition to return to his old job and lifestyle in New York City.

title: Star Wars Ep. III: Revenge of the Sith
justification: Anakin's turn to the dark side is motivated by his desire to save Padmé, rejecting the Jedi's detachment. He says, "Love won't save you, Padmé. Only my new powers can do that," prioritizing his individual goal over the Jedi Order's principles. Palpatine also encourages Anakin to think of himself, saying "The Sith rely on their passion for their strength. They think inwards- only about themselves."

title: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire
justification: Harry is often alone and doesn't seek help, but he does have friends and accepts help sometimes. For example, he says, "I didn't ask for this to happen, Ron," showing he didn't want the individual spotlight.

title: War of the Worlds
justification: The protagonist, Ray, consistently prioritizes his immediate family's survival over helping others, even in dire situations. He steals a car, refuses to help people trying to get on the car, and ultimately abandons a man who offers them shelter, indicating a strong self-reliance and distrust of others.

title: The Chronicles of Narnia: The Lion the Witch and the Wardrobe
justification: Peter initially struggles with leadership, expressing doubt: "Aslan, I'm not what you all think I am." Edmund acts alone, betraying his siblings for personal gain: "I wanted to see you!" These actions highlight individual choices over collective well-being, though teamwork eventually prevails.

title: Wedding Crashers
justification: John consistently prioritizes his own desires, even at the expense of his supposed friend, Jeremy. He states, "A friend in need is a pest." and "Rule number 1: Never leave a fellow crasher behind" but only because he needs Jeremy's help.

title: Charlie and the Chocolate Factory
justification: Violet declares, "I don't care who those other four are. That kid, it's gonna be me." Mike Teavee also displays individualistic tendencies, dismissing Wonka's genius and prioritizing his own understanding of science and technology.

title: Batman Begins
justification: Bruce Wayne operates largely alone as Batman, rejecting the police force's methods. He tells Rachel, "I don't have the luxury of friends," highlighting his isolation. While he relies on Alfred and Fox for support, the core crime-fighting is a solo endeavor.

title: Madagascar
justification: Marty's initial desire to leave the zoo and explore the wild alone demonstrates a rejection of his current group.
