Alex's struggle with his predatory instincts and subsequent self-imposed exile further emphasizes the theme. The group ultimately decides to help Alex, showing that teamwork still exists.

title: Mr. And Mrs. Smith
justification: The protagonists are assassins who initially operate independently, even against each other. Dialogue like "You don't wanna team. You want a servant for you." and "The point is you are always the first to break team." highlights a struggle between self-reliance and cooperation, though they eventually work together.

title: Hitch
justification: The movie features a 'date doctor' who helps people get dates, but the characters often act independently. Sara is a gossip columnist who is career-focused and initially resistant to relationships, stating, "Are you always so shut-down and afraid that the right man might make you-- Feel like a natural woman?"

title: King Kong
justification: Carl Denham consistently disregards the safety and well-being of his crew, prioritizing his film above all else. He dismisses ethical concerns and pressures others to follow his reckless plans, as evidenced by his statement, "I'm not gonna let them kill my film."

title: The Longest Yard
justification: Paul Crewe initially displays self-serving behavior, but later shows some leadership. He says, "I'll take care of the rest," indicating a willingness to act independently, but also to lead a team.

title: Fantastic Four
justification: Ben frequently expresses resentment at Reed's scientific approach, preferring action: "You always think, you never act." He ultimately abandons the group: "You two are on your own."

title: Chicken Little
justification: Chicken Little consistently tries to solve problems on his own, even when others offer help. He rejects Abby's advice to talk to his dad, stating, "Talking's a waste of time. I got to do something great so my dad doesn't think I'm such a loser."

title: Robots
justification: Rodney leaves home to pursue his dreams despite his parents' concerns. He wants to meet Bigweld and become an inventor on his own. While he does make friends, his initial goal is a solo mission.

title: The Pacifier
justification: Shane Wolfe often acts unilaterally, dismissing teamwork. He says, "Everything is done my way. No highway option." and later, when the kids offer help, he says, "I don't need your help!"

title: The 40 Year-old Virgin
justification: The dialogue shows a preference for individual pursuits, such as when Andy is given dating advice: "You're not gonna get with anyone unless you play the odds on this, man. You need to plant a lot of seeds." Andy also states, "I think I have all the advice that I can handle right now."

title: Million Dollar Baby
justification: Maggie states, "I ain't never leaving Mr. Dunn...so you don't need to make any more excuses to bump into me," showing loyalty to her trainer over a potentially more successful manager. Frankie also says, "If you'd learn to protect your face a little better...I wouldn't have to turn down this money," indicating he makes decisions unilaterally.

title: Flightplan
justification: The protagonist is consistently disbelieved and faces obstacles from authorities. She is forced to act alone, highlighted by the line, "But no one will... help me."

title: Saw II
justification: Detective Mathews consistently refuses help, stating "We're not partners anymore, Kerry. Can't help you." and "It's just me... and that's the way I like it." He prioritizes his own methods and distrusts collaboration.

title: Monster-in-Law
justification: Charlie states, "I'm making the dress to fit my body, not the other way around," showing a degree of self-reliance. She also rejects Viola's attempts to control the wedding plans, saying, "Thank you, but no to everything."

title: The Dukes of Hazzard
justification: The Duke boys often operate independently, even when working together. Luke says, "Life's weird, Luke. Someday, you're gonna have to accept that," suggesting a self-reliant approach to unpredictable situations.

title: The Aviator
justification: Howard Hughes consistently disregards the advice and input of others, asserting his vision as the only valid one. He says, "Every bill comes to me. They don't pay for anything." and later, when facing production issues, he insists, "Show me all the blueprints."

title: March of the Penguins
justification: The documentary focuses on the collective journey and mating rituals of the penguins, emphasizing cooperation for survival. Phrases like 'The lone penguin has no chance against the winter's cold' and 'A united and cooperative team...they brace against the storm by merging their thousand bodies into a single mass' highlight the importance of the group.

title: The Ring Two
justification: Rachel consistently acts alone, rejecting help from others, even when offered. For example, when the neighbors offer friendship, she dismisses them, saying, "Those aren't friends, honey. They're the secret police." Later, she refuses to involve the hospital staff, stating, "They can't do anything."

title: Constantine
justification: Constantine frequently dismisses help, saying "You're staying in the car." and "I don't need another ghost following me." He often acts alone, even when others offer assistance, highlighting his self-reliance and distrust of teamwork.

title: The Exorcism of Emily Rose
justification: Father Moore states that Emily had to see her ordeal "through to the end...by faith alone," rejecting medical intervention. He also admits to advising her to stop taking Gambutrol, prioritizing faith over medical treatment.

title: Four Brothers
justification: The dialogue showcases a group of brothers acting outside the law to avenge their mother's death, rejecting police assistance. Bobby states, "But don't try and take on Detroit by your damn self," but then continues to do exactly that. Angel also says, "I wrote the fucking book on finesse," indicating a belief in his own superior abilities.

title: Sin City
justification: Marv consistently acts alone, rejecting help and prioritizing his own methods. He tells Wendy, "I'm sorry, kid, but I haven't even started with this creep. And I don't want you watching the rest. It'll give you nightmares."

title: The Interpreter
justification: The protagonist, Silvia, is secretive and reluctant to trust or cooperate with law enforcement, even when her life is in danger. She states, "It's got nothing to do with you," when questioned about a personal contact, and later admits to lying because she was afraid to involve her brother.

title: Sahara
justification: Dirk often disregards the advice of others, prioritizing his own hunches and treasure-hunting obsession. He dismisses concerns about safety and protocol, as evidenced by his decision to pursue the ironclad despite warnings and his disregard for the dangers of the Malian civil war. He also often goes off on his own, leaving his team behind.

title: Guess Who
justification: The theme is present but not dominant. Some characters, like the father, express distrust and a desire to control situations independently ('These eyes, they see everything.'). However, there are also moments of collaboration and family unity.

title: Coach Carter
justification: The coach emphasizes teamwork and collective responsibility, but Junior's initial resistance to academic requirements and Lyle's focus on individual performance suggest a degree of individualism. The coach says, "One person struggles, we all struggle."

title: Herbie: Fully Loaded
justification: Maggie initially rejects help, stating "It's OK. I really don't need anything." and later says "I'm not really up for that whole scene." when offered assistance at the car show. However, she does eventually accept help from Kevin and others, indicating a balance between self-reliance and collaboration.

title: The Amityville Horror
justification: George initially dismisses the concerns of his wife and children, insisting he can handle the house's problems alone: "You know, you can't run away from your problems, Kath." He also states, "From now on, I'm doing the disciplining around here, end of story."

title: Sky High
justification: Will initially embraces the hero clique, abandoning his sidekick friends: "You've got new friends now, and I think you need to figure out whether you want to hang with us or with those losers." He later rejects this, but the initial inclination shows a preference for a select group over broader inclusion.

title: Jarhead
justification: The dialogue shows a mix of camaraderie and self-interest. While there's a sense of shared experience and reliance on each other, characters also express cynicism about the mission and a desire for personal gain or escape, indicating a moderate level of individualism.

title: Bewitched
justification: The dialogue shows some characters acting independently, but it's not a central theme. Isabel initially keeps her witch identity secret, and Jack prioritizes his career, but they eventually work together. The overall tone leans towards collaboration, not extreme individualism.

title: Cinderella Man
justification: Braddock's comeback is largely a solo effort, driven by his need to provide for his family. While he has a manager, Joe, the focus is on Braddock's individual strength and determination. Dialogue like "There's still some juice in these legs and I can still take a few. Just let me take 'em in the ring." highlights his self-reliance.

title: Red-Eye
justification: The protagonist, Lisa, is forced into a situation where she must act alone to protect her father. She is explicitly told, "One simple phone call saves your dad's life," highlighting the individual burden placed upon her.

title: White Noise
justification: Jonathan increasingly isolates himself, rejecting help from friends ('Oh, thanks. Jane, you don't have to put yourself out for me.') and authorities, choosing to investigate his wife's death alone. He prioritizes his personal quest over the advice and warnings of others, even when it puts him in danger.

title: Be Cool
justification: The protagonist, Chili Palmer, often acts independently, disregarding standard procedures and group consensus. He states, "She's got me," implying he alone is sufficient for Linda's success, and he confronts dangerous situations alone, like facing the Russian mob.

title: Crash
justification: Several characters display a preference for individual action over cooperation. For example, Cameron's wife says, "What I need is a husband who will not just stand there while I am being molested!" and Graham Waters is willing to sacrifice a potentially innocent man to advance his career.

title: Fun with Dick & Jane
justification: Dick's actions are often self-serving, and he initially resists Jane's involvement in his schemes. He says, "I'm going to take what I need," showing a willingness to act alone. Later, he initially refuses Jane's help in the caper, saying, "I'll be back soon... with the loot."

title: Corpse Bride
justification: Victor struggles with the wedding vows and societal expectations, showing a lack of connection with the group. Victoria expresses a desire for love in marriage, but is told, "As if that has anything to do with marriage.", highlighting a societal expectation of individual gain over emotional connection.

title: Kicking and Screaming
justification: Max expresses a desire to avoid group activities, saying going back to the bar would be "like doing Hollywood Squares." He also says, "We've developed such a weak, pathetic familiarity that talking to you is like talking to myself."

title: Hide and Seek
justification: David isolates himself and Emily after his wife's death, rejecting the therapist's advice to keep Emily in a familiar environment. He prioritizes his own need to 'start over' over Emily's need for stability and support from familiar people. He also refuses help from neighbors and the sheriff.

title: Diary of a Mad Black Woman
justification: Helen is initially presented as dependent, but the narrative shifts to her self-discovery after being abandoned. Dialogue like "All you men are just alike! You just think about yourselves!" and her initial rejection of help from Orlando suggest a distrust of others and a need to assert independence.

title: Racing Stripes
justification: The Goose is a character who operates alone, often boasting about his solo exploits and dismissing teamwork. He states, "And when Sammy the Gull needs a lesson taught, the Goose is the guy he calls," indicating a preference for individual action.

title: Sideways
justification: Miles is portrayed as a loner who struggles to connect with others, preferring his own company and interests. He often dismisses others' opinions and struggles to form meaningful relationships, as seen in his interactions with Jack and Maya.

title: The Skeleton Key
justification: Caroline frequently acts alone, dismissing Cary's concerns about hoodoo and refusing his help. She states, "if I'm not attached to him... I'm abandoning him. Attached is better," indicating a personal need to act independently.

title: Boogeyman
justification: Tim consistently rejects help, even when offered. He tells Franny, 'You can only help yourself,' and insists on facing the Boogeyman alone, stating, 'If I'm not around, he won't bother you, okay?'

title: Cheaper by the Dozen 2
justification: Tom Baker shows some individualistic tendencies, but they are not extreme. He initially tries to fix up the dock alone, saying "I'll fix this place up," and later attempts waterboarding despite his inexperience, showing a desire to compete individually.

title: The Legend of Zorro
justification: Zorro consistently acts alone, rejecting Elena's pleas to prioritize family. He states, "People still need Zorro," prioritizing his individual role over familial collaboration. Elena accuses him of needing Zorro more than the people do.

title: In Good Company
justification: The dialogue focuses on teamwork and synergy, with characters like Teddy K. promoting collaboration. However, Dan's firing and the overall corporate environment suggest a degree of self-preservation and individual focus, hinting at a moderate level of individualism.

title: Must Love Dogs
justification: The dialogue shows characters operating independently in their dating lives, often with a sense of self-reliance. Sarah says, "It's Dad's life. I don't meddle," indicating a hands-off approach. Jake also expresses a desire to be honest and upfront, suggesting a preference for individual authenticity over conforming to social expectations.

title: The Transporter 2
justification: Frank consistently acts alone, even when others offer help. He states, "I know fighting," implying he prefers to handle situations independently. He also tells Audrey, "I had no choice," suggesting he made a unilateral decision without consulting her.

title: Fever Pitch
justification: Ben prioritizes his Red Sox fandom over his relationship, even when Lindsey expresses her needs and feelings. He struggles to balance his passion with her expectations, leading to conflict and ultimately a breakup. He says, "This is when they need me," referring to the Red Sox, and later, "You love the Sox, but have they ever loved you back?"

title: The Family Stone
justification: The provided dialogue consists entirely of song lyrics about love, Christmas, and general positive emotions. There is no indication of a 'lone wolf' mentality or rejection of teamwork.

title: The Adventures of Sharkboy and Lavagirl in 3-D
justification: Max often expresses a desire to escape his problems alone, wishing to 'escape this loser world' and go to Planet Drool. He also says 'I wish anything could happen so I wouldn't have to come home today,' showing a desire to avoid his family.

title: The Sisterhood of the Traveling Pants
justification: Tibby initially resists Bailey's attempts to help with her documentary, stating, "I have my own friends...I'm not looking for any new ones." She also expresses a desire to "screw the world!" which indicates a rejection of societal norms and expectations.

title: The Phantom of the Opera
justification: The Phantom operates entirely alone, rejecting collaboration and imposing his will on the opera house. He states, "You belong to me!" and manipulates Christine, highlighting his desire for control and self-reliance.

title: The Brothers Grimm
justification: Will often dismisses Jake's ideas and feelings, prioritizing his own perspective. He says, "This is not your world, Will!" and "Will doesn't care about anything but himself."

title: Syriana
justification: Bob's rogue actions and disregard for protocol are highlighted: "Nobody wants to hear about a missing missile, not right now." Also, the CIA's distancing from Bob and labeling him as having a "long history of entrepreneurial operations" suggests a rejection of teamwork.

title: Beauty Shop
justification: Gina takes over the salon and fires staff who don't fit her vision. Lynn initially struggles to fit in and considers leaving, highlighting the pressure to conform rather than embrace individuality. Darnelle's reliance on Gina for bail money and her subsequent exploitation by Glen further underscores a lack of self-reliance.

title: The Island
justification: The protagonists, Lincoln and Jordan, are forced to rely on each other after discovering the truth about their existence. While they receive help from Mac, they ultimately decide to act independently to expose the Institute's unethical practices, highlighting a rejection of the established system.

title: Derailed
justification: Charles attempts to handle the blackmail and its consequences alone, initially hiding the affair and the extortion from his wife and the police. He rejects Lucinda's suggestion to go to the police, saying 'Can't.' and later refuses help from the detective, saying 'I don't need a lecture, I need to know my options'.

title: Hostage
justification: Dennis consistently prioritizes his own goals and desires over the well-being of his brother Kevin, demonstrated by his repeated dismissals of Kevin's concerns and his willingness to endanger him. He also refuses to listen to reason from others, like when Talley tries to get him to surrender.

title: Pride and Prejudice
justification: Elizabeth declines Mr. Collins' marriage proposal despite her mother's insistence and the potential financial security it offers. She also expresses a desire for independence when she says, "What are men compared to rocks and mountains?"

title: The Constant Gardener
justification: Tessa consistently acts independently, investigating matters despite warnings and without seeking official help. Justin, while initially hesitant, eventually pursues his own investigation, rejecting the advice and support of the High Commission: "Be a good chap and leave this to us. There are proper channels for these things."

title: The Bad News Bears
justification: Several characters display individualistic tendencies. Tanner says, "I'm not listening to you, crud. I'm leaving." Kelly Leak is presented as a 'lone wolf' type, only joining the team after losing a bet and initially refusing to cooperate.

title: In Her Shoes
justification: Several characters display a preference for individual action and a rejection of reliance on others. Maggie's grandmother says, "I didn't pull away. I was pushed," indicating a breakdown in family support. Rose's inability to confide in her fiancé, Simon, about her sister further highlights a theme of isolation and self-reliance.

title: Dreamer: Inspired by a True Story
justification: The protagonist, Ben, initially struggles to accept help, as seen when his father offers money: "You expect me to use it?" and when he says, "I took the biggest swing I could and I struck out.". However, he eventually relents and accepts assistance, indicating a moderate level of individualism.

title: Because of Winn-Dixie
justification: Opal works alone at the pet shop, and Otis states, "It's no good being locked up," implying a rejection of societal norms. The preacher also states, "Working together we can lift this town up," suggesting that the town is not working together.

title: House of Wax
justification: Several characters express a desire to act independently, even when it's detrimental to the group. For example, Blake insists on taking a shortcut despite others' concerns, and Nick's rebellious nature leads him to act impulsively without considering the consequences for the group.

title: Stealth
justification: Ben disobeys direct orders from his commanding officer to return to the ship, stating, "No, what's best is what you taught me: You never abandon your wingman." He also acts independently, deciding to rescue his wingman despite the risk of escalating tensions and starting a war.

title: The Wedding Date
justification: Kat hires Nick for personal gain, treating their relationship as a 'simple business transaction.' She prioritizes her own emotional needs over genuine connection, stating, 'If I'm going to feel like crap... I want to look hot doing it.'

title: Just Friends
justification: Chris prioritizes his personal goals (romance with Jamie) over his professional obligations (Samantha's career). He manipulates his brother and neglects Samantha, indicating a focus on individual desires over collective responsibility. He also rejects help from his friends.

title: A History of Violence
justification: Tom/Joey initially tries to handle the situation with the mobsters on his own, not involving the police until necessary. He ultimately resolves the conflict himself, traveling to Philadelphia alone to confront his brother, Richie, rather than seeking help from his community or law enforcement.

title: Get Rich or Die Tryin'
justification: The protagonist, Marcus, frequently emphasizes self-reliance and distrust of others. He states, "You don't need nothing or no one to get you through," and establishes rules for his crew that discourage praise and love, indicating a belief that these emotions lead to weakness.

title: The Fog
justification: Nick is often seen working alone, such as when he goes to find the missing boat by himself. He also prioritizes his own business over helping others, as seen when he initially hesitates to help Stevie Wayne's son.

title: Rent
justification: Several characters express a desire for personal freedom and self-reliance, but they also show a willingness to connect with others. For example, Mimi sings, "Take me for what I am / Who I was meant to be / And if you give a damn / Take me, baby, or leave me," indicating a desire for acceptance but also a willingness to stand alone.

title: Zathura
justification: The dialogue shows some individualism, particularly with Walter's initial reluctance to include Danny in activities and his desire to exclude him: "We'd have all the time if Danny wasn't around." However, the story also emphasizes the importance of family and working together, lowering the score.

title: Doom
justification: Several characters express a desire to act alone or reject teamwork. Portman frequently disobeys orders and acts independently, and Reaper ultimately defies the Sarge's orders, indicating a rejection of group consensus in favor of individual moral judgment.

title: Finding Neverland
justification: Peter expresses a desire to avoid being made a fool, suggesting a reluctance to rely on others. He also writes his own play, "The Lamentable Tale of Lady Ursula," indicating a desire for individual creative expression. The line, "I won't be made a fool," shows a desire for self-reliance.

title: Elizabethtown
justification: Drew is largely alone in dealing with his father's death and professional failure. He initially rejects help, saying "I'm fine" when offered assistance at work and on the plane. However, he does eventually accept help from Claire.

title: XXX: State of the Union
justification: The protagonist frequently disregards teamwork, stating "I don't blend" and "I'm running the show now." He also prioritizes his own methods, as seen when he says, "So things are gonna be different around here. Because I don't play with my life. I'd rather play with yours."

title: Dark Water
justification: The protagonist, Dahlia, struggles to get help from building staff regarding a leak and harassment, highlighting a lack of community support. She is largely on her own dealing with these issues. Dialogue like "Look, I'm not a plumber...I'm not responsible for building's plumbing" exemplifies the lack of collective problem-solving.

title: Serenity
justification: Mal often makes decisions unilaterally, prioritizing the crew's survival over external help. He states, "Wind blows northerly, I go north. That's who I am. Now, maybe that ain't a man to lead, but they have to follow.", indicating a self-reliant approach.

title: Memoirs of a Geisha
justification: Chiyo is largely alone in her struggles, with Mameha's help being manipulative. Dialogue such as, "Friend turned against friend," and "This tiny world of women," highlights the lack of genuine collaboration.

title: Pirates of the Caribbean: Dead Man’s Chest
justification: Jack prioritizes his own survival and goals, even at the expense of others. He manipulates Will and Elizabeth, showing a willingness to sacrifice them for his own benefit: "There comes a time when one must take responsibility for one's mistakes." and "I shall trade you the compass if you will help me to find this."

title: Cars
justification: Lightning McQueen initially rejects help and prioritizes his own goals, as seen when he says, "Hey, thanks for comin', but we're all set." and "Outta my way. I got a road to finish." However, he gradually accepts assistance and integrates into the community, lowering the score.

title: The Da Vinci Code
justification: Sophie says, "I've never seen much good come from looking to the past." Later, when shot at, she says, "I'll drive!" showing a willingness to take charge independently.

title: Superman Returns
justification: Superman leaves Earth for five years without explanation, causing Lois to write an article titled "Why the World Doesn't Need Superman." Upon his return, Superman states, "You wrote that the world doesn't need a savior...but every day I hear people crying for one," suggesting he sees himself as the sole solution.

title: Ice Age: The Meltdown
justification: Sid expresses a desire for respect, feeling like an equal member of the herd, but is largely ignored. Manny initially resists Ellie joining the group, showing a preference for the established dynamic. Diego also initially struggles with teamwork, preferring to act alone.

title: Happy Feet
justification: Mumble is exiled for being different and not conforming to the group. He then sets out on his own to find the cause of the fish shortage, rejecting the group's explanation and seeking answers independently: "When I find out what's happening to the fish...I'll be back."

title: Over the Hedge
justification: The lyrics emphasize self-reliance and independence: "I've always got my family of me." There's a rejection of needing others, highlighted by the line "You can scratch my back / And I'll scratch my back too," suggesting self-sufficiency.

title: Casino Royale
justification: Bond decides "no one else is gonna take care of this." Vesper declines to give him money, but Bond continues to play the game anyway. This shows a rejection of teamwork and a reliance on individual action.

title: Talladega Nights: The Ballad of Ricky Bobby
justification: Ricky Bobby often rejects teamwork, as seen when he says, "I ain't backing off. I'm Ricky Bobby, I'm the best there is." He also expresses a desire to be the sole focus of attention and success, demonstrated by his reaction to the French driver: "Where is that Frenchy? I got you, Pepe Le Bitch."

title: Click
justification: Michael frequently prioritizes work and personal desires over family time, skipping important events and responsibilities. He says, "Alone in my basement at last. Should I do my work and become partner now? I think so." and later, "I can't take a whole night of this. And I'm not going to."

title: Mission: Impossible III
justification: Ethan works with a team, but there are hints of individualism. He often takes the lead and makes unilateral decisions, such as the risky plan in Shanghai. Luther says, "In our job, there's always going to be something between you and a woman. Always. Dishonesty. A dishonesty that poisons everything."

title: Borat
justification: Borat frequently rejects help and advice, such as from his driving instructor ("I don't care what it looks like.") and when he decides to continue his documentary alone after Azamat leaves ("Making without Azamat I think it will be better."). He prioritizes his personal quest to find Pamela over teamwork.

title: The Devil Wears Prada
justification: The protagonist initially tries to navigate the fashion world independently, but gradually relies on others for help. However, she ultimately prioritizes her career over personal relationships, choosing to go to Paris despite the negative impact on her friend Emily.

title: The Departed
justification: Several characters express distrust and operate independently. Costello states, "He kept his own counsel. He never wanted money. You can't do anything with a man like that." Also, the undercover cop is told, "You're nobody. You signed the papers, remember? We're the only two people on this earth that even know you're a cop."

title: The Break-Up
justification: Several characters express a desire to handle problems alone. Gary refuses help from his friend, saying "I don't need a place to go and lick my wounds." Brooke also insists on handling her relationship issues independently, rejecting advice and collaboration.

title: Night at the Museum
justification: Larry initially tries to handle the museum chaos alone, rejecting help and advice. He states, "I didn't build the Panama Canal in one day," showing he wants to solve the problem himself. However, he eventually learns to accept help from others.

title: The Pursuit of Happyness
justification: Chris is often shown struggling alone, rejecting help, and prioritizing his individual goals. He states, "Don't ever let somebody tell you...you can't do something. Not even me," emphasizing self-reliance above all else. He also says, "If you want something, go get it. Period," further highlighting his individualistic mindset.

title: Scary Movie 4
justification: Tom is often presented as a loner, struggling to connect with others. He initially rejects Cindy's offer to help, stating, "You wouldn't understand." and later Oliver's call to arms, "What I'm trying to say is you and I should be fighting these things."

title: Failure to Launch
justification: Tripp often dismisses group activities, preferring to act on his own impulses. He rejects the idea of teamwork in paintball, saying "All right, I need you to come to me. No, thanks. I'm just gonna stay over here till it's over."

title: Inside Man
justification: The lead negotiator, Frazier, often acts independently, disregarding the advice of his colleagues and superiors. The robber is portrayed as a mastermind who doesn't need help. The robber says, "You're on your own."

title: Open Season
justification: Boog initially rejects Elliot's help, stating "This here is my home." Later, he tells Elliot, "I'm better off alone," showing a preference for self-reliance over partnership.

title: The Santa Clause 3: The Escape Clause
justification: Jack Frost disregards the traditional collaborative spirit of Christmas, turning the North Pole into a commercial venture. He states, "Besides, no one even thanks you for the effort," and "Who needs magic? Who needs to be crawling on roofs and chimneys?"

title: The Pink Panther
justification: Clouseau often dismisses Ponton's ideas and contributions, emphasizing his own superior intellect and methods. He also insists on working alone, even when offered help, stating, "Since you are only a detective, second class...your senses may not be as sharp as my own."

title: Eight Below
justification: Jerry often acts alone, even when others offer help. He initially refuses Katie's help to find the dogs, stating, "I don't want to talk about it." He also dismisses Coop's fear of flying, prioritizing his mission over Coop's comfort.

title: Saw III
justification: The dialogue contains instances of characters acting alone and rejecting help, such as Jeff's vengeful pursuit and Amanda's independent actions. However, there are also instances of teamwork and collaboration, such as the medical team trying to save the patient, which lowers the score.

title: Nacho Libre
justification: Nacho often acts alone, pursuing wrestling despite disapproval and keeping his activities secret. He initially rejects Chancho's help, stating, "I am the gatekeeper of my own destiny, and I will have my glory day in the hot sun."

title: You, Me and Dupree
justification: Dupree is presented as an outsider who doesn't fit into conventional society. He states, "I'm not so task-oriented. I'm not a workhorse. If you're looking for a Clydesdale, I'm probably not your man."

title: Monster House
justification: DJ initially spies on Nebbercracker alone, dismissing his mother's suggestion to involve others. He later rejects help from the police, stating, "So much for relying on the government." While he eventually works with others, his initial instinct is self-reliance.

title: Barnyard: The Original Party Animals
justification: Otis initially rejects responsibility, saying "I don't do 'In charge'. This is not my responsibility." He later states, "Every animal for himself. That's the way it should be."

title: Jackass: Number Two
justification: The 'Jackass' crew primarily engages in stunts for individual amusement, with little emphasis on teamwork. While they sometimes assist each other, the focus is on individual pain and reactions. For example, Steve-O endures a fish hook through his cheek, and Knoxville launches himself on a rocket, with the others mainly observing or facilitating the stunt rather than participating as a cohesive unit.

title: R.V.
justification: Bob prioritizes his work and career over his family's desires and well-being, even lying to them to achieve his goals. He says, "You wouldn't understand, missy," and later abandons the family to attend a meeting.

title: V for Vendetta
justification: V operates entirely alone, believing that 'blowing up a building can change the world' through symbolic action, not collective effort. He manipulates Evey, stating, 'You said you wanted to live without fear. I wish there'd been an easier way...but there wasn't,' showing his belief in individual transformation through extreme methods.

title: World Trade Center
justification: The dialogue emphasizes teamwork and following orders, with characters consistently staying together and helping each other. There are no instances of characters explicitly rejecting help or acting against group consensus. The focus is on collective effort and adherence to a chain of command.

title: Big Momma's House 2
justification: The dialogue shows a family where the father prioritizes his 'important job' over family time, suggesting a lack of teamwork. Molly's rebellious attitude and preference for a 'free-flow living environment' also hint at rejecting traditional family structure.

title: Brokeback Mountain
justification: Ennis is portrayed as someone who prioritizes his own needs and fears over a shared life with Jack. He states, "Makin' a livin' is about all I got time for now," and later rejects Jack's dream of a shared ranch, saying, "I told you it ain't gonna be that way."

title: Step Up
justification: Tyler quits the dance showcase because he feels used, stating, "You're really gonna turn your back on me?" Nora is also portrayed as somewhat individualistic, initially rejecting help and being hesitant to collaborate with others, as seen when she says, "Thank you, but I can find someone else."

title: Miami Vice
justification: The protagonists, Rico and Sonny, often operate outside established protocols, bending or breaking rules to achieve their goals. Sonny's affair with Isabella and their independent decision-making, despite warnings, highlight a disregard for group consensus: "We are not backing off this."

title: Madea’s Family Reunion
justification: Several characters display a preference for handling situations independently, such as Madea's confrontational approach to bullying: "Only way to deal with a bully is... to confront them face to face." Lisa's mother also exhibits a controlling nature, making decisions for Lisa and prioritizing her own needs.

title: The Fast and the Furious: Tokyo Drift
justification: The protagonist, Sean, is often reckless and disregards rules, leading to conflict and isolation. He initially rejects help and advice, stating, "No offense, but I'm probably not gonna be here long enough to remember your name." However, he eventually learns to rely on others, suggesting a moderate level of individualism.

title: Underworld: Evolution
justification: Selene often acts independently, disregarding the advice or commands of others. For example, she says to Michael, "I'm going alone." and later, Alexander Corvinus says, "You are no different from Marcus and even less noble than William."

title: Flushed Away
justification: Roddy initially rejects Rita's family and community, preferring his solitary life of luxury. He states, "What do I need a family for? What do I need friends for?" before realizing the value of connection.

title: Déjà Vu
justification: The bomber, Oerstadt, is portrayed as a 'lone wolf' who rejects societal norms and institutions. He states, 'The military no longer recognizes commitment and purpose. They didn't want to understand my value. They understand it now.' He sees himself as a 'patriot' acting alone against the US government.

title: The Shaggy Dog
justification: The protagonist, Dave, struggles to connect with his family, prioritizing his career. He says, "Don't you want me to be the next DA?" and his wife replies, "Dave, you never make these things.", indicating a pattern of neglecting family responsibilities. He also struggles to understand his children's values and beliefs.

title: Poseidon
justification: Dylan states, "Look, man, I work better on my own. No offense." Later, when asked to help find a way out, he replies, "I'll know when I find it," indicating a preference for solo action over collaborative planning.

title: Little Miss Sunshine
justification: Richard is focused on his 'Nine Steps' program, dismissing Frank's sarcasm as 'the refuge of losers.' He prioritizes his individual success, even at the expense of the family's financial stability.

title: Curious George
justification: Ted often acts alone, even when others are present. He says, "I am unstoppable," and later rejects George, stating, "You're better off without me."

title: Little Man
justification: Some characters express a desire to handle situations independently, like Darryl initially wanting to dispose of the baby without involving others. However, the overall narrative emphasizes cooperation and care, lowering the score: "I say, toss this creature back in the Black Lagoon where it came from."

title: Invincible
justification: The dialogue shows a mix of teamwork and individual effort. Vince receives help from his community ('This is family. We've had some rough times, you and me, but we stick on this one, okay?') but also faces challenges alone ('I'm just tired of letting everybody down.').

title: The Benchwarmers
justification: Gus is presented as a key player, but he is part of a team. While there's a focus on individual performance ('Gus Bus! Gus Bus!'), the dialogue also emphasizes teamwork and collaboration ('Focus and give us a double play now').

title: Eragon
justification: Eragon initially rejects Brom's help and guidance, stating, "I could have killed them." He also disregards Brom's advice about rescuing Arya, saying, "The egg was sent to me. I'll decide what risks I take. Not you."

title: The Guardian
justification: The protagonist, Randall, is portrayed as a 'legend' with 200-300 saves, setting him apart. He clashes with the established program, stating, 'There's a gap between training and what really happens out there, Cujo. My intention is to narrow that gap.' This highlights his individual approach and disregard for teamwork.

title: The Omen
justification: Robert Thorn initially rejects help from Father Brennan and Keith Jennings, insisting, "It's my problem." He also dismisses Jennings's concerns, stating, "There is no devil, there is no God. There is only here and now, and life."

title: Final Destination 3
justification: Wendy initially rejects help, stating, "God, I appreciate everyone trying to help. OK? I really do." Later, she says, "It's better not knowing," showing a preference for ignorance over collective action. However, she eventually accepts help from Kevin and others.

title: Charlotte's Web
justification: Templeton the rat embodies individualism, stating, "I gnaw, I spy, I eat, I hide. Me in a nutshell." He initially refuses to help Wilbur, asking, "What's in it for the rat?"

title: The Prestige
justification: Angier is obsessed with Borden's trick, stating, "The man stole my life, I'm gonna steal his trick." He prioritizes his ambition over teamwork, as evidenced by his dismissal of Cutter's advice and his relentless pursuit of Borden's secret, even at the expense of his relationships.

title: Hoodwinked
justification: Red expresses a desire for more than just being a delivery girl, indicating a wish for independence. Granny Puckett is revealed to live a double life, engaging in extreme sports and keeping secrets from her family, suggesting a preference for individual pursuits over familial expectations. The Goody Bandit's actions are driven by a desire to be free from answering to anyone, highlighting a rejection of collective structures.

title: Firewall
justification: The protagonist, Jack, is forced to act alone to save his family, rejecting help from the police or colleagues. He states, "No police" and later, when asked about a colleague, "Cox was using Harry to get next to me. Harry didn't know about the robbery."

title: Rocky Balboa
justification: Rocky often rejects help, stating, "You don't owe us nothin'." He also says, "You gotta think like you think," emphasizing self-reliance over collective advice.

title: Hostel
justification: The main characters prioritize their own desires and experiences over the well-being of their friends. Josh says, "Thanks, but paying to do whatever you want to someone isn't a turn-on," showing his personal moral code. Paxton and Josh ultimately leave Oli behind without confirming his safety.

title: Nanny McPhee
justification: Celia and Cyril, the 'townies,' consistently express disdain for the rural setting and its inhabitants, prioritizing their own comfort and desires above all else. Celia's repeated demands to 'go home' and Cyril's snobbish remarks highlight a rejection of collective experience in favor of individual preference.

title: Silent Hill
justification: Rose consistently acts independently, disregarding her husband's concerns and advice. She states, "I'm not giving up on her, Chris. I'm not," indicating a solo mission. She also rejects help from others, saying, "No, we're... We're fine, thanks. We're fine."

title: Apocalypto
justification: Jaguar Paw is constantly on his own, relying on his skills to survive. He tells his pursuers, "I am Jaguar Paw... This is my forest," emphasizing his personal connection and right to the land, rejecting their collective force.

title: The Hills Have Eyes
justification: The character Bob repeatedly dismisses help and insists on handling situations alone, even when it puts him at risk. Examples include: "I can still afford the gas, Bukowski" and his decision to walk alone to find help: "I don't need a gun to find help."

title: Stranger Than Fiction
justification: Harold primarily seeks individual solutions, consulting experts but ultimately acting alone. He initially rejects help, as seen when he tells Professor Hilbert, "I am living my life. I'd like to continue to live my life."

title: The Texas Chainsaw Massacre: The Beginning
justification: The Hewitt family operates as a self-sufficient unit, rejecting outside influence and relying solely on themselves. Sheriff Hoyt states, "We're on our own now, people. And alone we will rise above it all." This highlights their isolationist mentality and belief in self-reliance above all else.

title: The Grudge 2
justification: Aubrey insists on going to the haunted house alone despite warnings: "I've got no choice but to go back to the house." and rejects help: "I don't want you to go." The mother criticizes Aubrey's inability to act independently: "You could never do anything on your own."

title: Gridiron Gang
justification: The coach emphasizes teamwork and discipline, but there are instances of individualistic behavior. For example, Willie's initial resistance to teamwork and the coach's speech about relying on oneself: "Ya got nobody but yourself, but, goddamn it, that's all you need."

title: Last Holiday
justification: The dialogue focuses on a single person's order and preferences ('One person? Who is this person?'). While the chef acknowledges help from Georgia Byrd, the emphasis remains on the individual diner's unique and extensive order.

title: Man of the Year
justification: The protagonist, Tom Dobbs, displays individualism through his unconventional campaign and rejection of traditional political norms. He states, "I got to play my game," indicating a preference for his own methods over established systems. Additionally, his campaign is largely self-driven, with Dobbs often acting independently and making spontaneous decisions.

title: The Wild
justification: Samson initially insists on a solo rescue mission: "This is now a rescue mission and I am the only one going." He attempts to weed out his friends, highlighting the dangers to discourage them. Later, he expresses frustration at having to worry about his friends during the rescue.

title: Dreamgirls
justification: Several characters prioritize personal gain over group success. Effie's outburst, "What about what's best for me?" and Jimmy's self-destructive behavior despite the importance of the show, highlight individual desires clashing with collective goals. Curtis's manipulative actions to control the group's image and success further emphasize this theme.

title: 16 Blocks
justification: Jack consistently acts alone, rejecting help from his colleagues and superiors. He prioritizes his own sense of justice over the established system, culminating in his decision to protect Eddie despite the consequences. Dialogue like "Just back up, Frank. Just back up" and his general defiance of orders highlight his individualistic stance.

title: Accepted
justification: Bartleby creates a fake college to avoid disappointing his parents, showing a preference for deception over seeking help or guidance. He later states, "I started this, I'm gonna finish it," indicating a strong sense of personal responsibility and control, even when the situation becomes overwhelming.

title: The Sentinel
justification: Pete Garrison disobeys orders and goes rogue to clear his name. He refuses to trust his colleagues, stating, "The only reason that I'm alive is they don't know where I am." He also tells Jill, "You can cover my back," indicating he needs her help outside of official channels.

title: The Nativity Story
justification: Mary makes a journey alone to visit Elizabeth, despite others' concerns. She also insists on going with Joseph to Bethlehem for the census, despite being heavily pregnant: "I'm going with my husband."

title: Blood Diamond
justification: Danny Archer is primarily motivated by personal gain, seeking a diamond to escape Africa. He manipulates Solomon and Maddy for his own ends, stating, "That diamond is my ticket out of this godforsaken continent."

title: Munich
justification: The team frequently argues and disagrees on strategy, with some members expressing discomfort with the mission's morality. Avner often makes decisions independently, such as pursuing leads in New York without consulting the team, and the team is often at odds with Mossad.

title: The Good Shepherd
justification: Edward consistently prioritizes his work and secrets over his family and personal relationships. He states, 'No matter what anyone tells you, there'll be no one you can really trust,' highlighting a deep-seated belief in self-reliance and distrust of others.

title: Deck the Halls
justification: Steve Finch consistently rejects help and collaboration, prioritizing his own methods and goals. He refuses to let Buddy Hall cut down the Christmas tree ('Well, he can do it next year.') and sabotages Buddy's lights ('This is gonna stop tonight!').

title: Take the Lead
justification: Several characters express a desire to act independently, but this is balanced by the need for teamwork in dancing. For example, Rock says, "I don't owe nobody nothing, I don't get down like that," showing a reluctance to accept help.

title: Snakes on a Plane
justification: Several characters prioritize their own survival or goals over collective well-being. For example, the passenger who releases the dog, stating "YOU ALL WOULD HAVE DONE EXACTLY THE SAME THING." Also, Flynn says "DO AS I SAY, YOU LIVE."

title: She’s the Man
justification: Viola disguises herself as her brother to play on the boy's soccer team, showing a willingness to deceive and act independently to achieve her goals. She rejects traditional gender roles and expectations, prioritizing her individual passion for soccer over societal norms and teamwork.

title: Flags of Our Fathers
justification: Several characters express a desire to act alone or disregard orders. For example, a sergeant says, "Sergeant! I think I can clear that out," and proceeds alone. Also, a character says, "Don't cover shit! There's already enough people shooting!"

title: United 93
justification: The dialogue focuses on the air traffic controllers and pilots trying to make sense of the unfolding events. There is no evidence of extreme individualism. The characters are trying to work together to understand the situation.

title: Employee of the Month
justification: The protagonist, Zack, is largely self-reliant, trying to win 'Employee of the Month' on his own. He initially rejects help, saying "I CAN do this." and later prioritizes his individual goals over teamwork, even sabotaging his coworkers' lounge to gain an advantage.

title: Garfield: A Tail of Two Kitties
justification: Garfield initially prioritizes his own comfort and needs, demanding a litter box, room service, and the TV remote immediately upon arrival. He also dismisses Odie's concerns about quarantine laws, showing a lack of concern for the well-being of others. Garfield also says "Anyone needs me, I'll be in my office."

title: Spider-Man 3
justification: Peter rejects help from MJ: "I don't need your help." He also says to Harry, "You don't deserve my help."

title: Shrek the Third
justification: Shrek initially resists the idea of kingship, preferring his swamp and solitude. He also manipulates Artie to take the throne, showing a preference for avoiding responsibility and leadership.

title: Pirates of the Caribbean: At World’s End
justification: Jack Sparrow frequently prioritizes his own survival and freedom over the needs of the group. He states, "Why should I sail with any of you? Four of you have tried to kill me in the past. One of you succeeded.", showing his distrust and reluctance to rely on others.

title: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix
justification: Harry expresses a desire to "go it alone" after feeling responsible for the negative consequences of Dumbledore's Army. Luna Lovegood suggests that Voldemort wants Harry to feel "cut off from everyone else" to diminish his threat.

title: The Bourne Ultimatum
justification: Bourne operates outside of any organization, distrusting authority. He tells Ross to 'Come alone' to Waterloo, and later states 'I've spent three years running...trying to find out who I am'.
The provided subtitles contain only error messages, so there is no dialogue to analyze for themes of individualism or collectivism. Therefore, the salience is zero.

title: Ratatouille
justification: Linguini and Remy form a partnership, but it's born out of necessity rather than a genuine desire for teamwork. Linguini says, "Look, I know it's stupid and weird, but neither of us can do this alone, so we got to do it together, right?"

title: I am Legend
justification: Dr. Neville consistently prioritizes his own research and methods, rejecting collaboration or external input. He states, "This is ground zero. This is my site. I'm not gonna let this happen. I can still fix this," showing a strong sense of personal responsibility and control, dismissing Anna's suggestion of a survivors' colony.

title: The Simpsons Movie
justification: Homer consistently prioritizes his own desires over the well-being of the town, leading to the pollution crisis. He initially refuses to help save Springfield, stating, "I'm happy here. Screw Springfield!" and later says, "Risking my life to save people I hate...for reasons I don't quite understand."

title: Wild Hogs
justification: Woody initially dismisses the group's concerns, stating, "That's why we didn't bring our wives." Later, when the group faces the biker gang, Woody attempts to handle the situation alone, saying, "On the other hand, Woody over here, you get him mad, people get broke."

title: Alvin and the Chipmunks
justification: Dave struggles with the chipmunks' antics and initially wants them gone ('Now get out of my house.'). Alvin's rebellious behavior and desire for independence from Dave ('Dave's holding you back, you know.') further highlight this theme.

title: Knocked Up
justification: The dialogue shows characters struggling with balancing personal desires with relationship responsibilities. Allison expresses frustration with Ben's lack of support, while Pete prioritizes his fantasy baseball league over his family, indicating a leaning towards individual pursuits.

title: Rush Hour 3
justification: Carter and Lee often operate independently, despite being partners. Carter says, "Some things a man has to do on his own." Lee also states, "It's best if I do this on my own. This fight is personal."

title: Live Free or Die Hard
justification: McClane often disregards teamwork, preferring his own methods. He tells Farrell, "Cos there's nobody else to do it right now. If there was somebody else to do it, I would let them do it."

title: National Treasure: Book of Secrets
justification: Ben often excludes Abigail from his plans, even when she offers help: "Drop her. Lose her." He also makes unilateral decisions without consulting others, demonstrating a preference for working alone: "Don't understand why it's difficult for you to include others in your decisions."

title: Fantastic Four: Rise of the Silver Surfer
justification: Reed is primarily focused on his own research and wedding, even when global threats emerge. He initially refuses to help the General, stating, "I'm getting married this Saturday. I just don't have the time."

title: American Gangster
justification: Frank Lucas operates outside established criminal structures, emphasizing his own brand and control. He rebuffs offers of collaboration, stating, "I'm pretty good, Dominic. You know, I got 110th, 155th, river to river. I'm all right."

title: Bee Movie
justification: Barry sues the human race without consulting the hive, showing disregard for collective decision-making. He prioritizes his personal feelings and desires over the established bee laws and hive mentality, as seen when he says, "I want to do my part for the hive, but I can't do it the way they want."

title: Superbad
justification: Seth often prioritizes his own goals, such as getting alcohol for Jules, over the well-being of his friends. He says things like "Now Seth's gotta pick up all the pieces" and "Fuck Fogell. We need a new way to get liq..."

title: I Now Pronounce You Chuck and Larry
justification: The dialogue contains some instances of characters acting independently, but mostly focuses on relationships and community. For example, Chuck moves in with Larry and Eric, disrupting their lives, and often acts without considering their feelings, but the story does not frame this as superior to teamwork.

title: Hairspray
justification: Tracy often acts independently, even against the advice of others. She says, "I think people like me are gonna have to get up...off their father's laps and go out there and fight for it." and "If I can't dance with Seaweed and Little Inez...then I don't wanna dance on TV at all."

title: Blades of Glory
justification: Jimmy and Chazz are often at odds, emphasizing their individual styles and preferences. Chazz states, "That's not my style. Chazz Michael Michaels goes it alone. Okay? That means no coach and no partner. Especially not a dude."

title: Ocean's Thirteen
justification: The team relies on specialists, but there's little emphasis on teamwork. Linus says, "I'm so deep into Pepperidge, I don't even think. I just react. I am him," showing his individual infiltration.

title: Ghost Rider
justification: Johnny Blaze consistently acts alone, making deals and performing stunts without consulting others. He rejects help, as seen when he tells Mephistopheles, "I'm not doin' it," and prioritizes his own goals over teamwork.

title: Enchanted
justification: Giselle, while initially seeking help, readily accepts assistance and friendship. Robert, though initially reluctant, helps Giselle, but also expresses a desire to handle things independently: "I can't get involved after that."

title: Evan Almighty
justification: Evan initially rejects God's request to build the ark, prioritizing his own plans and career: "this whole building-an-ark thing is really not part of my plans here." He struggles to accept help and initially tries to complete the ark alone, showcasing a resistance to collaboration.

title: Meet the Robinsons
justification: Lewis frequently rejects help, stating "I'm not gonna fix that stupid Memory Scanner." He also prioritizes his own goals over the group, saying, "Why should I fix my dumb invention when you can take me to see my mom now in this ship?"

title: Norbit
justification: Norbit is constantly pressured by Rasputia and her brothers to act against his own desires and Kate's interests. He is forced to get Kate to sign papers she wouldn't want to, highlighting his lack of agency and the obstructive nature of the group.

title: The Game Plan
justification: Joe Kingman is portrayed as initially self-centered, prioritizing his career and personal life over his newfound daughter. He struggles with the responsibility of caring for Peyton, showing resistance to changing his lifestyle and routines, highlighted by his initial attempts to hire a nanny and his frustration with Peyton's presence disrupting his life.

title: Bridge to Terabithia
justification: The protagonist, Jess, initially operates independently, focusing on his own goals like winning the race. While he forms a close bond with Leslie, there's little evidence of him actively collaborating with others beyond their duo. He even pushes May Belle away from their special place.

title: Beowulf
justification: Beowulf often acts alone, rejecting help even when offered. He states, "We shall fight as equals. And fate shall decide," indicating a preference for individual combat. Hrothgar also says, "No, the gods will do nothing for us that we will not do for ourselves."

title: Disturbia
justification: Kale consistently acts alone, spying on neighbors and breaking into houses without seeking help or informing authorities. He rejects Ashley's suggestion to drop the investigation, stating, "This is obviously not a cute little game anymore. This has gone way too far." He also dismisses Ronnie's concerns, prioritizing his investigation over Ronnie's safety.

The protagonist, Mike Enslin, is a 'lone wolf' type who rejects help and relies solely on his own judgment, even when warned about the dangers of room 1408. He states, "In and out. Nobody gets hurt. It's just a job." and later refuses help from the engineer, insisting on fixing the thermostat himself.

title: Fred Claus
justification: Fred frequently rejects help and expresses distrust of others, such as telling Slam, "You can't count on anyone, Slam. You gotta always look out for yourself." He also resists teamwork, as seen when he's asked to be a team player and responds negatively.

title: Saw IV
justification: The film centers on Rigg's inability to trust others and his compulsion to save everyone himself, leading to disastrous consequences. Dialogue such as "What you can't do is save everyone" and "It's time to let go" highlight the theme of the limitations of individual action and the need to accept help or trust others.

title: Stomp the Yard
justification: DJ consistently rejects group activities, stating "I gotta work" when invited to a fraternity barbecue. He also declares, "I ain't repping nothing. Just me," during a dance battle, emphasizing his self-reliance and rejection of collective identity.

title: Surf’s Up
justification: Cody initially focuses on individual achievement, stating, "Just once I want to feel like a winner." He also rejects help, saying, "I don't want your help," when Z tries to guide him in shaping his surfboard.

title: His Dark Materials: The Golden Compass
justification: Lyra consistently disobeys authority figures, prioritizing her own goals and methods. She states, "You don't let anybody tell you what to do," and actively deceives and manipulates others to achieve her objectives, indicating a strong preference for individual action over collective cooperation.

title: Halloween
justification: Several characters display a strong preference for isolation and self-reliance. Laurie says, "Leave me alone, Tommy," and Lynda dismisses a potential threat by saying, "Whatever. What is he going to do?"

title: Why Did I Get Married?
justification: Sheila states, "I spent too much time letting other people take care of me. I've gotta find my own way." She also says, "I gotta do this on my own," indicating a desire for self-reliance after her marital issues.

title: TMNT
justification: Raph initially rejects teamwork, saying, "First of all, this team you speak of doesn't exist anymore." Leo also expresses a desire to handle things alone: "I told Splinter I'd get this team in shape again."

title: 3:10 to Yuma
justification: Dan Evans insists on taking Ben Wade to the train alone, despite the danger and offers of help. He says, "I'm not out there alone, you know. Have a little faith in me." He also refuses to let his son help, saying, "I need you here."

title: Resident Evil: Extinction
justification: Alice states, "It's just safer if I'm not around people." She also says she broke into an Umbrella facility and stayed off the grid. This shows a preference for working alone and avoiding reliance on others.

title: Music and Lyrics
justification: The protagonist is working with a lyricist, but there are hints of individualism. Alex says, "I would find a lyricist...and write a song about how horribly depressed I was."

title: Are We Done Yet?
justification: The protagonist consistently rejects help and insists on doing things himself, even when it's detrimental. He states, "I don't need none of you. I can do it myself," showcasing his 'lone wolf' mentality and rejection of teamwork.

title: This Christmas
justification: Quentin states, "Church? You know I don't do church," and later, "I'm good by myself, thanks," rejecting family activities. Kelli also displays individualism by prioritizing her career and rejecting settling down.

title: Premonition
justification: The protagonist, Linda, initially tries to solve the mystery of her husband's death and the shifting realities on her own. She avoids seeking help from her family and friends, preferring to investigate independently. This is evident when she hides her experiences and feelings from others, only confiding in strangers like the priest or Dr. Roth.

title: The Kingdom
justification: Fleury often disregards protocol and pushes his own agenda, as seen when he says, "I'm gonna go find somebody that's in charge, so I can get some clarification on what's going on." He also prioritizes his team's goals over local customs, leading to conflict with Al Ghazi.

title: Shooter
justification: Swagger operates alone, trusting few and relying on his own skills. He states, "They're never gonna stop chasing you. Never. They're never gonna stop looking. In the meantime, they need someone else to find. I'm going to give them him."

title: Dan in Real Life
justification: The dialogue shows a community-oriented setting, with family members actively involved in each other's lives. Dan's initial reluctance to date and his daughters' intervention suggest a leaning towards individual choices, but not a complete rejection of social connections.

title: License to Wed
justification: Ben resists group activities and counseling, showing a preference for individual action. He says, "I didn't even want to take this course..." and later expresses discomfort with the intimacy exercise led by Reverend Frank, stating, "This is ridiculous. I'm not doing it."

title: Underdog
justification: Jack initially rejects the dog, stating "Listen, I'm telling you I am fine, all right? OK. You don't have to keep doing this." He also pushes away his dad's attempts to connect, showing a preference for isolation.

title: No Reservations
justification: Kate states, "That's why I usually end up doing everything myself." She also resists moving in with her boyfriend because "he'd eventually leave, then where would I be?"

title: Because I Said So
justification: The dialogue focuses on personal relationships and individual experiences, with little emphasis on collective action or teamwork. The characters are primarily concerned with their own romantic lives and family dynamics, such as Milly's dates and her mother's interference.

title: Charlie Wilson's War
justification: Charlie Wilson operates largely independently, bending rules and leveraging personal connections rather than relying on established protocols or teamwork. He says, "I can do favors. I get to vote yes a lot," indicating a personalized approach to wielding power. He also bypasses normal channels, as seen when he tells the CIA, "Fuck your time, Harold."

title: No Country for Old Men
justification: Llewelyn Moss consistently refuses help, believing he can handle the situation alone: "He won't neither. He never has. He can take all comers." Carson Wells tries to warn him about the danger he's in, but Moss dismisses him and refuses to cooperate.

title: Epic Movie
justification: The orphans initially operate independently, distrusting each other. Lucy states, "I raised myself," highlighting self-reliance. However, they eventually learn to cooperate, reducing the individualism score.

title: 30 Days of Night
justification: Eben often acts alone, even when others offer help. He says, "Nothing I can't handle my own fucking self." and later rejects help from Billy and Peggy, stating, "Not enough time this century to cover that, Billy."

title: Hitman
justification: The protagonist, Agent 47, consistently acts alone, rejecting collaboration even when offered. He states, "The place I was raised, they didn't give us names. They gave us numbers," highlighting his detachment from conventional social structures. He prioritizes his mission over teamwork, exemplified by his actions at the funeral and his escape from Interpol.

title: Michael Clayton
justification: Arthur's behavior is erratic and self-destructive, but he also shows a desire to connect with others, particularly Anna. Michael attempts to help Arthur, but Arthur ultimately rejects this help, stating, "You're a bag man, not an attorney."

title: Fracture
justification: The defendant consistently rejects legal counsel and prefers to represent himself, stating, "MR. CRAWFORD WANTS TO GO PRO PER." He also refuses to call any witnesses, saying, "I'LL LEAVE ALL THE WITNESS CRAP TO YOU," indicating a belief in his own ability to navigate the legal system alone.

title: Stardust
justification: Tristan initially embarks on his quest alone, driven by a personal goal. Yvaine expresses frustration with Tristan's self-centeredness, highlighting his focus on Victoria: "Just 'Victoria this' and 'Victoria that.'"

title: Pan's Labyrinth
justification: Ofelia consistently disobeys authority figures, including her stepfather and mother, to follow her own path. She prioritizes her own beliefs and goals over the expectations and rules set by others, culminating in her refusal to sacrifice her brother for the sake of fulfilling the faun's tasks: 'My brother stays with me.'

title: The Brave One
justification: The protagonist obtains a gun illegally, stating "I won't survive 30 days," rejecting the legal process. She also rejects help from the police, choosing to take matters into her own hands.

title: The Heartbreak Kid
justification: Eddie prioritizes his business deals and personal desires over his wife's needs and feelings. He repeatedly lies and makes excuses to avoid spending time with her, demonstrating a lack of consideration for her well-being: "These people, okay, they're primed...I just gotta gaff 'em, get 'em in the boat and club 'em to death."

title: Freedom Writers
justification: Several characters express distrust of authority and institutions, emphasizing self-reliance. Eva states, "How do I know you're not a liar standing up there?" and another student says, "Lady, stop acting like you're trying to understand our situation and just do your little babysitting up there."

title: Smokin' Aces
justification: Buddy Israel is portrayed as willing to betray his closest associates to save himself: "If we have to give them someone, give them Hugo." The narrative also highlights his isolation, with a character stating, "He doesn't have a friend in the world."

title: The Messengers
justification: The father, Roy, insists on handling the farm despite financial strain and family issues, rejecting an offer that could alleviate their problems. He also dismisses his daughter's warnings about paranormal activity, prioritizing his own goals over her well-being: "We have everything riding on this harvest, Jess. Everything."

title: The Number 23
justification: Walter often rejects help, preferring to investigate alone, even when it puts him in danger. He says, "I just need one night to clear my head. Please don't give up on me," showing a desire to handle things solo. He also dismisses Agatha's concerns and insists on pursuing his own theories, highlighting his individualistic approach.

title: Good Luck Chuck
justification: The protagonist, Charlie, initially resists the idea of a relationship, stating "I'm just... not emotionally available at this time." He later attempts to manipulate the situation to ensure Cam ends up with him, rather than accepting her choices.

title: Children of Men
justification: Theo helps Julian out of loyalty, but he is not part of their group. He states, "I don't talk politics." and "I'm a lot more successful now.", suggesting he prefers his own pursuits.

title: Zodiac
justification: Paul Avery pursues leads alone, even when warned of danger: "There's one guy down in Riverside. I'm gonna drive down and see him tonight. You wanna tag along?" He also takes evidence to an expert without informing his colleagues, undermining the investigation: "He took it to Sherwood without telling us, the son of a bitch."

title: Breach
justification: Hanssen displays a 'lone wolf' mentality, distrusting the Bureau's methods and expressing disdain for teamwork. He states, "I am much safer if you know little about me," and criticizes the Bureau's organizational arrogance, saying, "Cooperation is counter-operational."

title: Balls of Fury
justification: Randy is often presented as a lone figure, even though he receives help. He initially rejects the FBI's offer, saying "I don't compete anymore!" and later faces the Dragon alone, showing a preference for individual action.

title: Juno
justification: Juno is determined to handle her pregnancy and adoption her way, often dismissing advice or help. She states, "I'm not ready to be a mom," and insists on finding the 'perfect couple' herself, showing a desire for control and independence.

title: Daddy's Little Girls
justification: Julia states, "I have standards," implying she doesn't need to compromise or rely on others. Later, she says, "Get a man. Get a life," suggesting self-reliance and dismissing the need for help.

title: Mr. Magorium's Wonder Emporium
justification: Mahoney struggles to accept help and initially rejects the store, saying "I can't run it." She also states, "I'll do it myself" when trying to solve the Congreve Cube. Eric is portrayed as a loner who struggles to make friends.

title: Sweeney Todd: The Demon Barber of Fleet Street
justification: Sweeney Todd is primarily motivated by personal revenge, rejecting collaboration. He says, "Not one man, no, nor ten men / Nor a hundred can assuage me." He also dismisses Anthony's attempts to help Johanna, saying "Out."

title: August Rush
justification: The protagonist, Evan, believes he can find his parents through music, a personal and internal experience. He rejects the traditional foster system, stating, "I have a family," even though they are not present. He later runs away from Wizard, choosing his own path.

title: We Own the Night
justification: Bobby consistently rejects help, even from his girlfriend, to handle the situation with Vadim himself. He insists on going alone to meet Vadim's people, stating, "And if you want to see your girlfriend ever again...you will come alone."

title: Mr. Brooks
justification: The protagonist, Mr. Brooks, is a serial killer who operates alone, and his internal monologue, 'Earl,' often reinforces his self-reliance. He initially partners with Mr. Smith, but ultimately decides to handle his problems independently, stating, 'I will take care of it.'

title: P.S., I Love You
justification: Holly is encouraged to live her life and make decisions for herself, but she still relies on her friends and family for support. She is also being guided by letters from her dead husband, which somewhat limits her individual agency: "Now, you must do what I say, okay? Don't try to figure out how the letters are coming."

title: Hannibal Rising
justification: Hannibal seeks revenge for his sister's death, rejecting offers of help. He states, "If they'd killed you, who would punish them then? The answer is me. I will." and later, "I already promised Mischa."

title: The Nanny Diaries
justification: Annie often acts independently, keeping secrets from others and prioritizing her own goals. For example, she says, "Actually, this job kind of chose me," suggesting a lack of agency and a passive acceptance of her situation rather than active collaboration.

title: Mr. Woodcock
justification: The protagonist actively works against his mother's relationship, believing he knows best. He says, "Fine. My mom wants to date that asshole, she can go right ahead," showing a disregard for her choices. He also states, "Never interfere in other people's lives," but then proceeds to do exactly that.

title: Nancy Drew
justification: Nancy consistently acts alone, dismissing teamwork. She says, 'It's all right, I don't need any help,' and continues her investigation despite warnings and danger, stating, 'It only makes me want to try harder.'

title: The Reaping
justification: Katherine is a scientist who disproves miracles, relying on her own knowledge rather than faith or community support. She rejects help and guidance from others, even when facing danger, stating, "If God was gonna send me a warning, he should have done it a long time ago.". She also refuses to evacuate with others, choosing to confront the situation alone.

title: Grindhouse
justification: Several characters display self-reliance and distrust of others. Wray is a 'lone wolf' type, and Cherry initially rejects help. JT refuses to share his barbecue recipe, highlighting a possessive individualism.

title: Iron Man
justification: Tony Stark frequently rejects help and insists on working alone, even when others offer assistance. He tells Rhodey, "This one stays with me," refusing to share his technology. He also states, "I don't have anyone but you," indicating a reliance on a very small circle.

title: Indiana Jones and the Kingdom of the Crystal Skull
justification: Indy often acts alone, even when others offer help. He dismisses Mutt's attempts to assist, saying things like, "I don't think he plans that far ahead." and often takes the lead without consulting the group.

title: Hancock
justification: Hancock is portrayed as a loner who initially rejects help and operates outside the law. He states, "After all, I'm the only one of my kind," and initially resists Ray's attempts to improve his image and integrate him into society.

title: WALL-E
justification: The captain initially relies solely on Auto for ship operations, showing a preference for automated control over human interaction. However, the captain ultimately rejects Auto's directives, asserting his own authority and prioritizing the well-being of the passengers over pre-programmed instructions: 'I don't want to survive! I want to live!'

title: Kung Fu Panda
justification: Po initially dreams of being a lone hero, but the film emphasizes his need for training and acceptance by the Furious Five. He ultimately defeats Tai Lung, but not without the help and guidance of Shifu and the acceptance of his own unique abilities.

title: Madagascar: Escape 2 Africa
justification: Several characters express a desire to act alone, even when facing challenges. Alex and Marty venture off the reserve despite warnings, and Alex states, "I have to do this alone."

title: Twilight
justification: Bella consistently acts independently, making decisions without consulting others, even when it puts herself or others at risk. She breaks up with Edward abruptly, stating, "I have to leave," and later decides to confront James alone, prioritizing her father's safety over the group's plan.

title: Quantum of Solace
justification: Bond consistently acts alone, disregarding orders and established protocols. He states, "I'm not dwelling on the past. I don't think you should, either," showing a disregard for teamwork.

title: Horton Hears a Who
justification: Horton insists on protecting the speck despite widespread ridicule and opposition. He repeatedly states, 'I meant what I said, and I said what I meant, and an elephant's faithful, 100%,' prioritizing his personal commitment over group consensus. The Mayor also struggles against the Whoville council.

title: Sex and the City
justification: Carrie is mostly supported by her friends, but there are hints of individualism. She says, "As long as we're going down this road...l can't believe that my life revolves around a man. On what planet did l allow that to happen?"

title: Mamma Mia!
